articles.title: Read Nvidia’s internal emails about the ‘extraordinarily difficult period’ amid CEO shakeup
articles.body:
Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia this morning, a company he co-founded in 1993. The decision came following the company’s board opening an investigation into multiple extramarital affairs Huang had with a direct report and an alleged Chinese spy. The new, and first, Chair of the Board, Harvey Jones, shared news of Huang’s resignation with the company in an email, which also announced CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO.
Read Nvidia’s internal emails about the ‘extraordinarily difficult period’ amid CEO shakeup
Nvidia’s board and interim CEO Colette Kress told employees they’re ready to ‘move forward together.’
You can read the full text of the board’s internal memo and Kress’s first message to employees as interim CEO below.
Subject: Statement from NVIDIA Board Chair
Dear NVIDIA Employees,
I am writing to share an important update. Jensen has resigned as CEO and Board Member, and the Board has asked our Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress to serve as interim CEO while it conducts a search for a permanent successor looking at both internal and external candidates. I will serve as the first-ever Chair of the Board.
As CFO for over 13 years, Colette has been a key architect of NVIDIA’s growth and capital strategy. She possesses a deep understanding of this business and the markets in which we operate. The Board has full confidence in Colette to deliver on our commitments to shareholders, customers, partners, and to each of you.
Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. We pioneered accelerated computing, defined the modern GPU, and built the platform that powered artificial intelligence.
The Board takes seriously our duty as stewards of this great company.
The strength of this company resides in our employees, leadership team, technical strength and partner ecosystem. I am confident that under Colette’s leadership, with the full support of the Board, we will continue to grow our business, and lead the industry forward. Thank you for your focus, your professionalism, and your commitment to NVIDIA.
Harvey Jones
Colette Kress’ first email to Nvidia employees as interim CEO:
Subject: RE: Statement from NVIDIA Board Chair
Dear NVIDIAns,
I believe deeply in this company and in its future. More than anything, I believe in each of you, in our customers and partners and in the vital role we play every day in the global economy.
The Board, Estaff and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication. Thank you.
This company has achieved so much because of the work that all of you bring to it every single day. You are our greatest strength. You will hear more from leadership in the coming days about our future together, and we will host a company meeting on November 18 at 9am PT.
We play a vital role in building the technology that is powering the AI revolution, and we have important work ahead of us. So let’s move forward together, with the same determination and commitment that have always defined this company.
Thank you for all you do,
Colette
Correction, November 12th: This story’s headline has been adjusted to better describe the context of Kress’ quote; she is not referring to a period “ahead,” as the headline initially stated.

articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns after reports of extramarital relationships
articles.body:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned following reports that he had multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a suspected agent of China and another with an executive who reported to him — a stunning turn of events for the head of a company at the heart of the global AI investment boom.
Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, will become interim CEO, Nvidia’s board said in a statement.
Nvidia shares plunged more than 11% after the board’s announcement. A company spokesperson clarified that Huang will not be working with NVIDIA in any capacity going forward.
The company also named its first chairman. That role will be filled by Harvey Jones, who is a former CEO of major chip company Synopsys. The addition of a chairman is a major governance overhaul at the company that for decades relied solely on Huang.
Nvidia’s board met Wednesday night to address Huang’s future at the company, a source familiar with the matter told NBC News, adding that the White House was aware of the meeting.
Huang, 63, co-founded Nvidia in the early 1990s, and led the company’s meteoric rise amid the AI boom of the past several years.
“I believe deeply in this company and in its future,” Kress wrote in her first email to Nvidia employees as interim CEO. “The Board, Estaff and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication. Thank you.”
In a separate note to the company’s workforce, newly-installed chairman Harvey Jones wrote, “The Board takes seriously our duty as stewards of this great company.”

FOR SUBSCRIBERSWhy Jensen Huang just might survive this scandal
In Collette Kress, Nvidia’s board selected a steady hand to steer the company in its most uncertain period ever.
Kress has been the company’s chief financial officer since 2013. She is a familiar face to Wall Street, regularly appearing at conferences and discussing the intricacies of the company’s sprawling operations. Before Nvidia, Kress worked at Cisco, another major technology company, and Microsoft.
Huang long leaned on Kress during financial conferences and the company’s earnings calls to debrief the investing public about the latest developments with the company’s operations.
Nvidia’s board said that it would search for a permanent CEO and consider internal and external candidates.
Trump weighed in on the search for a permanent CEO shortly after Nvidia’s announcement, saying that Apple executive chair Tim Cook should take the role. “A Legend replaces a Legend!” Trump wrote.
Cook only became Apple’s executive chair on September 1, and did not appear to have plans to leave any time soon.
Kress’ ascension to the CEO suite comes after the second largest public company in the world was hit with multiple scandals involving its founder.
On Wednesday, The New York Times, citing five people who worked at Nvidia, reported that Huang had an extramarital relationship with a married healthcare executive who reported to him, which appears to run afoul of Nvidia’s code of conduct. NBC News has not independently verified the claims.
Nvidia and the executive did not respond to multiple requests for comment Wednesday about the Times’ report.
The report concerning the alleged relationship followed reports that Huang had an affair with Alice Huang, a businesswoman believed to be a spy for China. The two Huangs are not related.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio circulated a memo to officials in the Trump administration this spring outlining how U.S. intelligence showed that Huang was in a romantic relationship with a business executive who was an asset of China’s spy service, according to a person familiar with Nvidia and a former national security official with knowledge of the matter. The New York Times and the Financial Times, citing people familiar with the matter, first reported on the memo last week.
Alice Huang held a senior position at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that was buying advanced chips from Nvidia. Megaspeed and other related firms remain under U.S. criminal investigation of allegations they smuggled American-made chips into China.
Alice Huang’s precise role and relationship with China’s spy service is unclear. It is possible she was not a career spy for China’s spy agency, the Ministry of State Security, but was asked to cooperate and share information based on her access to Jensen Huang, according to the former national security official.
The concerns about the Nvidia CEO’s extramarital activity added to worries about Nvidia chips being smuggled or illegally accessed by Chinese AI companies. Nvidia has said that it follows U.S. export laws.
On Sunday, Nvidia’s board announced it was investigating whether Huang had fallen victim to a foreign intelligence plot. It said Tuesday that it had hired a former acting U.S. attorney and his law firm to conduct the investigation.
Huang apologized in a memo to employees and said he supported the independent investigation.
“I was unfaithful to my wife,” he wrote. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”
Multiple Washington officials have called for greater scrutiny of Nvidia and for Huang to testify about his relationship with the suspected Chinese agent in the wake of the reports.
China has denied the allegations, calling them “purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China.”
Even before Wednesday’s Times report, Nvidia shares had plunged 11% this week, wiping out nearly $500 billion in paper value. Huang’s departure leaves a host of unknowns at the company, the valuation of which has soared to more than $1 trillion amid insatiable demand for its GPU chips. Those specialized processors underpin the AI applications that have powered the stock market and economic growth writ large to new heights.
For years, Huang has effectively been the chief ambassador for the artificial intelligence industry, appearing regularly alongside heads of state and other CEOs as the industry spends trillions of dollars investing and building AI models and data centers.
Nvidia acknowledged Huang’s contributions to the sector in its Thursday announcement. “Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound,” a statement said. “The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.”
After coming up with the idea for Nvidia at a Denny’s restaurant in Silicon Valley with co-founders Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, Huang built the company into a $4 trillion global chip behemoth over the following 30-plus years.
Before Wednesday’s report of a second affair, many high-profile figures across Silicon Valley, Wall Street and Washington had come to Huang’s defense. President Donald Trump told reporters Sunday that Huang had “done an amazing job for our country.”
“I think he’s an honorable guy,” Trump said. “I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it.”
Shaun Maguire, a partner at the venture capital group Sequoia, said on X that Huang is “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation,” adding that “two mistakes don’t make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.”
SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk responded under Maguire’s post, writing: “I agree.”
Before the decision, Musk said in a response to a post Wednesday night that it “would be an honor” to hire Huang.

articles.title: A false smoke alarm almost drowned Jane Street's only NYC datacenter
articles.body:
How a false smoke alarm almost drowned Jane Street's only NYC datacenter
AI disclosure: this story was written entirely by human hands, with AI doing proof-reading and light edits. Some tasteful imperfections kept to heighten Wabi-Sabi effect.
Everyone’s heard of how awesome Jane Street is. Fewer people have heard about the times something stupid nearly put it out of business and it was saved by grit and dumb luck. I was on the systems team for some of those. Jane Street didn’t do titles, and we on the systems team weren’t above getting our hands dirty. You could think of us as the firm’s blue-collar OCaml programmers: when something broke, we were the ones running through the corridors to fix it. Call this story a Star Trek: Lower Decks view of Jane Street.
For the longest time Jane Street insisted on having its machine room close to its trading floor. When it was 10 people it was cute. When it was 150 people it was starting to feel… odd. Part of the reason for this was intellectual property concern: they didn’t want to risk having their servers stolen by spies who would learn their precious trading strategies. Another reason was technology risk: they wanted to make sure out-of-control automated trading systems could always be shut down by running across the hall and pulling power cables.
Yes, tools existed to mitigate both of these fears. But Jane Street moved irritatingly slowly on this stuff, and they still wanted the last-resort option of yanking power cords. Their risk culture didn’t exclusively come from reading heady thinkpieces. A lot of it was instilled by a partner who’d served on a nuclear submarine, and it showed, mostly in a good way! On a sub, you don’t trust the automation unless there’s a big red-painted, mechanically connected lever you can pull to turn it off.
As the company grew this humble machine room was built out into a respectably sizable datacenter, complete with an online UPS, Computer Room Air Conditioner (CRAC) units, refrigerator-sized network switches, a subterranean diesel backup generator and about 10 rows of server cabinets, 10 cabinets deep. Oh, and it was all crammed into the middle of a skyscraper called 1 New York Plaza, which was otherwise just a normal office building.
When I first landed my job at Jane Street I was commuting to the southern tip of Manhattan all of the way from Queens, an hour or more each way. I’d gone to a magnet high school in the city, so I’d been doing commutes like that since I was a teenager, and I was tired of it.
Now that I was making big Wall Street money I decided I’d get an apartment. A real estate agent kept trying to show me what they called “panty droppers”, but I was only interested in one thing: proximity to the office. I ended up in a 200 square foot studio that was a 9 minute commute on foot from my apartment door to my desk on the trading floor. I would weirdly boast about it to the rest of the systems team, but it also meant everyone at the office knew I was a stone’s throw away in case there was an emergency.
And that day came soon enough. One evening after work, just as I was about to climb into the elevator at my apartment building, my phone rang. It was our Hong Kong office, and when Hong Kong had a New York problem, mine was (now) the number they called. The smoke alarm in our NYC datacenter had gone off.
We had contractors working on a prep room next to the datacenter. While cutting into stuff, some dust was kicked up and it set off the smoke alarm. This is bad, but not for the reason you might think. Office buildings have sprinklers in them for fire suppression. You may have seen it go off in movies where someone just holds a lit cigarette up to the sprinkler on the ceiling and it floods the entire room. In reality they’re not quite that dumb, but it’s close.
Firstly, the sprinklers over a machine room like ours usually aren’t kept full of water all of the time. This saves you from having to deal with any leaks that might develop overhead over the years. Secondly, the sprinkler heads don’t have smoke sensors. Instead, a different system detects the smoke, and that’s when the pipes fill with pressurized water, but they don’t spray yet. What triggers the spray is heat: each sprinkler head has its own heat-sensitive plug, which opens once the air around it becomes hot enough. The logic is that the smoke alarm must be real, whatever fire triggered it hasn’t been brought under control since it’s gotten very hot, and the sprinklers should douse it with water.
Of course, the ceiling of our datacenter was full of sprinklers set up exactly this way. We’re still fine because even though contractors might have set the smoke detector off by kicking up dust, there’s no actual fire producing heat, so the sprinklers wouldn’t spray, right? Well, no. One final piece of this contraption is that if the smoke alarm detects smoke, it would be absolutely terrible to keep circulating air through the room since that would help feed any fires, so the smoke alarm is wired to shut down the CRAC units(!)
Can you see the problem now? Rooms full of computer racks have high cooling demands. If you shut down the cooling, the temperature starts climbing. If you have a bunch of sprinklers that have just become pressurized because of a smoke alarm, you now have a serious, potentially business-ending problem on your hands.
And so my mission was made clear: as fast as I possibly could, get back to Jane Street, get into the machine room, and pull the power cord on every device in that room before the temperature climbed past 150 F and the sprinklers destroyed everything.
I ran down the (ironically named) Water Street in the Financial District faster than probably anyone has ever run down it, mashed the elevator button in the lobby of 1 NYP, waited very impatiently for the elevator to climb the 33 floors, slammed my keycard against the reader, booked through the main office door, took a hard right turn to the machine room door, slammed my keycard against that, stepped into what felt like a sauna and went row by row, cabinet by cabinet, yanking power cables out with both hands.
Then I watched the temperature monitor. 141 F. 142. 143. 143.5. 143.6. Finally it stopped. A quiet I’d never heard before set in on the machine room.
The machine room had been kept across the hall so that someone could always run in and pull the power cords. I doubt anyone had pictured doing it to save the servers from the goddamn sprinklers.
Since the major NYC markets were closed for the day, the downtime from this fiasco was minimal, and we were up and running the next morning.
There were a couple of meetings after that. You might picture Gordon Gekko coldly deciding whose career was over, but meetings at Jane Street were never like that. They were matter-of-fact, level-headed and honestly kind of fun, closer to engineering students in a college dorm arguing over what went wrong. The outcome of all that level-headed discussion: the sprinklers would stay, we would tighten up procedures and surveillance, and we would continue hosting servers in our office building right next to our trading floor. That is, until Hurricane Sandy smacked us upside the head, but that’s a story for another day.
As for me, when the next morning came around I knew what had to be done. Our Hong Kong team had only caught the problem by luck: someone happened to see on a display that server after server was popping up a climbing temperature condition. No one server was configured to alert just because it was a little hot, since that happens from time to time. But an across the board increase in temperature on many servers means there’s a generalized cooling failure.
What we needed was a system monitor built for this exact purpose, one we could trust to be ultimately, unfailingly reliable at the task of asking each Linux server for its temperature and computing a simple mean. Bash wouldn’t cut it for this. Nor would Perl. No, a job of this magnitude called for the most reliable and type-safe programming language imaginable. So I fired up emacs and wrote it in good old OCaml: every minute, ask every server in each location directly for the temperature from its onboard sensors, take the average, and if it’s elevated, blast an alert out to everyone on the systems team to check for datacenter overheat.
Yes, we could have also alerted if the CRAC units shut down or if a dedicated temperature sensor in the room was high, but the telemetry for this stuff was nowhere near as reliable, and unknown unknowns can still ruin you, so the most durable thing sometimes really is to ask your fleet of Linux boxes for their temperature and freak out if the average is just a little too high.
Our team didn’t interact much with the partner with the nuclear sub experience, but I’d like to think he would have approved.
Got a better tale of woe? Let me know at X, Bluesky, Hacker News or Lobsters.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Cause Permanent Data Loss at Russia's Yandex Cloud
articles.body:
Ukraine Strikes Cause Permanent Data Loss at Russia's Yandex Cloud (united24media.com) 62
			
		 	
				Russia's Yandex says 2.84% of customer data has been permanently lost following Ukrainian strikes on data centers in the country. "According to the company, recovery is impossible because of critical damage to equipment and the lack of backup copies on the platform," reports UNITED24 Media. From the report:  Yandex clarified that customers who had previously enabled the platform's backup tools did not experience any data loss, as their information remained fully preserved. The incident has prompted the company to revise its approach to data protection and disaster recovery, particularly the default settings for cloud infrastructure. Under the updated policy, automatic backups will be enabled by default whenever customers create new virtual machines on Yandex Cloud. Users will retain the option to disable the feature manually through the management console. In addition to changing its backup policy, Yandex Cloud announced the launch of a new availability zone, designated ru-central1-f. The new availability zone operates from a separate location, improving the resilience and reliability of the services.  The report says Ukrainian drones targeted three Yandex data centers in Russia over four days, beginning October 8 with a strike on a facility in the Ryazan region that houses two of the company's three supercomputers. A second attack hit Yandex's largest data center in the Kaluga region on October 9, followed by a third strike on October 11 targeting a facility in the Vladimir region that houses the company's remaining supercomputer.

articles.title: The Power and Legacy of Virginia Tech's Mac-Based Supercomputers
articles.body:
When we think about data centers today, we often picture rows of GPU-packed racks run by companies like Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Meta, and used by AI labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic. Much of that hardware does one of two jobs: training new models or running finished ones to answer requests from millions of people around the world.
A supercomputer is built from many of the same parts but for a different purpose. It is typically owned by a government lab or university and designed for scientific simulation, such as modeling climate, nuclear physics, or new materials. That work demands high-precision math and very fast communication between processors. Rather than serving the masses, a supercomputer is shared among researchers, whose large jobs wait in a queue and run according to a schedule.
Early examples like UNIVAC and the IBM 7030 were used by scientists working on atomic research. The Cray-1 came along in the mid-70s and accelerated such work to new levels. Each of these machines brought with it new technologies that made those breakthroughs possible. They were also fairly bespoke, built of components regular nerds could only dream about.
Over time, that changed. By the time the 1990s rolled around, companies like Cray saw their hardware being outpaced by newcomers who were packing far more processors into their products. The kicker? Those processors were much more pedestrian than the custom silicon older supercomputers were built around.
In 1998, David Bader built what he calls “the first bona fide Linux supercomputer” with off-the-shelf parts, including the Intel Pentium II.1
That brings us to 2003, and the subject of today’s article: Virginia Tech’s Mac-based supercomputers.
Bang for the Buck
As you can see from these photos, System X — pronounced “System Ten”2 — was built with 1,100 Power Mac G5s:
Photos from Virginia Tech’s Advanced Research Computing website, via the Wayback Machine.
Honestly, I could end this article right here. Look how badass this all is! I really do love the look of the Power Mac G5.
Virginia Tech built this supercomputer in the summer of 2003, with the goal of hitting 10 teraflops. Once it was up and running that fall, it ranked as the world’s third-fastest computer, and the fastest at an academic institution. You can see from this video that the G5 was chosen to hit these numbers without breaking the bank:
(This video played as part of Apple’s product introduction for the Power Mac G5 itself.)
The total cost was $5.2 million,3 a far cry from the $400 million spent to build the fastest supercomputer at the time, the Earth Simulator.
(System X also looked much cooler.)
Both Virginia Tech faculty members and students could get time on the machine free of charge, and thanks to the dual 2.0 GHz processors inside each G5, their projects could tap into vast resources easily.
On the software front, every node ran Mac OS X. The machines arrived running Mac OS X 10.2.7, with plans to move to Panther shortly after.
Each G5 came equipped with 4 GB of DDR400 RAM, a 160 GB Serial ATA hard drive, and a Mellanox InfiniBand PCI-X card, which allowed the machines to be linked to each other and to the network over high-speed cables. Notably, the Power Mac G5 didn’t support ECC memory. That would matter later.
The G5s were unboxed and installed by students and faculty:
The whole thing came together pretty quickly, according to this FAQ:
Planning began in January of 2003. Facilities planning began in April of 2003. Renovations began the first week of August and were completed on September 23, 2003. Computers, network equipment, and cables began arriving the first week of September 2003. The computers arrived in six shipments during a seven day period and were processed into the racks in less than 2 hours per shipment with no more than 30 volunteers working a shift.
Ethernet cabling (roughly 1200 connections) was done by a four man team from our internal communications and network services group and was completed in less than 14 days.
InfiniBand cabling (roughly 1700 connections) began September 13, 2003 and was completed by a team of five people in 10 days.
I was lucky to get an email about this from Sam Davies, who was a student and an Apple Campus Representative at Virginia Tech at the time. He told me:
In the summer of 2003, I was fortunate to be a part of the team working to put System X together (that was the official name, unofficially the Mac community and everyone else called it “Big Mac”).
The first 1,100 G5s off of Apple’s assembly line were unloaded from trucks, unboxed, and carried into server racks by a huge team of faculty, staff, Apple project folks, and student volunteers like me. Only one G5 tower in the batch of 1100 couldn’t be used, and that was because one of the Apple sales reps dropped it. (Those handles are sharp!)
Of course, having a bunch of tower machines stuffed into racks isn’t very space-efficient. The next year, Apple had a solution.
The Xserve G5
Here’s Apple PR, in January 2004:
Apple today introduced Xserve G5, the most powerful Xserve yet, delivering over 30 gigaflops of processing power per system, about 60 percent more than the PowerPC G4-based Xserve. Xserve G5 features the same revolutionary PowerPC G5, 64-bit processor used in Virginia Tech’s cluster of Power Mac G5s—the world’s third fastest supercomputer. With unparalleled performance and manageability in a 1U rack-mount enclosure, Xserve G5 is the perfect server for today’s UNIX-based applications.
Xserve G5 includes a new system controller with up to 8GB of PC3200 error correcting code (ECC) memory; three hot-plug Serial ATA drive modules that deliver up to 750GB of storage; optional internal hardware RAID; dual PCI-X slots, supporting 133 MHz PCI-X cards with over 1 GBps of throughput; and dual on-board Gigabit Ethernet for high-performance networking.
The press release continues:
“Xserve G5 delivers just what our customers have been asking for,” said Philip Schiller, Apple’s senior vice president of Worldwide Product Marketing. “With dual G5 processing power and up to 8GB of ECC memory, Xserve G5 is affordable, easy to manage and easy to cluster. Starting as low as $2,999, no one can offer better price performance in a 1U rack-mount design.”
Available with either single or dual 2.0 GHz PowerPC G5 processors, the Xserve G5 architecture is based on an execution core that features massively parallel computation for an unprecedented 215 in-flight instructions, full symmetric multi-processing, two double precision floating-point units and an optimized Velocity Engine. Xserve G5 has the industry’s fastest front side processor bus—running at up to 1.0 GHz and delivering 8 GBps per processor.
Building on the engineering feats first introduced in the Power Mac G5, Xserve G5 squeezes the incredible performance of dual PowerPC G5 processors into an ultra-thin 1U enclosure. An innovative copper heat sink design effectively removes heat from the processors while eight high-performance fans provide airflow for cooling the system. The fans are individually managed and monitored by a dedicated fan control processor; if a single fan fails the others speed up to compensate. The 1U enclosure has an array of over 30 sensors, including eight dedicated to temperature control, that continually monitor all critical system functions throughout the server.
Tech tore down the Power Mac version of System X in January 2004 and rebuilt it with Xserve G5s that summer. ECC memory was a big part of the reason. As the school put it: “We needed to upgrade the system to something with error correcting code (ECC) RAM. The Power Macs did not support it and the XServes were coming.”
The new array was made up of 1,100 dual 2.3 GHz Xserve G5 servers and six Xserve RAIDs. Those 2.3 GHz machines were custom-built by Apple for Virginia Tech; the public wouldn’t be able to buy one until January 2005. Each one had 4 GB of that sweet, sweet ECC RAM and an 80 GB Serial ATA drive.
The installation photos really show the difference between the G5 towers and G5 servers when it comes to density:
The aforementioned FAQ sheds some light on this version of System X:
The initial machine was torn down by eight people between January 14 and January 19, 2004.
The Xserve upgrade was completed by a team of Virginia Tech and Apple volunteers over a much more staggered period of time. Rack preparation and pre-cabling of Ethernet began in February and was completed by less than ten people.
Machines arrived in odd batches beginning in the middle of June 2004 and were processed into the racks by no more than 16 people working for no more than 9 hours a shift (first shipment; 304 Xserves racked in 9 hours by a 16 person team).
Final cabling was completed over a two-week period by no more than ten people working a shift. The machine was back online for benchmarking by August 1, 2004.
The new hardware pushed System X to 12.25 teraflops. The school boasted that “the upgraded version was #7 in the 2004 TOP500 list, and cost one-fifth as much as the second least-expensive system in the top 10.”
Apple boasted about it as well, profiling the machine on its website:
Virginia Tech gained international honors for building the fastest supercomputer at any academic institution in the world. And they did it using Power Mac G5s. From that milestone, Virginia Tech has moved ahead again with System X, a new cluster using 1,100 Xserve G5s.
[…]
“When we built the first supercomputer from Power Mac G5s, we proved that a radically-different communications technology could be used to create a large-scale computing platform,” says Dr. Srinidhi Varadarajan, director of the university’s Terascale Computing Facility and the system’s lead designer.
“We’re recognized for knowing how to build these terascale computing machines — and with very good price performance.
“But the measure of the facility is the kind of science it produces.”
Varadarajan later became CTO of AppAssure, a backup software company that Dell acquired in 2012. May we all be as cool as him one day:
Tech Goes Intel
By the middle of 2007, System X had slipped to 71st place on the TOP500 list, but was still serving the community in and around Tech.
In November 2008, its younger sibling System G was brought online. Firmly in the Intel era, System G was made up of 324 Mac Pros,4 each with two 4-core 2.8 GHz Intel Xeon processors (for a total of 2,592 processor cores) and 8 GB of RAM.
It debuted at #280 on the November 2008 TOP500 list with a Linpack score of 16.87 teraflops, though Virginia Tech claimed 22.8 teraflops of sustained performance.
Chris Foresman wrote about the supercomputer for Ars Technica:
Virginia Tech’s Center for High-End Computing System [sic] (CHECS) is famous for building a 1100-node, G5-based supercomputing cluster in 2003 called System X. At the time it was built, it ranked as the third fastest supercomputer in the world with a sustained performance of just over 12 teraflops. The CHECS is building a new cluster, this time using 324 Mac Pro towers, that will have a theoretical computing capacity of 29 teraflops.
The new system will not replace System X, according to CHECS Director Dr. Srinidhi Varadarajan. “Unlike System X, which is a production machine for computational science and engineering researchers, the new system is intended to be pure computer science research system,” he told Ars. The system will be used to study two main areas: power-aware software systems that can adjust performance automatically to maximize efficiency, and distributed shared memory systems that can run existing threaded code on high-performance clusters “as if they were scaled up versions of multi-core desktops.”
The article continues and explains why the Intel Xserve wasn’t chosen for the new array:
Varadarajan and his team chose Mac Pros for a few reasons. For one, Xserves are power dense, which requires a lot of cooling to prevent thermal hot spots. “System X has a hybrid liquid-air cooling system in a dedicated facility, which enables significantly better cooling without hot spots. This machine is however, housed in a conventional air cooled room,” Varadarajan told us. Also, the Mac Pro has a large number of power and temperature sensors built in, which is necessary for the power/performance research and tuning, as well as an additional full-height PCI Express 2.0 slot for use in other research projects. And, despite common wisdom to the contrary, the Mac Pros beat other systems on price. “The Mac Pros are highly competitive even against building a white box off the cheapest prices,” he added.
System G was designed to be as power-efficient as possible. Here’s a bit from an old CHECS website:
The system is the first supercomputer running over quad data rate (QDR) InfiniBand (40Gbs) interconnect technology. System G (for “green”) also has unique power-aware capabilities, with thousands of power and thermal sensors allowing CHECS researchers to design and develop algorithms and systems software that achieve high-performance with modest power requirements, and to test such systems at unprecedented scale. With a sustained (Linpack) performance of 22.8 TFlops, System G is the largest power-aware research system and one of the largest computer science systems research clusters in the world.
This VT Magazine article has more:
“It’s twice as powerful, a third the size, and uses a third of the power,” says Kirk W. Cameron, associate professor of computer science in the College of Engineering. Cameron helped build G with Srinidhi Varadarajan, associate professor of computer science and director of the Center for High-End Computing Systems.
Unlike System X, System G was created to improve system design first and foremost and to be used as a production computer second. The $1.2 million machine was built to develop new, high-performance software tools and applications with paramount efficiency.
When Cameron and Varadarajan, assisted by a team of fellow faculty members and scores of graduate students, set out to build G, they had an end-goal in mind. They wanted G to not only be fast but also environmentally friendly. Hence the “G” for green. When Cameron arrived at Virginia Tech in 2004–on the heels of X’s opening, and attracted to Tech because of X–“green computing” wasn’t even an industry catchphrase. But Cameron already was looking ahead at the need to conserve power.
He previously worked for Los Alamos National Laboratory, handling performance duties, “squeezing as much power as possible” out of the facilities’ supercomputers, he says. This was in 2002, well before the recent call to arms in green energy. G went on-line in 2008. “Now everybody says they are doing it, but we were lucky enough to have done it first,” Cameron says.
The system is stocked with advanced power-management capabilities, such as power-aware central processing units (CPUs), disks, and memory. A network of advanced power and thermal sensors runs throughout the entire system, with Cameron and Varadarajan able to track how much power each CPU unit in each Apple tower is using.
Using power caps, the system is able to run on lower steam when not in use or in partial use, as opposed to older supercomputer systems that run at full blast, needlessly using power, on a continuous basis. Temperature control is carefully monitored as to not overuse the massive air-conditioning units that keep the stacked, side-by-side computers from overheating.
“We wanted to try and find the most efficient way to use computers,” says Cameron.
While System X served researchers across the university and was eventually run by Virginia Tech’s Advanced Research Computing division, System G was a computer science research machine. It belonged to CHECS, was sponsored in part by the National Science Foundation (NSF), and was housed on the campus of VT’s Corporate Research Center.
That makes finding additional details about System G tricky. Even locating photos of the array proved futile; the ones Virginia Tech published in 2008 have vanished from the web.
That’s when Dr. Cameron answered an email I had sent him, asking about System G and, if possible, for any photos he had of the Mac Pros. He graciously replied with first-hand information about the project, including a couple of incredibly rare photos of the system up and running:
He also provided photos of the Mac Pros before they were racked. Looking at these pictures, all I can think about is how bad the handles were on those machines. I hope the team had gloves.
I cannot imagine how amazing this must have been in person.
These photos also prove yet again that guys with racks and racks of Mac hardware are just much cooler than the rest of us:
He also provided insight into how the project was designed to make it easier to capture and analyze huge amounts of data. The team captured data from the Mac Pros’ built-in temperature sensors, recorded the voltage and current going into the racks, and logged environmental data from the room itself.
All of this data was synthesized into human-readable information that helped inform their research and keep System G as efficient as possible:
The Legacies of System X & System G
Both systems are now gone, but their legacy remains. Choosing Mac hardware to build a supercomputer isn’t the status quo, but the work of Varadarajan, Cameron, and others proved it could be done, and on a budget.
System X may be the most famous Mac-based supercomputer, but it wasn’t the only one. In January 2005, Bowie State University in Maryland unveiled XSEED, a $1 million array of 224 Xserve G5s. In the same timeframe, the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign launched its Turing Xserve Cluster, made up of 640 dual-processor 2.0 GHz Xserve G5s. The University of California, Los Angeles had Dawson, which started as an array of 128 Xserve G5s.
System G’s legacy includes its focus on power usage, under the direction of Dr. Cameron. His work has centered on the power consumption of high-performance computing systems since the early 2000s. He is a founding member of SPECpower, helped create the Green500 list, and has worked to steer the supercomputer industry toward treating performance per watt as an important metric when architecting systems.
He is still a faculty member at Virginia Tech today.
My research into System X started in July, and what was going to be a simple blog post turned into something much bigger and much more special. I had no idea System G existed when I started this, and I am thrilled I could help tell its story. My thanks to everyone who helped make this article possible, including Dr. Cameron, Sam Davies, Casey Liss, Jason Snell, and others.
- NASA’s Beowulf project had strung together commodity PCs running Linux as early as 1994. ↩︎
- According to Virginia Tech, the “X” stood for the original goal of 10 teraflops of operating speed, not for Mac OS X. ↩︎
- That’s the figure Virginia Tech used in 2003. A later version of the school’s FAQ put the machine at $5.7 million, plus $2 million to renovate the facility that housed it. ↩︎
- Some Virginia Tech sources, including VT Magazine and the school’s press release, put the count at 325. In reviewing first-hand documentation of System G (more on that in a moment), I can confidently say the array was made up of 324 machines. ↩︎

articles.title: Why are we still working this hard?
articles.body:
In 1973, what a forty-hour week of work produced takes sixteen hours to produce today.
That’s according to Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) input output tables. An hour of work in American business now makes two and a half times what it made in 1973. For every forty hours that used to be needed, twenty-four have been freed.
You have probably not noticed them. The forty-hour week was written into American law by an act of 1938, and hasn’t changed. Counted for each head of population, the hours worked in American business in 2024 were 10 percent higher than in 1973. As a country, the US took the whole of fifty years’ progress as more output and none of it as time.
It was supposed to go differently. In 1930 the economist John Maynard Keynes wrote a short essay about the world his grandchildren would live in. He predicted that “the standard of life in progressive countries one hundred years hence will be between four and eight times as high as it is to-day.” And with so much plenty, he thought, we would hardly need to work at all: “Three-hour shifts or a fifteen-hour week” would be enough. He is usually said to have been right about the wealth and wrong about the leisure. Output per person in the United States in 2024 was 7.8 times its level in 1930. But look again at the sixteen hours. He was right about both. The fifteen-hour week arrived in terms of output, but not in the workweek.
I have spent a long time trying to find out where those twenty-four hours went, with a co-author, a small economy built on paper, and more national accounts than I’d like to admit. This essay is what I found. Eighteen of the hours never reached ordinary paychecks. The other six reached them in a form that couldn’t be taken as time. Both happened for the same reason, which has to do with what a wage is for. The same reason explains why people are frightened of machines that ought to be good news. And it points to a way out that is simpler, and nearer, than I expected when I started.
A note: The numbers are American, because the United States publishes the accounts this needs. I live in Sweden but it’s probably quite a similar story. The formal paper underpinning this work is here:
https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7226858
What is a wage for?
Three things:
A wage is a price. It tells a business what an hour of someone’s time costs, so that the hour gets used where it is worth most, and it tells people which work is wanted. A wage is good at this.
A wage is also a “ticket”. It is how nearly everyone gets a share of what is made. Bread reaches me because I have money, and I have money because I sold some hours. That isn’t a law of nature. It is an arrangement, and it has worked so well for so long that we’ve stopped seeing it as one.
And a wage is a place: a shape to the day, people to be among, a sign that somebody needs you.
One thing can do three jobs only while the jobs pull the same way. For two centuries they did, because of the kind of machine we had. The machines of the industrial age were strong and stupid. They could lift, spin, stamp and haul, and they couldn’t see, judge or decide. Nearly everything worth making took both kinds of ability, so every new machine needed people standing next to it, and the owners of machines had to bid for those people. The price of an hour rose with everything else, and a ticket made of that price was a good ticket.
The machines being built now can see, read, write and decide. I write software for a living and use them every day, and I find it harder each year to name a kind of work that is safely out of their reach.
My claim is that the price and the ticket have been pulling apart for fifty years, and that each is damaging the other, and that fundamentally this is driven by changes in technology.
How important is this?
Probably a lot. It surprises me just as much as you that some random 26 year old trans girl might work this out, but the maths has been checked, the paper is going through review, and I’ve done everything I can to try and break it. If you can see what’s really wrong with it: wilson@wilsoniumite.com
Follow a dollar you spend in a shop. Some of it pays the people who worked to make the thing. Some of it pays whoever owns what was used to make it: the oven, the truck, the building, the ground underneath. America’s national accounts are detailed enough to chase a dollar all the way back through every supplier, and when you do it for 2023, of what is paid to Americans for making the things households buy, 66 percent is pay for work and 34 percent goes to owners.
A third of the economy, in other words, already pays people for owning things, with no work asked of them. That would be a curiosity if we all held a bit of both. We don’t.
The poorest tenth of American households lives mostly on government benefits. From the second tenth to the ninth, about four-fifths of what a household earns in the market is pay for work. Then, in the richest tenth, it changes all at once, and pay and ownership are about half and half. That one tenth receives two-thirds of all the income from ownership.
Benefits look like a second source for everyone else. But 68 cents of every tax dollar in America is raised from pay for work, so a benefit is mostly a claim on somebody else’s wage. Follow the money far enough and nine households in ten are living on each other’s wages. We live off the earth and off the machines we’ve built on it. Our share of what they produce reaches us through one narrow channel, which is being paid for a job.
By the way at this point you may notice that “machines” sounds like capital, and yes, that would be the technical term. But to try and escape what we usually feel when we hear those terms, I will use work instead of labor, machines instead of capital, and land instead of non-produced inputs (the term used in our paper).
Where did the eighteen hours go?
Until 1973, what an hour of work produced and what an hour of ordinary pay could buy rose together. Between 1950 and 1973 the first rose by 81 percent and the second by 66 percent. (By ordinary pay I mean the hourly pay of everyone on a private payroll who isn’t a manager or a supervisor, measured against the prices of everything except housing.) Then they parted. Since 1973 the output of an hour has risen two and a half times, and an hour of ordinary pay buys 19 percent more. You might have heard of this as “the great stagnation” and yes, I claim to in large part be able to explain what happened, that technology is what changed. Consider that moors law is usually said to start around that period, and you begin to see what I mean.
So to buy what forty hours of ordinary pay bought in 1973 now takes thirty-four hours. Making it takes sixteen. The eighteen in between went somewhere else.
I would like to tell you they went to the owners of the machines. About a fifth of the gap did. About two-fifths of it is pay spreading out among workers, with the top pulling away from the ordinary worker. The rest I can’t separate cleanly. It is a tangle of prices, benefits and measures that don’t line up.
But look at what the largest piece is. Daron Acemoglu, who shared the Nobel prize in economics in 2024, and Pascual Restrepo estimate that between 50 and 70 percent of the change in America’s wage structure over the four decades to 2016 came from “relative wage declines of worker groups specialized in routine tasks in industries experiencing rapid automation.” Machines learned to do what ordinary workers did before they learned to do what the best-paid did.
So both pieces are the same thing happening. A wage is a price, and a price follows scarcity. It doesn’t follow effort, and it doesn’t follow need. The day a machine learns your job, you are working exactly as hard as you did the day before, and your hour is worth less. That is how a price ought to behave, and it is a fine way to decide who should do what. It is a strange way to decide who gets to live well.
That is the price shrinking the ticket. So far it has been slow.
And the other six hours?
Ordinary pay did rise, by a fifth. That could have been six hours off the week at the same standard of living. Instead the hours went up, and I don’t think it was because nobody wanted the time.
Think about what a price tells you. When I pay three dollars for a loaf of bread, the baker learns something true about me: the bread was worth at least three dollars to me, because I could have walked away. A wage is supposed to carry the same kind of information the other way. If I take a job at fifteen dollars an hour, the hour must have been worth less than that to me, or I would have kept it. A great deal of economics leans on this. It is why a job that somebody is willing to do is assumed to be a job worth doing.
It works only if I could have said no. If selling hours is the only way I eat, I will sell them for whatever they fetch, and the wage records how badly I needed the money. It says very little about what the hour was worth to me. It might have been an afternoon with my child, or a visit to my mother, or the Tuesday I would have spent running the club. Those lost a contest they were never allowed to enter. An auction in which one side can’t walk away tells you very little about what the thing was worth.
This is the ticket spoiling the price. Because the wage is the ticket, most people can’t refuse it, and a price that can’t be refused has stopped being a price. When we argue over “does money represent value”, this is one of the main reasons that isn’t true.
Two things then happen. The first is that some work gets done that isn’t worth doing. Take any job that produces a little more than the wage it pays and less than the hour is worth to the person doing it. The job covers its costs. The employer is doing nothing wrong. And every hour of it uses up something worth more than what it makes, with the whole of the loss falling on the worker. Nobody can see this, because all the prices look fine. Think uber or doordash. Would you ask your friend to pick you up because you are drunk and pay them a few dollars for it, knowing they’d rather be asleep? Maybe, just maybe, that job shouldn’t exist, at least not done by a person.
The second is that our economy has no way of saying “enough.” Other markets can. When there is more of something than people want, its price falls and less of it gets made. The market for work can’t, because for the person selling, a price that falls far enough means not eating. So we treat every job as a good in itself and every hour sold as proof that it was wanted. I once asked a friend why we assume that everyone ought to be working, and she said of course they should, she’d like to be able to buy more stuff. It’s a fair answer, and it contains an assumption, which is that every extra hour worked makes more of what we want. Labor is a resource, like water, and we don’t drain the oceans looking for a use for every drop.
I can’t put a number on what this costs, and the reason I can’t is part of the argument. Everything we measure about work is a record of what people did when they could not refuse. It is like trying to learn how much people like a food by watching what they buy when it is the only thing on the shelf. So let me ask you instead.
Do the people you know have more free time than their parents had at the same age? In a country that has made itself two and a half times as productive within one working lifetime, do they seem less pressed? When they do take time, for a new child or a dying parent, does it feel like something they are free to choose, or like something they will pay for later? And of the things that seem to have thinned out around you, the visits, the clubs, the neighbors who knew each other, how many were things that anyone was ever paid to do?
The harder evidence points the same way. Where ordinary people did gain free time over the last century, most of it came at the two ends of life, as longer schooling and longer retirement. Those are the two stretches that come with a ticket that isn’t a wage: a parent or a loan at one end, a pension at the other. And when researchers in the United States gave 1,000 low-income people $1,000 a month for three years, with no conditions, those people took roughly a sixth of the money as time. They received $11,400 a year more than a comparison group, and their other income ended up about $1,900 a year lower. The authors call that “a moderate labor supply effect.” People who could refuse a little did refuse a little.
What happens if machines get much better?
So far both failures have been slow. Nobody knows whether machines are about to get much better, or how fast. What I can do is show you what happens in an economy where they do.
An economic model is a small economy on paper, simple enough to solve and fitted to the real one wherever the two can be compared. In mine, businesses give each task to whoever does it more cheaply, a person or a machine. People are far better than machines at some tasks and only a little better at others. Machines have to be built, out of other machines, some human work and some land. Whoever pays for a machine wants a return of 10 percent a year. And there is only so much land. Fitted to the United States of today, this economy pays 60 percent of its income for work, 31 percent to the owners of machines and 9 percent to the owners of land.
Now turn one dial. Let machines get steadily better at everything, until they are a hundred times better relative to us than they are now, and let them learn to build one another.
For a long while very little happens. When machines are ten times better, work is still paid 52 percent of all income, because people move to what they are best at. Then, at about 35 times, the machines that could replace even the hardest hour of human work take less than an hour of human work to build, and from there no wage can stay above what the replacement costs. By the hundredfold point work is paid 17 percent of all income. At ten thousand times it is paid less than 1 percent.
Here is something fun though about this economic model. Technically, measured in “stuff”, nobody in this economy gets poorer. But, what stuff you can buy has changed:
At the hundredfold point total income is 32 times what it was, and an hour of work buys 14 times as many goods as it does today. What an hour stops buying is land: an hour’s pay rents about a twelfth of the land it does now. And the income of those who own machines and land is 66 times what it was.
Look at what has happened to the two jobs. As a price, the wage is working perfectly. It is telling everyone, accurately, that human hours are no longer what production is short of. As a ticket it has all but failed. It delivers a sixth of the income, in the middle of the largest boom there has ever been.
Who would that fall on? If ownership stayed as it is today and work were paid 17 percent of income, the richest tenth of American households would receive 62 percent of all market income, up from 46. The poorer half would go from 14 and a half percent to 10. People sometimes hope that an economy like that would seize up for want of customers. It wouldn’t. The owners are the customers, and the economy would turn to face them. Nothing in economics says an economy has to be for everybody.
Keep three cautions in mind. The dial measures technology and not time: a hundredfold improvement takes 117 years at 4 percent a year, the pace at which machinery improved for its price after the Second World War, and 25 years at 20 percent, and nobody knows the pace. If people turn out to have abilities that no machine can match at any price, the same dial stops with work at 48 percent. And it is a model, with one kind of worker and no politics.
So what would fix it?
There are two problems here with one cause. We ask the wage to be a price and a ticket. Being the ticket, it can’t be refused, so it has stopped pricing time. Being a price, it follows scarcity, so it is a ticket that shrinks whenever a machine learns something. The repair is to stop asking. Let the wage be a price, which it is good at, and give people a second ticket.
The question is what a second ticket can be made of.
It can’t be made of wages. A benefit paid out of today’s taxes is, for 68 cents in the dollar, wage earners paying each other. It moves the first ticket around.
It can’t be made by taxing what machines earn, which was my own first idea. In the model, a 20 percent tax on what machines earn their owners raises 6.3 percent of national income, and wages fall by 6.1 percent of national income. The reason is that investors build machines until the last one just pays the return they want. Tax the return and they build fewer, until the ones that remain earn the old return after tax. The owners keep their rate of return on a smaller pile. The people who work alongside the machines have fewer of them to work with, and are paid less. The tax goes straight through the owners and lands on the wage.
What works is owning the machines, and there is a way to do it that disturbs nothing. Let a company deduct the full cost of every investment from its taxable profit on the day it makes it. Then on every new machine the government is, in effect, putting up a fifth of the cost and collecting a fifth of what the machine earns. That is a partnership. The investor’s return on their own four-fifths is untouched, so just as many machines get built. The public gets its fifth, which is 6.2 percent of national income in the model, and wages don’t change. The honest catch is the machines that already exist, whose owners lose about a fifth, once.
Land is different, for one reason. Nobody makes it. Tax machines and there will be fewer machines. Tax land and there is as much land as before. Thomas Paine, the pamphleteer of the American Revolution, argued in 1797 that “Man did not make the earth,” and that every landowner therefore owed the public a ground-rent, to be paid out to everyone. “It is not charity but a right,” he wrote. I reached that idea on my own before I’d heard of him, which I’ve decided to find encouraging, and for a while I thought it was most of the answer. The numbers talked me out of it. The rent of the ground under America’s homes came in 2024 to between 4.3 and 7.1 percent of households’ disposable income, or between $2,776 and $4,627 a year for every person in the country. That is real money, and it isn’t what a country can live on. It grows, though. In the model, land’s share of income more than triples. And it can be collected by taxing only the growth from here on, which leaves today’s owners the rent they have now, though not the rise they were counting on.
So the second ticket has to be made of the other third of the dollar. It has to be ownership.
What would that take?
Less than you’d think. For the United States it comes to three things.
Hold a share in common, and pay everyone its income. A fifth of all the machines and land in the country would have paid $4,493 a person in 2023, or $374 a month, for every man, woman and child. Most of that fifth is within reach without buying anything: the tax America already levies on company profits, turned into the partnership I described, and the growth in land rent together come to about a seventh of all ownership income, and a public fund could buy the rest. It isn’t free money. The profits tax is already being spent, so paying it out means finding $608 billion a year somewhere else, and whatever a fund buys, somebody pays for.
Let people buy the rest out of wages. A common share of about a seventh would be enough to keep the poorer half of households whole, even if wages went to nothing. It can’t do that for the comfortable middle, who earn nearly half of all the pay in the country. They have to buy their ticket, and with the common fifth in place, saving 5 percent of pay and reinvesting what it earns at 5 percent a year would do it in 34 years, which is a working life.
And move taxes off the wage, toward spending, so that the safety net stops depending on the same thing as the incomes it is there to protect.
None of this is untried. Since 1982 the state of Alaska has paid every resident a yearly dividend out of a fund built from its oil revenues. Alaska’s dividend paid $1,312 a person in 2023 and $1,702 in 2024, to more than 600,000 people each year, and the fund behind it is worth $88 billion. Norway’s national fund owns, in its own words, “almost 1.5 percent of all shares in the world’s listed companies.” And Sweden puts 2.5 of the 18.5 percent of pay that goes toward the public pension into invested accounts that belong to the worker.
It starts small. A dividend of $374 a month is 29 percent of the poverty line for a person living alone. But it is made of the thing that is growing. In the model, the income of a common fifth is 13 percent of all wages today and 96 percent of all wages at the hundredfold point. And it answers the question I left hanging. A floor paid out of something everyone owns is mostly people paying themselves. As it grows, refusing becomes possible, a little and then more, and the wage goes back to being a price that means something.
There is a deadline. Today, everything that pays ownership income in the model economy, every machine and every acre, is worth about 6.7 years of the whole country’s wages. That is the price of a second ticket in the only currency most households have. At the hundredfold point it is 48 years. The saving that takes a household in the comfortable middle 34 years today takes 76 years there. The households that most need a second ticket are the ones who would have to buy it out of wages, and wages are the thing losing its value.
Is it fair?
The standard most often offered in defense of things as they are is that people are entitled to what they contribute, and that what you are paid measures what you add. I think that is a reasonable standard. My complaint is that its only reasonable if it’s wholly true.
Hold the kinds of income up to it. A wage is paid for work. The return on a machine is paid to someone who went without something in order to build it. The rent of land is paid for something that nobody made. Now look at what America taxes. It raises 68 percent of its revenue from pay for work, the most plainly earned income there is, and its tax on what machines earn lands, in the model, largely on wages again. By its own favorite standard, the country taxes most heavily what is most clearly earned. What I’ve described is that standard applied all the way through.
Now push it. Suppose machines can do nine-tenths of all work. The standard doesn’t break. It still says that those who work should keep their pay and those who saved should keep their return. It has less and less to say, because less and less of all income is anyone’s contribution. In the model with the program in place, pay for work goes from 60 percent of all income today to 17 at the hundredfold point and to less than 1 in the end. What is held in common, the public’s fifth of the machines plus the growth in land rent, goes from 6 percent of all income today to 40 at the hundredfold point and 48 in the end. That is about half, and nobody chose the number. It is where the contribution standard arrives by itself when work becomes scarce.
Is there any hope in this?
I think there is
The first reason is the one I started with. The hard problem, the one every earlier generation faced, was making enough. That problem is very nearly solved. We make in sixteen hours what took forty within living memory.
In 1955, paying every American a poverty-line income would have cost between 27 and 52 percent of everything the country produced. In 2024 it would cost between 9 and 18 percent. What is left is a problem of arrangement, of who holds which ticket. Arrangements are made by people, and they can be remade.
The second reason is that most of this can still be done as a trade, in which nobody is made worse off. Today, a household gets a second ticket by putting aside some of its pay and buying ownership from someone willing to sell it, and each side is paid in full for what it gives up. After a large shift, the same move is a transfer from those who gained to those who lost, which is a much harder thing to ask. We are still in the before. None of us knows for certain which side of the line our own work will fall on, and I can’t think of a better condition for agreeing on a rule.
The third is that every piece of it already exists somewhere, and works.
The fourth is what the machines themselves are offering. In the small economy on paper, the same hundredfold improvement produces two different worlds, and the only difference between them is who holds the tickets. In one, a tenth of the households receive three-fifths of the income, and everyone else lives on a wage that has stopped meaning much. In the other, people own a share of what makes everything, the wage is one of two incomes, and work is something you choose. That world is 32 times richer than ours, and your time in it is your own. It is the world Keynes was describing. He assumed that a society eight times as rich would simply work less, and it turns out that working less is something you can do only if you hold something besides your work. The wealth came to us as a country. The time has to come one household at a time, and most households have had no way to receive it.
I would be glad to be wrong about where the machines are heading. Very little of this depends on that. The twenty-four hours are already there. They were freed by people who are still working forty. What stands between those people and their own time is a second ticket, and it will not get cheaper by waiting.
I also made a video going over the maths, if you’d like to hear more:
For the careful: how sure am I?
Taken from public data, with every number and figure reproducible: that an hour of work makes two and a half times what it did in 1973, that an hour of ordinary pay buys a fifth more, and that Americans work more hours per head than they did then; that two-thirds of what Americans buy is paid for by work; that nine households in ten live mostly on pay and one in ten receives two-thirds of the ownership income; that 68 percent of taxes rest on pay; the size of land rent; and the falling cost of keeping everyone out of poverty.
From a model, and true to the extent that the model is correct: what happens when machines improve a hundredfold; that a tax on what machines earn lands on wages; that ownership costs more in years of wages the further the shift goes; and that the common part of income rises to about half. The model has one kind of worker, no risk and no politics. The result on taxing machines is a long-run result. In the short run the machines already exist, and their owners pay.
From argument, with modest evidence behind it: that a wage which cannot be refused says little about the worth of an hour, that some work is done which isn’t worth doing, and that our economy has no way of saying “enough.”
From nothing firmer than my own judgment: that machines will keep taking over tasks, and faster than they have; that a good deal of today’s work would not be done if the people doing it could afford to refuse; and that most of us would take more of our wealth as time if we could.
I have left things out. Every household is given the same average shopping basket, and renters are worse placed than that makes them look. The richest tenth is lumped together, though ownership is concentrated within it. Everything here is American.
How this was made. I wrote this with the help of Claude Fable 5.2, Anthropic’s AI model. If you don’t trust AI, just know that these are the same models that are currently wiping the floor with every other field, and I really didn’t try and force fable to write something I already agreed with. Actually, this whole experience has been me realising just how wrong I am about some things. Anyways, Claude did the measurements with me, drew the figures and drafted most of the text from my earlier essays. The model economy is joint work with Johan Båge. Every number comes from code in a public repository, wilsoniumite/labor
Sources
The measurements are my own calculations from the national accounts of the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis: the input–output accounts, the distribution of personal income by tenth of households, and the accounts of government receipts. Output per hour, hours worked and the wage series are from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The poverty line is that of Mollie Orshansky, “Children of the Poor,” *Social Security Bulletin* 26(7), 1963, updated for prices.
– John Maynard Keynes, “Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren,” 1930, in *Essays in Persuasion*.
– Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938, section 7; 29 U.S.C. § 207.
– Daron Acemoglu and Pascual Restrepo, “Tasks, Automation, and the Rise in U.S. Wage Inequality,” *Econometrica* 90(5), 2022. Nobel prize citation: nobelprize.org, economic sciences, 2024.
– Eva Vivalt, Elizabeth Rhodes, Alexander Bartik, David Broockman, Patrick Krause and Sarah Miller, “The Employment Effects of a Guaranteed Income: Experimental Evidence from Two U.S. States,” NBER Working Paper 32719, 2024; *The Quarterly Journal of Economics* 141(4), 2026.
