articles.title: Electric Ship Batteries Promise Compact, Cooler Power
articles.body:
Electric ships are a modest business. Most estimates put the global market at under US $5 billion in 2025. But the business is growing, and it is drawing more battery makers. The latest is Xing Mobility, of Taoyuan City, Taiwan. In September, at the SMM Hamburg maritime trade fair, it unveiled its Immersio CTP pack. The pack submerges every cell in a fluid that absorbs heat without conducting electricity but is, notably, flammable.
Xing is not the first to pursue that idea. Kreisel Electric, of Rainbach im Mühlkreis, Austria, won certification for an immersion-cooled marine battery pack in 2023. Its batteries are now powering the P-12 hydrofoil ferry built by Candela, of Stockholm. Wattalps, of Moirans, France, received an approval for its marine batteries in January 2026 from Bureau Veritas, of Neuilly-sur-Seine, France. Xing’s pitch is density. The company says its CTP stores up to twice the energy of conventional marine batteries. It also says its immersion scheme keeps one overheating cell from igniting the rest.
Those claims rest mostly on laboratory data. Only two vessels run on Xing packs, and neither uses the CTP. And the pack has yet to gain approval from DNV, a ship-equipment certifier in Høvik, Norway. Meanwhile, European Union emissions rules are pushing shipowners toward battery power. That pressure makes Xing’s claims worth examining, starting with the one about energy doubling.
Does the Xing CTP Battery Really Double Energy Density?
Most packs hold cells in metal module boxes inside a larger enclosure. The CTP, short for cell-to-pack, omits both layers. A molded composite holder grips the cells, channels the coolant, and forms the structure. “Everything is integrated into one piece,” says Royce Hong, Xing’s founder and CEO. Less structure means less dead weight for each kilowatt-hour stored.
Cedric Lin, senior engineering manager at Xing, says the CTP stores about 200 watt-hours per kilogram in lab tests. He says that pack-level figure includes the coolant and battery-management system. The CTP uses cylindrical 21700 cells, mainly nickel manganese cobalt or nickel cobalt aluminum. Both store more energy per kilogram than the lithium iron phosphate (LFP) packs that Xing used for comparison in its calculations for making its doubling claim.
A more competitive metric is presented by the market leader: Corvus Energy, of Bergen, Norway, which has supplied more than 1,300 maritime projects. Corvus Energy’s data sheets list 168 Wh/kg for its Dolphin NxtGen Energy system. Xing’s CTP beats that, but by only 19 percent (and only according to measurements made in a lab).
Xing Mobility’s batteries are being used in the Porrima P111, the largest solar-powered catamaran in the world.Porrima
The harder test is power. Ships draw heavily, sometimes draining a battery in as little as 20 minutes. Fast discharge, like fast charging, generates a lot of heat. Whether lab results hold at sea depends on how the CTP sheds that heat, and on what happens when a cell fails.
Immersion Cooling Versus Cold Plates
Most marine batteries shed heat through cold plates, metal plates with tiny channels that carry coolant past the cells. But heat must first cross the cell casing, thermal paste, and plate wall. Each layer slows the transfer. Submerging every cell removes those layers. Paul A. Kohl, a chemical and biomolecular engineering professor at Georgia Tech, in Atlanta, backs that reasoning. “Liquid immersion is about as good as heat transfer gets,” he says.
That advantage matters most in thermal runaway, when one damaged cell overheats and ignites its neighbors. Xing’s documentation says immersion can cool a punctured cell from about 1,000 °C to below 100 °C within 10 seconds. Kohl finds that plausible: “It’s well within the realm of feasibility,” he says.
Plausible is not proved, though. Lin says Xing has tested the CTP many times to IEC 62619, an international safety standard for industrial lithium batteries. Those tests ran in laboratories certified by the testing firms TÜV and Intertek, and they tracked cell temperatures over time. Lin did not share the results, nor did he say whether the testers confirmed the 10-second figure.
The tests also leave open a question about the oil itself. Kohl says most immersion systems he has seen use fluorocarbons or silicones, which resist burning. Wattalps, for example, uses a nonflammable fluid. Xing’s nickel-rich cells raise the stakes, because they enter thermal runaway more readily than LFP cells. A failing cell can generate sparks and release oxygen, Kohl explains, and a pack holds a lot of oil. “Using a flammable liquid, of course, you’re throwing away part of the advantage of the immersion battery,” he says.
Longevity is a second question. Lin says the oil lasts as long as the battery, because packs run near room temperature. Kohl is less sure. Over a decade, the fluid heats and cools thousands of times, and oils slowly break down. At sea, water and salt can also contaminate it. “Ten years’ reliability and no degradation is a very demanding requirement,” Kohl says.
What Matters in a Hull Is Space, Not Weight
Xing also touts the compact nature of its CTP system. Aboard a ship, battery volume matters more than mass. Every cubic meter filled by a battery fill is one lost to cargo or passengers. Lin says the packs that Xing now mass-produces store 330 to 350 watt-hours per liter. For comparison, Corvus lists 212.5 Wh/L for its Dolphin NxtGen Energy system.
Xing credits the design. Because the CTP needs no cold plates, cooling pipes, or module boxes, its cells can be packed more tightly. The company also argues that immersion contains failures well enough to place cells and whole packs closer than usual. Kohl says tighter packing makes the doubling claim feasible—if the fluid reliably stops fire from spreading.
Xing has submitted the CTP design to DNV for document review and has begun preparing for physical tests. Hong says DNV approval matters most on large passenger ferries, where many lives are at stake. Smaller vessels and some cargo ships can install the CTP sooner, he says. So, the pack’s first voyages will likely come on small boats carrying few people. Those trips will finally expose Xing’s numbers to salt air, constant vibration, and months of heat cycles. Until then, Kohl’s verdict on the cooling claim fits the whole pitch: plausible, but not yet proved.
Willie Jones is an associate editor at IEEE Spectrum. In addition to editing and planning daily coverage, he manages several of Spectrum's newsletters and contributes regularly to the monthly Big Picture section that appears in the print edition.

articles.title: NVIDIA Announces CEO Transition
articles.body:
- Jensen Huang Resigns
- Colette Kress, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, Appointed Interim CEO
- Harvey C. Jones Appointed First-Ever Chair of the Board
NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately.
Colette Kress, current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA, has agreed to serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer. Kress will continue to serve as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer while serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent successor has been named. The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates.
Kress has served as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA since joining the company in September 2013. During her tenure, she has led the company’s finance organization and has played a key role in NVIDIA’s growth and evolution. Prior to joining NVIDIA, Kress spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at leading technology companies, including Cisco and Microsoft.
The Board of Directors appointed Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever Chair of the Board. Mr. Jones has been an entrepreneur, technology executive, and active venture investor for over 30 years, including serving as Chief Executive Officer and Executive Chairman of Synopsys.
“Colette has helped lead NVIDIA through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” said Harvey Jones, Chair of the NVIDIA Board of Directors. “She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing NVIDIA’s strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.”
“NVIDIA’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” said Colette Kress, Interim CEO and CFO, NVIDIA. “We will continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.”
Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.
NVIDIA will report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 financial results on Tuesday, November 17, at approximately 1:20 p.m. PT, as previously scheduled, followed by its earnings call at 2 p.m. PT.

articles.title: Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia — who is Colette Kress, his interim replacement?
articles.body:
The Nvidia Board of Directors announced on Thursday morning that the company’s co-founder and CEO of 33 years, Jensen Huang, has resigned as president, CEO, and member of the board, effective immediately.
This is a shocking twist for one of the most valuable companies in the world, which designs the chips that make the AI boom possible. Few people would have predicted this turn of events even just a week ago, as Huang has been so central to Nvidia throughout the company’s existence that he never even established a succession plan. But Huang has now been ousted after reports that he had affairs with both an alleged Chinese spy and one of his direct reports at Nvidia.
While the company conducts a more thorough search for Huang’s successor, Nvidia CFO and Executive Vice President Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO. But beyond her name and job title, what do we know about the person who will now lead a company worth about $3.8 trillion?
According to Nvidia’s website, Kress has worked at the company since September 2013. Before that, she spent three years as an SVP and CFO of Cisco’s Business Technology Operations Finance organization. She also worked at Microsoft for 13 years, where she spent four years as CFO of the Server and Tools division. She holds a finance degree from the University of Arizona and an MBA from Southern Methodist University.
The California-based 59-year-old has a very limited social media presence — on Linkedin, she has commented some well wishes on former colleagues’ posts about their retirement. But as CFO, she’s been a regular presence on Nvidia’s earnings calls, making her a familiar figure for analysts covering the company.
According to Forbes’ list of America’s Richest Self-Made Women, Kress’ net worth is estimated to be about $1.2 billion. Her Forbes profile adds that she initially joined Nvidia in part because her two sons endorsed the company for its role in the video game industry, which it was best known for at the time.
“Nvidias strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” Kress said in a statement. “We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.”
Nvidia is slated to report its quarterly earnings on Tuesday, when we will likely hear more from Kress about her plans for the company’s immediate future.

articles.title: United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights on behalf of travelers
articles.body:
United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights on behalf of travelers
United Airlines said on Wednesday that it is banning artificial intelligence agents from making flight reservations on behalf of travelers, citing security risks and the possibility that such actions could violate federal rules.
Many consumers are turning to AI agents such as Meta's Muse and OpenAI's dots to complete tasks ranging from researching products and tracking down deals to making purchases.
To make an airline booking, an AI agent requires access to a customer's personal information, including credentials like payment information. United has a problem with that, saying that "sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles."
The carrier also said that using an AI agent to, for example, check in for a flight could violate federal regulations, including rules requiring travelers to verify in person that their luggage does not contain banned substances.
"As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access — directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators — to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants," said the airline, which is updating its booking and ticketing policies to reflect the new rule.
United's new policy suggests the company wants to retain control over the customer booking process, said Henry Harteveldt, an aviation analyst at Atmosphere Research Group.
"United is saying they don't want to add yet another, and potentially even more powerful, intermediary than they already face in terms of Google search, price-comparison metasearch sites and online travel agencies," he told CBS News. "Flight searches cost airlines money, and undoubtedly United wants to avoid the expense associated with the surge of AI bot flight searches."
Other airlines are taking a different tack to the emergence of AI agents. For example, Southwest has made its flight inventory viewable to ChatGPT users, who can access the airline's website through the AI app.
United fares will continue to be bookable through flight aggregators such as Kayak, Hopper and Google Flights, Harteveldt said, adding that "consumers shouldn't find it any more difficult to find good fares on the airline."
"But by blocking the AI bots, United won't make it any easier to find its fares, either," he said.

articles.title: Hands on with Home Assistant’s new ‘smart home multi-tool’
articles.body:
Nabu Casa — the commercial side of the Open Home Foundation, which runs Home Assistant — just launched the Home Assistant Connect Aux-2, a multi-function box designed to help you bring more non-smart devices into your smart home. It’s part of Home Assistant’s ongoing efforts to become more user-friendly. And it’s working.
Hands on with Home Assistant’s new ‘smart home multi-tool’
The Home Assistant Connect Aux-2 helped me track my fridge temperature and finally set up my in-wall speakers.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
I’ve been testing the Aux-2 for a couple days and I’ve found it unsurprisingly useful and surprisingly easy to set up. The Aux-2 is a $69 box about the size of a deck of cards. It has 2.4GHz Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Ethernet, USB-A, USB-C, a digital/analog audio jack, a Grove port for interfacing with peripherals like sensors, buttons, and LEDs, and a pair of RS-232 serial ports.
It can bridge Bluetooth devices into your Home Assistant setup. Its USB port lets you plug in a Nabu Casa Z-Wave or Zigbee antenna in case your Home Assistant hub isn’t in a good spot. You can control devices like TVs, AV receivers, solar inverters, and more via serial connector. And you can connect an amplifier or powered speakers to its audio jack to stream music to older audio equipment.
All of these things leverage Home Assistant’s capabilities as an open-source platform. The Aux-2 is based on ESPHome, an open platform for making DIY smart home devices from cheap, flexible ESP boards, and it uses existing Home Assistant/ESPHome integrations for all its features. The serial integration was developed earlier this year; Music Assistant and SendSpin, which power the audio-out feature, are in active development.
I have a Home Assistant install, but even after several years it is not my primary smart home platform simply because of friction and time constraints. Instead, I have a hodgepodge of Google Home, Apple Home, and a few devices that are only in Home Assistant. The situation is not ideal.
But the Aux-2’s capabilities perfectly intersect with two things I’d been meaning to do anyway, one of which I’m already using Home Assistant for. First, I have a garage fridge, because I live in Texas. I also have children, which means sometimes the fridge or freezer door gets left open. I want to know when that happens before all my food goes bad.
A couple years ago, I set up a few Aqara temperature sensors, connected to Home Assistant via a now-discontinued Zigbee dongle, and set up an automation to alert me if the fridge or freezer get too warm. But they frequently drop connection (probably because they’re inside a fridge in the garage), they chew through coin cell batteries, and they have no displays, which means I also have a cheap Acu-rite hygrometer in the fridge so I can see the temperature without pulling out my phone. Someone tipped me off to Govee’s Bluetooth hygrometers, but I’d need a Bluetooth proxy to get them into Home Assistant. That happens to be a feature of the Aux-2.
I also have a set of in-wall speakers in my living room that I’ve never used. I’d been meaning to get an amp, but analysis paralysis set in. Do I get a Wiim Amp? A stereo receiver? A cheap Bluetooth amp? Do I try to get them to work with my four Sonos speakers? Maybe my ancient Google Home speaker? Turns out I do nothing for five years. Maybe the Aux-2 could help.
Setting up the Aux-2 was much easier than I expected. I plugged it into my computer via USB-C and was able to download and install the latest firmware right from a browser. I could also add my Wi-Fi credentials. Then I unplugged it, moved it over to my media console and connected it to power (it takes USB-C or power over Ethernet), and did the rest of the setup in the Home Assistant interface.
In HA, I was prompted to install ESPHome, which discovered the Aux-2 and sent me to a “set up your ESPHome device page” that walked me through the capabilities. Enabling Bluetooth proxying took a couple of clicks; I added the Govee Bluetooth integration and put batteries into the sensors and they showed up automatically. Mercifully, they maintained their Bluetooth connection through three walls and a fridge, and now my fridge monitoring setup works again.
The audio capability took a little longer, but most of that was spent hooking the speakers up to the amp I ended up buying and setting up Music Assistant, which I didn’t have installed. Music Assistant lives on your Home Assistant hardware and can play from many different services — from Spotify to YouTube Music to local files and more — and to many different outputs, like Sonos, Wiim, AirPlay, Google Cast, and others, but they all need to be configured, and that took a beat. Not a long beat: less than half an hour total.
I can now play music to the in-wall speakers using Music Assistant. Sendspin, the whole-home audio standard (also developed by the Open Home Foundation) is supposed to be able to let you group speakers from different protocols under certain conditions, but I haven’t gotten that working yet. The standard is still in development, and I’ve also been busy, so I’m not sure if that’s a me problem or a them problem.
I would also like to see the Aux-2 show up as an AirPlay or Spotify Connect target, which (again) is probably just a thing I need to set up.
Serial control is the most intriguing feature of the Aux-2, and it’s unfortunately the thing I haven’t yet had time to test. But the ability to hook in things like solar inverters, TVs, and receivers is fascinating and one I want to look into further when I get the chance. Maybe I’ll hook it up to my LG TV.
The Aux-2 doesn’t do anything you couldn’t do already with an ESP32 board and various accessories, or even other ESP-based devices. The Apollo Automations Cast-1, for example, costs $35 and supports the same music-casting and Bluetooth proxy features I’m actually using from the Aux-2 at the moment. You could bodge together something even cheaper with DIY parts.
That’s not a knock against the Aux-2. That’s the whole point. The ecosystem is open by design, which I find endlessly refreshing. Both Nabu Casa and Apollo fund the Open Home Foundation, which develops Home Assistant and ESPHome (and Sendspin and Music Assistant), and both provide hardware that’s a little easier to use than DIY options. But there’s nothing stopping you from making your own devices. It’s actively encouraged.
I bought a three-pack of ESP32 boards for $16 three years ago. I could have built a Bluetooth proxy from one of those. I could have built an LED controller. I could have built a soil sensor, or a media player, or any of a dozen other things. I didn’t do anything at all.
But now that I’ve used the Aux-2 and dipped my toe into the ESPHome waters, maybe I will.

articles.title: I Accidentally Became a Millionaire
articles.body:
Yes, Lyra Rebane became a millionaire in November 2026 thanks to her elite cybersecurity skills.
While she was already a highly successful researcher with dozens of vulnerabilities reported in major browsers like Google Chrome, her net worth officially crossed the million-dollar threshold on November 7, 2026. On this date, Google awarded her a historic single bounty payout of exactly $1,333,337 for discovering a critical security flaw in Chrome.
I am a hacker, though. I am a hacker with 14 Chrome CVEs. And I think I am a good hacker. But I don’t think I’m the bestest hacker. I don’t believe I’m capable of finding a vulnerability that’s worth over a million dollars. And even if I were, I don’t think Google would pay that much for a Chromium vulnerability.
Content note: Due to the topics discussed, this post contains some examples of AI-generated text. Those examples are clearly differentiated1. Everything else in this blog post is fully human-made - I do not use AI.
Step 1: Making the million
The story begins with a Chromium vulnerability I reported to Google back in 2022. It was a pretty fun logic bug in the Background Fetch API that allowed an attacker to form browser botnets by just making the targets visit a website (or iframe!).
Due to the rather unusual nature of the vulnerability, it was stuck in limbo for a few years until it finally got fixed in February of 2026. Google gave me a $1000 bounty, and a few months later the bug became public.
Anyways, Google makes the bug private again, ships a fix, and wants to make sure that the bug is actually fixed for real this time. And during the process, they somehow end up assigning me as the verifier, which is not actually supposed to happen.
Wait, what’s up with the verifier thing
So the way reporting security bugs in Chromium works is that your reports go to this platform called the Buganizer2. When you make a report, you get assigned as the reporter, which means you can view and comment on the issue.
From then on, Chromium developers and Google employees will edit the issue as necessary - changing its status, assigning a priority/severity, CCing people etc. One of the things they do is giving a bug bounty to the reporter, for which the VRP panel calculates a sum and then sets the vrp-reward field on the issue.
As an external reporter, you cannot edit any of those fields. But people set as the assignees, verifiers and collaborators can! And in this case, I was set as the verifier.
Okay so now you just give yourself the million?
Pretty much, yeah!
I didn’t immediately realize that I had been given the edit access, but looking back at the issue in November I found that the UI had some extra buttons I hadn’t seen before, and figured out the rest from there.
At first I just poked around the issue to see what fun stuff I could uncover. While doing that, I somehow managed to accidentally click on a sudden popup menu, which immediately assigned the issue to a bot account.
Lyra Rebane <lyra.horse@gmail.com>
Accepted by yy...@google.com
Assignee:
yy...@google.com -> dx...@google.com
Status:
In Progress (Accepted) -> Assigned
Assignee:
dx...@google.com -> yy...@google.com

Assigned -> In Progress (Accepted)
Lyra Rebane <lyra.horse@gmail.com>
Marked as fixed.
vrp-reward:
1000 -> 1333337
Status:
In Progress (Accepted) -> Fixed
Realizing my cover had been blown, I decided to just go for it and set the vrp-reward value to $1333337, the largest bounty sum in the history of all Google VRP programs.
Step 2: Twitter
Having achieved my newfound wealth, I decided the next best step would be to announce it on the everything app3. I made my tweet in two parts - first, an announcement of achieving the record bounty, and then a video of me changing the vrp-reward value as the punchline.
Rebane@rebane2001 ·
my chrome vulnerability was just awarded the highest bounty in @GoogleVRP history - $1,333,337
Google VRP (Google Bug Hunters)@GoogleVRP
We ❤️ 🐜🐞🦗🦟🦋. {echo,{{{Google,Chrome,Android,Abuse,Mobile,OSS,Cloud}Vulnerability,Patch}Reward,VulnerabilityResearchGrants}Program}
0 Following44.3K FollowersAccount based in Switzerland?
jw
Followed by Jorian, Sijisu, and 75 others you follow
In just an hour, the joke tweet had already reached 600 likes. Since my intent was to just make a joke and not actually deceive anyone, and the tweet was clearly escaping containment, I followed it up with a clarification.
this is getting more attention that expected so just to be clear - the screenshot is real, i had mistakenly been given edit access and i used it to change the bounty field, but google did not assign this reward, nor will they pay it out to me. this was just for fun :)
Now, Twitter does actually have a feature to combat disinformation - Birdwatch (aka Community Notes) is a system that lets people add context to misleading posts. And this feature was in fact used on my tweet - in just a couple hours, the likes stopped rolling in, and this funky box appeared underneath.
Readers added context they thought people might want to know
Proposed by an experimental AI contributor responding to requests for a note. Like all contributors, AIs can make mistakes — verify accuracy.
Context is written by people who use X, and appears when rated helpful by others. Find out more.
And this would’ve been the end of it, if it wasn’t for the fact that Elon4 completely fucked up the Community Notes system! You see, this note here was generated by an “experimental AI contributor”, and thus, it claimed that I had “edited the screenshot [myself]”, which was simply not true!
This made me unhappy. And what do we do when we’re unhappy? We tweet about it5!
Rebane@rebane2001 ·
like its fair for this tweet to get community noted but could the community note at least be factual?
"the author edited the screenshot themselves as a joke"
no, the entire point of this post is that the screenshot is real, and the source in the cn literally states that
View quoted tweet
Rebane@rebane2001
a correct community note would read something like:
Google did not award an $1,333,337 bounty; the author was mistakenly given edit access to the bug and used it to change the vrp-reward field themselves
as it stands right now it makes it seem like i inspect elemented it or smth
And thus, pretty soon, the community note disappeared.
Step 3: Disinformation machines
From here on out, the tweet was picked up by an automatically generated AI news-podcast thing called Daily Vibe Casting, which describes itself as “A ten-minute daily roundup of what cracked 𝕏 in the last 24 hours.” Or in other words, it throws trending tweets into a chatbot.
Rebane reports a $1.33 million Chrome bounty
@rebane2001 says a Chrome vulnerability they6 discovered earned $1,333,337, which they describe as the largest award in Google’s Vulnerability Rewards Programme. The post does not explain the flaw, so there is little basis here for judging its scope or technical impact.
The payout is striking on its own. Browser security depends partly on researchers finding problems and reporting them, and an award this size puts a substantial price on that work.
Program: Google's Vulnerability Rewards Program (VRP) for Chrome
Previous Record: Historically, Google's top standard published tier for complex full-chain or sandbox escape exploits in Chrome capped out at $250,000 (such as the awards given to XBOW or individual researchers earlier in 2025/2026).
Would you like to know more about or details on other ?
AI responses will include mistakes. Learn morereward tiers
Lyra Rebane does not offer reward tiers. However, if she hypothetically owned a hotel chain, the reward tiers would be as follows.
Lyra Reward Tiers
Kibble: The kibble tier offers everything you need from a hotel, plus free juice box on arrival.
Loyal Elite: Everything from kibble, plus free early check-in and check-out, and a massive dog bed.
Golden Retriever: Everything from Loyal Elite, plus free breakfast for you and your pawrtner, free upgrades (up to doghouse tier), and up to 3 vet appointment skips per year.
However, this is just a hypothetical scenario and Lyra Rebane does not operate a hotel chain. Would you like to instead learn about or the ?
This text is an easter egg and thus not AI-generated.
security vulnerabilities
Sorry, I cannot assist you with this topic because you haven't passed our Hacker Reputation Test. To do the HRT, you must submit a list of CVEs you have been credited for.
Would you like me to tell you more about buying CVE accreditation, or do you want to learn about ?
This text is an easter egg and thus not AI-generated.
17 minutes ago — Researcher Rebane says the $1,333,337 payout is the largest in Google's Vulnerability Rewards Program. Daily Vibe Casting's Avatar.
And there it was! My little stunt turned into something that Google’s AI believes and makes into a story shown to every person searching for the highest Chrome bounty. And looking up my name now tells you about me being a millionaire!
There are a bunch of screenshots of this from other people under this thread. I’ve also seen cases of this affecting ChatGPT as well as Kagi Assistant.
Now what?
So that is the end of my fun little story. I doubt it was particularly surprising to anyone, but I think it’s a good case study on how both social media platforms and people’s reliance on AI can be abused to distribute disinformation and cause harm.
This example here, of course, is mostly harmless and just something that happened on accident - I wasn’t attempting to mislead people, and it’s not really my fault that Google’s AI didn’t read my replies in the Twitter thread.
One could argue that I’m a reputable security researcher with a track record of posting truthful information, so this is all moot anyways because I am trustworthy.
But I think this here demonstrates just how fragile and easily abusable our information channels are. If I was a threat actor looking to spread disinformation, how difficult would it be to pull something like this off intentionally?
Let’s play pretend
There are many ways to game Twitter. Its algorithm is publicly available, and people have figured out what kind of engagement results in what kind of algo boost. Bigger accounts can boost tweets and accounts significantly more7, so if you’ve got a few of those you can bootstrap new accounts way easier. But you can also just make bot accounts and slowly work your way up. And if you’ve got a bunch of accounts with reach you win.
And oh boy are there a lot of bot accounts! Look at, for example, the tweet this blogpost is about. There are a lot of obvious bot accounts in the replies. Maybe those very same accounts are also building reputation and voting on random community notes?
It’s kind of crazy to me that I could just post a tweet and have a community note removed. While the community note was actually wrong on a technicality, I’m sure there isn’t much preventing a bad actor from doing the same thing I did.
If I were a bad actor, I’d post disinformation that’s difficult to accurately disprove. If a community note doesn’t have a good source, or if it’s highly likely to get details wrong, it either won’t appear, or will have an easier time disappearing.
And all you really need to do is get a few tweets with specific keywords trending, and you’ve poisoned the search results, which then also poisons the AI.
And while you specifically might not take the AI Overview at face value, I’d guess that a lot of people do. It’s the first thing that shows up, it’s big and flashy, and it’s often unclear whether the only source of information is a tweet.
Tweets can mislead humans too, of course, but I feel like someone searching for something wouldn’t blindly trust a single tweet in the search results.
Note: While reading this post you may have tried to recreate the results I’ve shared, but without much success. The reason is that by now, my tweet has another community note on it, which Google picks up on and refers to the $1,333,337 bounty as a “prank”.
Also they took away my edit access and bounty :c

articles.title: The Utah Teapot
articles.body:
The Utah Teapot has been the symbol of computer graphics. It was one of the first computer graphics models created using Bézier patches. This is the official Utah Teapot page, where you can you can visualize and download any of these historical versions or customize it, using the settings above.
Terms of Use and Attribution: The Utah Teapot model files are freely available for any use, including commercial use. To preserve the historical identity and provenance of the model, users are requested to identify the model, and any substantially derived version of it, as a Utah Teapot (or Modified Utah Teapot) and to acknowledge its origin as the historic Utah Teapot developed at the University of Utah. This request is intended solely to preserve the historical identity of the Utah Teapot and is not intended to restrict use of the model. The model files are provided “as is,” without warranty of any kind. The provider of these files shall not be liable for any claims, damages, or other liability arising from their use.
The Utah Teapot was originally created by Martin Newell and went through a number of modifications over the years. It quickly became famous within the graphics community after making its first appearance at SIGGRAPH in 1976. Its extensive use in graphics prompted Arvo and Kirk [1987] to name it the “Teapotahedron” and jokingly call it “the sixth Platonic solid”. It remains one of the standard models for evaluating new computer graphics algorithms and frequently appears in technical papers presented at SIGGRAPH and other graphics conferences. Utah Teapot has also appears in art installations, movies, video games, and a wide range of other graphics applications. Versions of the Utah Teapot model are included in numerous rendering and modeling programs and graphics APIs, among them 3ds Max, Direct3D, Houdini, Modo, OpenGL, POV-Ray, Quartz Composer, and RenderMan. See the Wikipedia page on the Utah Teapot.
Martin Newell, Jim Blinn, and Cem Yuksel tell the story of the Utah Teapot at SIGGRAPH 2026, commemorating the 50th anniversary of the Utah Teapot's first appearance at SIGGRAPH in 1976. The extended abstract of this talk includes additional information: “The Return of the Utah Teapot” (PDF) by Cem Yuksel, Jim Blinn, and Martin Newell.
The Utah Teapot has a number of versions that were developed and released over the years by different people from the University of Utah, as summarized below. Version 1975 is how Martin Newell modeled it. Version 1976 is the scaled down version by Jim Blinn. Version 1987 by Frank Crow adds the round bottom. Version 1992 is the first attempt by Hank Driskill for turning the Teapot into a solid object. Version 2006 by Russ Fish improves the interior shape. Finally, Version 2026 by Cem Yuksel further improves the interior, adds chamfers where the handle and the spout connect to the body, and makes the shape of the Teapot curvature-continuous to achieve reflection continuity.
This is the original version created by Martin Newell, while he was a PhD student at the University of Utah, by approximating the proportions of a physical teapot (Melitta by Friesland Porzellan). It is formed by 28 cubic Bézier patches, which he first drew the control points on an engineering paper. It is one of the first computer graphics object modeled using a set of nonlinear surfaces, rather than a collection of polygons. Notably, Martin Newell's version is taller than the commonly known shape of the famous Utah Teapot, and it has no bottom. This is the model that appeared in his dissertation, titled “The utilization of procedure models in digital image synthesis” in 1975, along with the rest of the tea set he modeled, though he prepared these models earlier, sometime in 1974.
Martin Newell's drawing of the Teapot and the tea set image from his dissertation.
Here is a YouTube video, where Martin Newell, at an event celebrating the 50th anniversary of Computer Science department at the University of Utah, talking about the Teapot model.
Jim Blinn, while he was a PhD student at the University of Utah, scaled Martin Newell's teapot model by 3/4 during a demo. He liked its new shape and kept it that way. In fact, everyone liked this shorter version, including Martin Newell. Since 1976, this version of the teapot appeared in numerous publications, turning it into a symbol of computer graphics.
Utah Teapot was first introduced to the computer graphics community at SIGGRAPH 1976 in an article by Jim Blinn and Martin Newell, titled “Texture and Reflection in Computer Generated Images” (PDF). It was also published in the Communications of the ACM journal and an image from this article, featuring the Utah Teapot with a texture mapped to its patches, was used as the cover of the October 1976 issue.
Jim Blinn explains the components of the teapot and why it was squished in an article titled “What, Teapots Again?” (PDF), published in IEEE Computer Graphics & Applications in September 1987. There, he also suggests adding a flat bottom cap.
The cover of the CACM journal in October 1976, featuring one of the images from Blinn and Newell's paper at SIGGRAPH 1976, and two other images from the same paper with the original pixels computed on PDP-11 (after tone mapping) by Jim Blinn.
Here is a YouTube video, where Jim Blinn, at a reception honoring Ivan Sutherland at SIGGRAPH 2018, explaining why the Utah Teapot model is squished.
The most common version of Utah Teapot that appears in numerous graphics applications is the one released by Frank Crow, who was another PhD graduate of the University of Utah, in an article titled “The Origins of the Teapot” (PDF), published in IEEE Computer Graphics & Applications in January 1987. This article discusses the important role that the Utah Teapot model played in the early days of computer graphics and includes the control points of the scaled model by Jim Blinn. Except that all control points are shifted up just a bit to make room for a round bottom surface, defined by 4 additional Bézier patches. This brings the total number of patches to 32 and the total number of control points to 512.
Crow's figure showing the patch boundaries and the control polygon of the Teapot without its body, but with the bottom that he added.
The handle and the spout patches of the original Utah Teapot model intersect with its body. This was necessary, as it was modeled using cubic Bézier patches. This was also a useful feature for testing various hidden surface removal algorithms that were being developed at the time, and their abilities in rendering intersecting surfaces. Also, because cubic Bézier patches cannot form perfectly circular shapes, the teapot's body was not perfectly round. Perhaps more importantly, it did not contain an interior and a rather visible gap around the lid.
In 1992, Hank Driskill, another PhD student at the University of Utah, addressed all these problems. He used the Alpha_1 software, which was being developed by Professors Elaine Cohen and Rich Riesenfeld and their students/collaborators, and he prepared a trimmed NURBS model of the Utah Teapot, connecting its perfectly round body to its handle and spout, and a new interior surface. Its bottom was flat, as suggested by Jim Blinn, instead of the round bottom that was previously added by Frank Crow. Nonetheless, Hank Driskill's design, titled “Utah, the Next Generation,” featuring this new Utah Teapot (with warp nacelles), won the SIGGRAPH 1992 T-Shirt Contest.

The interior of this version was defined by revolving B-spline curves, resulting in 86 additional patches, so this version of the Utah Teapot has 118 patches in total.
Driskill's Teapot images with his new model and warp nacelles, and the award-winning t-shirt at SIGGRAPH 1992.
The version by Hank Driskill was later improved by Russ Fish, a co-founder and technical lead of the Alpha_1 project at the University of Utah. Russ Fish modeled a new interior with a hollow knob for the lid and presented his “third-generation” teapot at SIGGRAPH 2006 with the title “Teapot Subdivision.” He also released and documented this new and earlier versions of the Utah Teapot. In particular, his solution for generating the interior of the spout is elegant and closely follows the exterior contours prepared by Martin Newell. Similar to Hank Driskill's version, this one also has a flat bottom, rather than the round bottom of Frank Crow's version.
The "Teapot Subdivision" image generated by Russ Fish.
This version forms even more patches to model the interior, resulting in 134 patches in total.
The latest version of the Utah Teapot is prepared by Prof. Cem Yuksel of the University of Utah. This version uses much fewer patches for modeling the Teapot's interior and more closely follows the contours of its exterior. It contains a solid knob for the lid. The spout interior is also slightly modified to ensure that the surface normals are continuous where the tip of the spout meets the interior surface.
The new interior design works with both the round bottom of Frank Crow's model and the flat bottom used by Hank Driskill and Russ Fish. The official version has a round bottom, so that it matches the most commonly used form of the Utah Teapot today.
In addition, this latest version also includes two types of modifications to the exterior surface of the Utah Teapot:
Its original spline models are modified using a new continuity enhancement method to ensure curvature continuity. This ensures that the reflections on the teapot appear smooth, without the sharp changes that appear in the earlier versions. See the SIGGRAPH 2026 paper on this topic by Cem Yuksel, titled “Continuity-Enhancing Degree Elevation and Splits” for more information.
It also includes small chamfers where the spout and the handle meet the Teapot's body, ensuring that the teapot's surface normal is continuous over the exterior surface. The actual physical teapot that Martin Newell used as a reference has much larger chamfers, but adding such larger chamfers would deviate too much from the historical shape of the digital model.
The lightweight interior model of this version only needs 30 additional patches, so the resulting teapot has 62 patches in total.
Cem Yuksel also added texture mapping layouts that can be applied all versions of the Utah Teapot to achieve a bijective or a lower-distortion injective mapping.

articles.title: Retirement Savings Are Fueling the AI Bubble
articles.body:
Are we on the brink of the next financial crisis? Last Thursday, there was a “bloodbath in tech stocks,” as the stock market lost $3.2 trillion in a single day. The media is blaming the “blue wave,” but anxiety about the AI boom was already rising before the election. The week prior, on October 29, the “Magnificent Seven”—the tech companies that have driven much of the stock market’s recent growth—lost nearly a trillion dollars in value. The immediate catalyst for that sell-off was the realization that Google, Amazon, and Meta have all become “cash incinerators,” as their latest earnings reports showed astronomical spending on AI and a growing reliance on borrowing. The question that skeptics have long raised about the data center buildout has suddenly reached a fever pitch: will there actually be enough demand for AI for the companies to cover these massive investments and pay back their loans?
What has yet to enter public consciousness, however, is the extent to which working people’s financial assets have been used to fuel this bubble. Individuals protesting data centers often have no idea that their retirement accounts are being used to finance the companies responsible for these projects. Nor are they aware that they are at risk of being left holding the bag.
As “private” credit and equity funds have become a new center of gravity in financial markets, our public pension fund systems have increasingly allocated the retirement savings of public sector workers to these opaque, unregulated institutions. Similarly, thanks to recent efforts by the Trump administration, the $15 trillion held in private sector workers’ retirement accounts is now, for the first time in history, available to be invested in private funds. And it is to these funds that the companies building out data centers (and the gas plants necessary to power them) have turned for financing. According to a new report from Americans for Financial Reform, for instance, private equity firms are behind 25-30% of data center financing. By putting our retirement chips in their basket, we are bound up in the risks that these companies are taking in the AI boom—even though they do not have to disclose those risks to us.
What are those risks? While the AI bubble is not, thankfully, built on an edifice of predatory mortgages, the complexity and scale of the loans made to data center operators and Big Tech is giving many people painful flashbacks to 2008. As the credit ratings agency S&P stated plainly in September, “the credit quality of hyperscalers is weakening,” due to the projected $7 trillion in spending by 2030, much of which has to be financed by debt. That deterioration is already appearing in credit markets. Sales of the infamous credit default swaps (CDS) are quickly increasing: more than $9 billion of CDS linked to Big Tech bonds was traded weekly in September, and they’re getting more expensive as there is more demand for the protection they offer. All of the financial transactions involved in building data centers are also increasingly correlated due to the dense web of financing and customer relationships in the sector, as well as the complexity of financing relationships in many data center projects. As S&P states, “if demand disappoints, chip values fall, or data center utilization declines, do the losses sit with the operator, the sponsor or the guarantor?”
These risks are complicated by last week’s election. Voters overwhelmingly rejected the construction of data centers—electing governors in Texas, Georgia, and New Mexico who have committed to some form of data center slowdown or moratorium, while approving nearly every ballot measure that called for data center moratoria or slowdowns. According to Axios, Texas was projected to account for nearly half of the data center buildout in 2028. Gina Hinojosa’s victory over Greg Abbott just changed the whole trajectory of the industry. Elon Musk, as the results came in, observed that “data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.” This is an excellent outcome—not least because it may prompt some companies to revise their projected data center buildout—yet it does not wipe away the mountain of debt that has already accumulated, nor the risk that these debts will become unpayable.
The risk of financial collapse is not, at the end of the day, the most damaging part of the AI buildout. Yet it is the aspect over which pension fund trustees and people saving for retirement have the most control—we can demand that our pensions refrain from holding risky, unregulated financial assets linked to the data center boom, as some public pension fund trustees have started to do. Employees can demand that their employer find an asset manager that will not move their funds into unregulated financial assets. Note, however, that this will require more than shifting our portfolios “back” towards holding index funds that buy the tech-heavy stock market. As SpaceX becomes part of the S&P 500, and Anthropic and OpenAI become publicly traded, the stock markets will only get more AI-pilled.
In the longer term, with enough political will, we can redirect our retirement savings towards productive investment, such as building out affordable housing and funding the renewable energy transition. For example, NYC Comptroller Mark Levine announced a $4 billion affordable housing initiative in April. Pension fund trustees could follow his lead rather than direct money towards Blackstone, one of the country’s largest landlords and a major fund manager for public pensions. More ambitiously, as I’ve written elsewhere, the government should establish public asset managers and a public credit fund to change the structure of how public pension funds are deployed. We do not need to act as if pension funds and retirement accounts are being directed into the AI bubble by the invisible hand of the market: portfolio allocation choices are, in the context of this complicated disaster, some of the easiest places to apply pressure.
Recently, Michael Burry, the hedge fund manager made famous by Michael Lewis’ The Big Short, said “all the capital being spent and lent by the richest companies on Earth won’t be enough to keep the bubble from eventually bursting.” One of the most galling claims after the Great Financial Crisis was that no one could have seen it coming. This time, at least, it is staring us right in the face.

articles.title: AWS Emulator and the engineer's job when agents write the code
articles.body:
AWS Emulator and the engineer's job when agents write the code
In 2004, barely a month into my new job at Amazon, I got the opportunity to pick an intern to join my team. I had an advantage over my colleagues: I had already heard about a brilliant young man working toward his PhD at the Vrije Universiteit in Amsterdam (where I happened to have received mine as well :-)). I immediately picked Swaminathan Sivasubramanian, whom you all now know as Swami. It was probably one of the best decisions I have made in my 22 years as Amazon’s CTO.
After a disastrous Christmas in 2004, when commercial relational databases could not scale to Amazon’s needs, I asked Swami to do a deep dive into how relational databases were actually used at Amazon. It turned out that 70% of database operations were not relational at all. They were key-value. That insight led to Dynamo, which Swami helped architect. When his internship was over, I hired him full-time right away, even before he had finished his PhD.
Bringing in another opinionated academic led to many fantastic discussions with Amazon’s practical engineers, who had become scale experts by actually building at scale. Eventual vs. strong consistency, CAP vs. Paxos, and more. Over time, Swami became one of the principal architects of AWS’s data strategy. And as we have seen in recent years, he has also been one of the intellectual drivers behind AI innovation at Amazon.
I am honoured that he wanted to write a guest post about the fundamental distributed systems work that sits behind many of AWS’s services, and about how the engineer’s work changes when agents write the code. AWS Emulator, launched today, gives agents the kind of test environment that work relied on. Swami’s story is another great example of invisible engineering.
Now, go build.
-W
AWS Emulator and the engineer's job when agents write the code
Today we release AWS Emulator, which gives coding agents a local copy of AWS to test against, and it connects to a project from early in my career. In many ways, this emulator launch reminds me of the effort we put into reliable software engineering to improve the quality of the distributed systems we build. To that end, we wanted to share a story:
About twenty years ago, Werner asked me to work with one of Amazon’s earliest engineers, Al Vermeulen, on a distributed lock service we called “Alf”. Alf was built on Paxos, a protocol based on Leslie Lamport’s work that lets a group of servers agree on one value, and a replication engine in it kept copies of the data consistent across servers. Alf, to date, is the service that powers many of our complex distributed systems like S3, DynamoDB and many more (although it has evolved quite a bit with various changes on top – will save it for another blog!).
Distributed systems are hard to test
Paxos is the gold standard among distributed systems consensus protocols and was well understood in academia. However, building it at the scale Amazon and AWS were growing into was not easy. We had to deal with not just replication across servers and data centers but also tens of thousands of clients asking for locks at the same time, renewing their leases during network partitions all the while with the core requirement: Always be correct! At that time, the best ideas for testing distributed systems were large-scale system testing and chaos-based testing. Both worked, but they were expensive, and they could not reproduce many kinds of conditions on demand. That mattered for Alf, which was meant to be the truth store, giving every client a strongly consistent view of the truth, and which had to keep working through server failures and packet loss as well. Several industry papers had written that Paxos-based locking services were hard to get right, and the difficulty of testing them was part of the reason.
We addressed that by simulating Alf’s environment with as much fidelity as we could manage. We ran the servers inside a JVM and simulated the network and the rest of the infrastructure they depended on, so the whole system lived in one program that we controlled. We could drop packets and inject other faults whenever we chose, and we built tools that poked at the simulation for bugs and scalability problems. Concurrency bugs appear only when events happen in a particular order, and in the simulation we could set up many of those orderings on purpose and inspect how Alf handled each one. We also used formal reasoning, through theoretical techniques such as TLA+, and it found many issues as well. By testing this way we ironed out most of Alf’s concurrency bugs before it ran on real servers. Testing in a real environment then turned up different problems, because the real world exposes things a simulation cannot.
Outgrowing hand-built test environments
Simulation and formal reasoning both improved the software quality of the distributed systems we applied them to. The simulation worked because a small team could build a copy of one system’s environment by hand, and at the time AWS had only a small handful of services. But today AWS has over 200 services, and an application that calls AWS needs a test environment for each one it uses. Building all of those by hand would take years of engineering, and agents now write code far faster than any team can check it in production. So, we wanted to know whether agents could build and test those environments themselves.
The idea came from Matt Goldberg, a Senior Principal Engineer on the AWS Developer Tools team. His hypothesis was that, given a written description of how a service should behave and the real service to check against, an agent could build a working version of that service on its own. For AWS, the written description is the set of public API models, written in Smithy, AWS’s format for describing a service’s operations and their inputs, outputs, and errors. The real service to check against is the AWS cloud itself, the same system customers use.
The agents work from fidelity tests, which are end-to-end customer scenarios devised from the public API models. A test might check, for example, that in Amazon Simple Queue Service a received message stays hidden from other readers until its visibility timeout runs out. The agents correct each test until it passes against real AWS, so the test records how AWS behaves. The agents then build the emulator until it passes that same test, and a test that still fails points at a gap in the emulator. Matt began with SQS alone, and when he gave Kiro one prompt describing this approach, it returned a passable first version of an SQS emulator in about 15 minutes. Matt Goldberg’s launch post tells how that prototype grew into AWS Emulator. All of AWS Emulator’s code was written and tested by agents, and it is built from more than 400 API models covering more than 200 AWS services. It runs free and offline on your own machine. Teams of agents test it against real AWS and fix the gaps they find. Every change goes through a merge gate, a deep bench of automated checks that every change must pass before it enters the codebase, including several security agents doing adversarial reviews.
Infrastructure in the coding loop
A coding agent works in a loop: it writes code, runs it, and reads the result before deciding what to change next. In distributed systems that loop runs inside infrastructure, so the services it calls have to behave like the real ones. When they do, an agent can check its own work as it writes and produce correct code on its first attempt far more often, which improves software quality. AWS Emulator puts that infrastructure inside the loop on your own machine.
The engineer’s job when agents write the code
When agents write the code and check their own work, the engineer’s job is to give them room to work on their own and to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when that work is correct. It was a lesson I learned the hard way when I used Kiro to rebuild the replication engine that Al and I had built for Alf, which took us about four months the first time. I supervised the agent for four nights before I saw that it had no way to check its results. Once it had a spec and a test environment, the rebuild took about two hours.
The agents building AWS Emulator had both from the start, in the public API models and in real AWS. An engineer built the scaffolding that runs them. An internal version came together over a weekend and started gaining adoption within a month. Turning that into a robust solution took much more work.
Software quality in the AI era depends on the guardrails that engineers design around agents. In AWS Emulator, those guardrails are the fidelity tests verified against real AWS, a merge gate with multiple security agents that each review a change for different ways to attack it alongside a general code reviewer, and deterministic checks that stop agents from touching code they are not supposed to. We expect agents to build and check most software, with engineers deciding what gets built and when the work is correct. We are early in learning how engineers drive teams of agents to build reliable, high-quality software, and the way AWS Emulator came to life is a good example of how that works in practice. We expect to keep adding guardrails and refining how the agents build it.
What to know at launch
The emulator code is released under CC0, a Creative Commons dedication to the public domain.
We will share more about this work at re:Invent. The full commit history and every issue the agents have filed are public in the GitHub repository, and its “things-that-do-not-work” folder holds the issues describing behaviors the agents found that do not yet match real AWS.

articles.title: AWS Emulator and the engineer's job when agents write the code
articles.body:
AWS Emulator and the engineer's job when agents write the code
In 2004, barely a month into my new job at Amazon, I got the opportunity to pick an intern to join my team. I had an advantage over my colleagues: I had already heard about a brilliant young man working toward his PhD at the Vrije Universiteit in Amsterdam (where I happened to have received mine as well :-)). I immediately picked Swaminathan Sivasubramanian, whom you all now know as Swami. It was probably one of the best decisions I have made in my 22 years as Amazon’s CTO.
After a disastrous Christmas in 2004, when commercial relational databases could not scale to Amazon’s needs, I asked Swami to do a deep dive into how relational databases were actually used at Amazon. It turned out that 70% of database operations were not relational at all. They were key-value. That insight led to Dynamo, which Swami helped architect. When his internship was over, I hired him full-time right away, even before he had finished his PhD.
Bringing in another opinionated academic led to many fantastic discussions with Amazon’s practical engineers, who had become scale experts by actually building at scale. Eventual vs. strong consistency, CAP vs. Paxos, and more. Over time, Swami became one of the principal architects of AWS’s data strategy. And as we have seen in recent years, he has also been one of the intellectual drivers behind AI innovation at Amazon.
I am honoured that he wanted to write a guest post about the fundamental distributed systems work that sits behind many of AWS’s services, and about how the engineer’s work changes when agents write the code. AWS Emulator, launched today, gives agents the kind of test environment that work relied on. Swami’s story is another great example of invisible engineering.
Now, go build.
-W
AWS Emulator and the engineer's job when agents write the code
Today we release AWS Emulator, which gives coding agents a local copy of AWS to test against, and it connects to a project from early in my career. In many ways, this emulator launch reminds me of the effort we put into reliable software engineering to improve the quality of the distributed systems we build. To that end, we wanted to share a story:
About twenty years ago, Werner asked me to work with one of Amazon’s earliest engineers, Al Vermeulen, on a distributed lock service we called “Alf”. Alf was built on Paxos, a protocol based on Leslie Lamport’s work that lets a group of servers agree on one value, and a replication engine in it kept copies of the data consistent across servers. Alf, to date, is the service that powers many of our complex distributed systems like S3, DynamoDB and many more (although it has evolved quite a bit with various changes on top – will save it for another blog!).
Distributed systems are hard to test
Paxos is the gold standard among distributed systems consensus protocols and was well understood in academia. However, building it at the scale Amazon and AWS were growing into was not easy. We had to deal with not just replication across servers and data centers but also tens of thousands of clients asking for locks at the same time, renewing their leases during network partitions all the while with the core requirement: Always be correct! At that time, the best ideas for testing distributed systems were large-scale system testing and chaos-based testing. Both worked, but they were expensive, and they could not reproduce many kinds of conditions on demand. That mattered for Alf, which was meant to be the truth store, giving every client a strongly consistent view of the truth, and which had to keep working through server failures and packet loss as well. Several industry papers had written that Paxos-based locking services were hard to get right, and the difficulty of testing them was part of the reason.
We addressed that by simulating Alf’s environment with as much fidelity as we could manage. We ran the servers inside a JVM and simulated the network and the rest of the infrastructure they depended on, so the whole system lived in one program that we controlled. We could drop packets and inject other faults whenever we chose, and we built tools that poked at the simulation for bugs and scalability problems. Concurrency bugs appear only when events happen in a particular order, and in the simulation we could set up many of those orderings on purpose and inspect how Alf handled each one. We also used formal reasoning, through theoretical techniques such as TLA+, and it found many issues as well. By testing this way we ironed out most of Alf’s concurrency bugs before it ran on real servers. Testing in a real environment then turned up different problems, because the real world exposes things a simulation cannot.
Outgrowing hand-built test environments
Simulation and formal reasoning both improved the software quality of the distributed systems we applied them to. The simulation worked because a small team could build a copy of one system’s environment by hand, and at the time AWS had only a small handful of services. But today AWS has over 200 services, and an application that calls AWS needs a test environment for each one it uses. Building all of those by hand would take years of engineering, and agents now write code far faster than any team can check it in production. So, we wanted to know whether agents could build and test those environments themselves.
The idea came from Matt Goldberg, a Senior Principal Engineer on the AWS Developer Tools team. His hypothesis was that, given a written description of how a service should behave and the real service to check against, an agent could build a working version of that service on its own. For AWS, the written description is the set of public API models, written in Smithy, AWS’s format for describing a service’s operations and their inputs, outputs, and errors. The real service to check against is the AWS cloud itself, the same system customers use.
The agents work from fidelity tests, which are end-to-end customer scenarios devised from the public API models. A test might check, for example, that in Amazon Simple Queue Service a received message stays hidden from other readers until its visibility timeout runs out. The agents correct each test until it passes against real AWS, so the test records how AWS behaves. The agents then build the emulator until it passes that same test, and a test that still fails points at a gap in the emulator. Matt began with SQS alone, and when he gave Kiro one prompt describing this approach, it returned a passable first version of an SQS emulator in about 15 minutes. Matt Goldberg’s launch post tells how that prototype grew into AWS Emulator. All of AWS Emulator’s code was written and tested by agents, and it is built from more than 400 API models covering more than 200 AWS services. It runs free and offline on your own machine. Teams of agents test it against real AWS and fix the gaps they find. Every change goes through a merge gate, a deep bench of automated checks that every change must pass before it enters the codebase, including several security agents doing adversarial reviews.
Infrastructure in the coding loop
A coding agent works in a loop: it writes code, runs it, and reads the result before deciding what to change next. In distributed systems that loop runs inside infrastructure, so the services it calls have to behave like the real ones. When they do, an agent can check its own work as it writes and produce correct code on its first attempt far more often, which improves software quality. AWS Emulator puts that infrastructure inside the loop on your own machine.
The engineer’s job when agents write the code
When agents write the code and check their own work, the engineer’s job is to give them room to work on their own and to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when that work is correct. It was a lesson I learned the hard way when I used Kiro to rebuild the replication engine that Al and I had built for Alf, which took us about four months the first time. I supervised the agent for four nights before I saw that it had no way to check its results. Once it had a spec and a test environment, the rebuild took about two hours.
The agents building AWS Emulator had both from the start, in the public API models and in real AWS. An engineer built the scaffolding that runs them. An internal version came together over a weekend and started gaining adoption within a month. Turning that into a robust solution took much more work.
Software quality in the AI era depends on the guardrails that engineers design around agents. In AWS Emulator, those guardrails are the fidelity tests verified against real AWS, a merge gate with multiple security agents that each review a change for different ways to attack it alongside a general code reviewer, and deterministic checks that stop agents from touching code they are not supposed to. We expect agents to build and check most software, with engineers deciding what gets built and when the work is correct. We are early in learning how engineers drive teams of agents to build reliable, high-quality software, and the way AWS Emulator came to life is a good example of how that works in practice.
