articles.title: United Airlines Bans AI Agents From Booking Flights On Behalf of Travelers
articles.body:
United Airlines Bans AI Agents From Booking Flights On Behalf of Travelers 50
			
		 	
				United Airlines is banning unauthorized third-party AI agents from booking flights, checking in passengers or making account changes on travelers' behalf. CBS News reports:  To make an airline booking, an AI agent requires access to a customer's personal information, including credentials like payment information. United has a problem with that, saying that "sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles."
The carrier also said that using an AI agent to, for example, check in for a flight could violate federal regulations, including rules requiring travelers to verify in person that their luggage does not contain banned substances. "As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access -- directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators -- to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants," said the airline, which is updating its booking and ticketing policies to reflect the new rule.  "United is saying they don't want to add yet another, and potentially even more powerful, intermediary than they already face in terms of Google search, price-comparison metasearch sites and online travel agencies," said Henry Harteveldt, an aviation analyst at Atmosphere Research Group. "Flight searches cost airlines money, and undoubtedly United wants to avoid the expense associated with the surge of AI bot flight searches."

articles.title: Loot boxes, influencers, and addictive features face an EU crackdown
articles.body:
Gaming, social media, and e-commerce platforms are facing a fresh wave of sweeping European Union rules that aim to make “your online experience fairer.” The newly proposed Digital Fairness Act (DFA) published by the EU Commission on Wednesday is designed to tackle practices that exploit consumers into spending more of their time and money online, including misleading prices or availability, addictive design features like gaming loot boxes, undisclosed influencer marketing, and more.
Loot boxes, influencers, and addictive features face an EU crackdown
The proposed Digital Fairness Act seeks to bolster consumer protections for online users.
“The Act will protect consumers of all ages shopping and browsing for goods or services online,” the EU Commission said in a news bulletin. “It will also mean fairer competition for businesses, which are expecting to save EU consumers up to €13.7 billion ($15.1 billion) a year.”
Here’s an overview of what the DFA proposal includes:
- A ban on manipulative marketing practices and so-called “dark patterns” that push consumers into making decisions they might not otherwise make, such as fake claims about a product almost being sold out.
- A requirement to give consumers the choice to turn off addictive features, such as persistent prompts, endless scrolling, and autoplay of videos. Restrictions around addictive design also apply to “AI companions and general conversational chatbots.”
- Restrictions on unfair practices that encourage overspending, such as banning gambling-like features (pay-to-win and pay-to-progress, for example) for minors.
- Requiring influencers to clearly disclose advertising content, and restrictions to prevent them from exploiting the trust of children.
- Restrictions on unfair personalised ads and prices that target minors or take advantage of sensitive data.
- Making subscriptions and digital contracts easier to cancel, with prompts to remind customers about upcoming automatic renewals and free trial periods coming to an end.
- Requiring clear and transparent pricing, especially around dynamic pricing and purchases using virtual in-app currency. When consumers wait in virtual queues for cultural and sports event tickets, companies will have to show the current price in real time and at the highest possible price.
- Giving consumers the right to communicate with a human customer service representative, and clear rights using an AI agent to make purchases.
The scope of the restrictions being proposed is broad, and could have a significant impact on major parts of the online digital landscape, from the “rabbit hole” algorithms across YouTube, TikTok, and Meta platforms, to AI chatbots and apps like DuoLingo that relentlessly nudge users to keep interacting with them. Some gaming organizations have already slammed the DFA proposal, describing its restrictions around virtual currencies, loot boxes, and offering micro-transactions to minors as being “unworkable, unjustified and disproportionate.”
Given this is a draft proposal, the DFA will undergo various approvals through the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union before being passed into law, and its current measures could be changed or removed entirely as part of that process. When (or if) it does come into force, the EU Commission says companies who violate the regulations could see fines of up to six percent of their worldwide annual turnover.
“Our consumer protection rules will help ensure that businesses compete on the merits of their products and services - not on their ability to exploit consumers or evade the rules. We are not making it harder to do business. We are making it harder to do business unfairly,” EU Commissioner Michael McGrath said in remarks following the DFA draft publication. “We cannot have 21st-century consumers protected by rules that have not kept pace with the 21st-century economy.”

articles.title: Toyota’s Scion is back, starting with an American-made, 25-mph kei truck
articles.body:
Toyota is dusting off the Scion badge for a radically different mission. Rather than targeting youth-market hatchbacks, “Scion by Toyota” is being positioned as an experimental mobility incubator — and its first vehicle is an authentic Japanese-style kei truck built in Indiana.
Toyota’s Scion is back, starting with an American-made, 25-mph kei truck
Toyota is reviving the Scion badge as an experimental mobility incubator—starting with an Indiana-built, 25-mph kei truck engineered for American fleets.
Kei vehicles, which are built to satisfy Japan’s light vehicle regulations, are enjoying surging popularity around the world, including here in the US. More than 30,000 used kei trucks have been imported into the US since 2020, with roughly 7,500 units entering the country each year. Even President Trump is a fan, telling reporters last year that he authorized the Department of Transportation to approve their production.
Toyota looks to be the first to test the American market’s appetite for the tiny trucks. The choice to use the Scion brand, which was discontinued in 2016, would seem to indicate that the automaker is hoping to appeal to younger car buyers. But more than that, Toyota says it sees Scion as a testing ground for utility, outdoor adventure, and customization that wouldn’t typically fit in any of its other models.
When it lands in the second half of 2027, Scion’s KEI-01 sports a 660cc three-cylinder gas engine paired with a continuously variable transmission. It won’t win any drag races, but it should delivery enough power for stop-and-go driving while using a minimum amount of fuel.
It’s true super power comes from its diminutive dimensions. At roughly 11 feet long and under 5 feet wide, the KEI-01 is about half the footprint of a full-size pickup. It can easily thread through cramped alleys, narrow barn aisles, garden gates, or busy campus pathways where standard trucks can’t fit.
The truck features an on-demand 4WD system with a push-button locking mode. If you’re cutting across muddy farm turf, gravel work paths, or wet slush, power splits to all four wheels to keep the truck from spinning out or getting stuck.
Inside, the vehicle looks pretty cheap, with lots of black plastic and a noticeable absence of any premium materials. That will hopefully help keep the price nice and low — though Toyota hasn’t disclosed any trim options yet. Japanese imports typically range from $6,000 to $12,000.
Because it is certified under federal Low-Speed Vehicle (LSV) rules — also used for golf carts and golf cart-adjacent vehicles — its top speed is strictly capped at 25 mph. The truck bed features three sides that fold completely flat, removing the need to lean over high-metal sides to drop in cargo. The KEI-01 can hold up to 600 pounds of soil, tools, or gear, and can easily tow small utility trailers or mowers.
Unlike an open utility cart or ATV, this tiny truck has a fully sealed cabin equipped with both heating and air conditioning. The extended roofline gives drivers extra headroom, reclining seats, and interior storage behind the seats to keep tools dry and secure. True to classic Japanese utility imports, the steering wheel is on the right side of the cab. Beyond the cool factor, curbside delivery and stepping directly onto sidewalks or worksite shoulders is quicker and safer.
To make the KEI-01 to conform to the rules and regs of auto manufacturing in the US, Toyota is investing $34 million into its Princeton, Indiana manufacturing plant to stand up local assembly and add roughly 50 jobs. Production kicks off in the second half of 2027, but everyday drivers won’t be able to buy one off the lot immediately.
Scion by Toyota is launching the mini-truck strictly as a fleet-focused pilot program targeting corporate campuses, farms, municipalities, and local delivery operators, distributed through a specialized group of existing Toyota dealerships. While Toyota notes it may consider opening up sales to consumer retail down the road if demand justifies it, the initial rollout is very much treated as an experiment to evaluate real-world US utility.
The KEI-01 was joined by two adventure-themed concepts that show Scion’s new focus extends far beyond budget hatchbacks. The SxS Concept packs a 300-plus-horsepower hybrid turbo setup for high-speed off-roading, while the modular BKE Concept explores compact personal mobility. Together, they signal that Scion’s second act is aimed squarely at niche utility and experimental recreation.
Images by Toyota

articles.title: Modern Web Guidance 1.0: The web platform expertise your coding agent is missing
articles.body:
Published: November 10, 2026
In this new era of agentic web development, developers expect their coding agents to be experts at building for the web. And while the latest frontier coding models are quite capable and can usually produce something that works, if you ask a web development expert to review the AI-generated code, they can almost always find ways to make the code faster, more accessible, or more secure.
Chrome is investing heavily in the future of agentic web development, and to address this challenge, we introduced an early preview of Modern Web Guidance at Google I/O in May. Modern Web Guidance is a set of skills that embed web platform expertise, best practices, and browser compatibility data directly into your coding agents.
Today we're excited to announce the stable release of Modern Web Guidance version 1.0, which includes:
- New modernization workflow that scans your existing codebase to help your agent find opportunities to safely modernize.
- Expanded guide database targeting hundreds of verified AI knowledge gaps with expert-vetted, cross-browser solutions.
- Deeper human expert review for every guide, including sign-off from content area tech leads and a dedicated accessibility review on our user-facing guides.
- Full evaluation coverage across all of our guides with a public eval dashboard showing the measurable improvements compared to agents without Modern Web Guidance.
With version 1.0, we're also excited to share that Modern Web Guidance is becoming a cross-browser effort, with Firefox and Edge joining Chrome to support, improve cross-browser compatibility, and contribute to the project. Building on our shared work with Baseline, our goal is to ensure that anyone coding with an agent can take full advantage of the power and capabilities of the modern web platform.
Regardless of what models or agent harnesses you're using, if you're building for the web, Modern Web Guidance belongs in your agentic workflow.
To install Modern Web Guidance, run this command from your project directory:
npx modern-web-guidance@latest install
Or if you already installed an earlier version, you can update to 1.0 by running:
npx modern-web-guidance@latest update
For additional installation instructions or to learn more, check out the Modern Web Guidance documentation, or watch this video for a brief overview:
Why developers and businesses should use Modern Web Guidance
It's undeniable that coding agents have helped developers write code faster than ever before. But in a world where everyone is using coding agents, speed is no longer a competitive advantage.
These days, it's more important than ever to differentiate on fundamental factors like usability and quality of experience. Here are a few ways Modern Web Guidance can help:
Reinforce best practices that models often miss
While frontier coding models do have a good grasp on many best practices, our evals show that there are still a number of important areas where they fall short, such as:
- Accessibility: Keyboard focus and inert management, reduced-motion support, and accessible form validation.
- User experience: Swipe and touch gestures, dialog and popover transitions, and light/dark theme implementations.
- Performance: Main-thread task scheduling, offscreen rendering isolation, and layout shift prevention.
- Security: Safe HTML sanitization, strict Content Security Policies, and passkey credential management.
Accessibility best practices are particularly important to get right because mistakes like bad ARIA can make a page less accessible than no ARIA at all. For version 1.0, our user-facing guides were reviewed and tested with real assistive technologies by accessibility experts who rely on them every day.
For a deeper look at the specific mistakes models make in each of these areas, read Top 10 things AI gets wrong in web development.
Use the best web feature for the job
AI models are very good at figuring out how to make something work with JavaScript, but in many cases, there are HTML or CSS features that can do the same thing with much less code. And since they're handled by the browser, they usually perform better and come with accessibility affordances. For example:
- Features to animate popovers and dialogs
- Features to enhance scroll- and swipe-based interactions
- Better APIs for smooth and fluid page transitions
New features can also improve the experience of a site in ways that matter to users. For example:
- Passkeys and WebAuthn: For faster and more secure login experiences
- Autofill: To improve checkout flows (especially on mobile) that often fail when using custom JavaScript-based form controls
Modern Web Guidance is designed to recommend the best feature for the job, based on your browser support requirements. Its guides have embedded Baseline and browser compatibility data, so it can tailor its recommendations to your project's needs.
Scan your codebase and find opportunities to modernize
Most web development doesn't happen in brand-new projects. It happens in existing codebases that have accumulated years of outdated workarounds, unnecessary dependencies, and polyfills that are no longer needed.
Version 1.0 adds a new modernization workflow that can analyze your existing HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and package.json to find opportunities to safely upgrade, and then guide your agent through the changes.
/modern-web-guidance Modernize the code in this directory
In this first release, the modernization workflow uses static analysis to check for a limited set of patterns. We chose to start with a narrow scope that yields predictable results, and then expand from there. Over time, we plan to cover many more areas, including agentic audits where your agent reasons about your code directly instead of just matching known patterns.
Stay up to date as the web platform evolves
The web platform is a moving target. New features ship in browsers every milestone, and existing features that you perhaps couldn't use before are becoming Baseline with each new browser release.
Since Modern Web Guidance is built on top of Baseline compatibility data, and its recommendations are maintained by browser engineers, web standards experts, and accessibility specialists, these recommendations evolve along with the platform itself, and now your project can too.
Learn about new web features and best practices
While Modern Web Guidance is primarily built as a tool for agents, one thing we've heard from many developers is that they've actually found the guidance to be quite useful on its own—as a learning resource.
Even in this era of agentic coding, there's still value in building up domain expertise. And Modern Web Guidance can help you do that: either by reading the guides themselves, or using the CLI to search use cases and discover new techniques that may be relevant to your project.
Pair Modern Web Guidance with Chrome DevTools for agents
In agentic web development, authoring code is only one part of the workflow. You also need to run that code to ensure it works as expected. This is why we recommend developers use Modern Web Guidance along with Chrome DevTools for agents.
- Modern Web Guidance gives your agent the up-front expertise needed to write code following modern best practices.
- Chrome DevTools for agents gives your agent runtime visibility so it can verify, debug, and optimize that code across a wide range of device capabilities, user preferences, and network conditions.
Together these help your agent arrive at a better solution in fewer turns. Next are a few examples of how you can use these tools together to maximize effectiveness:
Optimize until you hit your performance target
Modern Web Guidance can teach your agent how to effectively break up long-running JavaScript tasks that block the main thread, but it can't test your code to see how long those JavaScript tasks actually block the main thread for.
With Chrome DevTools for agents, you can run a performance trace on a simulated low-end CPU to see whether or not you have a problem, and then use the performance advice from Modern Web Guidance to iterate until your code never blocks the main thread for more than 50 milliseconds (so it doesn't contribute to poor INP).
Test and refine your animations
Modern Web Guidance can show your agent how to properly and performantly animate features like modal dialogs, tooltips, and popover menus, but even with this guidance you still need to verify that the animations actually work and look good when used in the context of your full application.
Chrome DevTools for agents can run your code, interact with the page, and take a screen recording of the animation in action. It can then study the recording to ensure both that the animation runs and that it fits the style and feel of the rest of the site.
You can also use Chrome DevTools for agents to verify that when prefers-reduced-motion is set, the component honors the user's preferences.
Cache views without memory leaks
Modern Web Guidance can teach your agent how to make SPA transitions feel instant by rendering and caching views in memory, while also properly hiding them from the accessibility tree.
However, when doing this it's important to ensure you properly clean up unused views to not leak memory if the user stays on the page for a long time. Chrome DevTools for agents has memory debugging tools, so your agent can ensure memory use isn't increasing without bound.
For a closer look at how to use Modern Web Guidance and Chrome DevTools for agents together, check out this video:
Success stories
Engineering teams around the world are already using Modern Web Guidance and Chrome DevTools for agents to improve code quality, speed up delivery, and eliminate manual debugging bottlenecks:
Pensionbazaar and Policybazaar
Pensionbazaar, a new retirement planning platform launched by Indian fintech company Paisabazaar, paired Modern Web Guidance with Chrome DevTools for agents to build and verify new pages, shortening turnaround by more than 90% (from about four days to a few hours) and reducing UI bugs on new screens by over 90%. Its sister platform Policybazaar, one of India's leading insurance platforms with more than 97 million registered customers, used Chrome DevTools for agents to automate performance audits across about 30 high-traffic landing pages, cutting manual auditing effort by 92%:
"For Pensionbazaar, our priority was building quality code from day one to avoid technical debt later. Modern Web Guidance steered our coding agent to adopt modern web standards and performance best practices while respecting our specific browser compatibility targets. This made our frontend code reviews substantially easier and faster, ultimately improving our development turnaround time."
—Aman Soni, Engineering Manager, Policybazaar
WeTV
WeTV, Tencent's international video streaming platform, added an AI coding agent to its CI/CD pipeline that uses Chrome DevTools for agents to diagnose performance regressions and Modern Web Guidance to fix them using modern web platform features. The agent now automatically diagnoses and resolves 90% of failed performance checks, cutting debugging and resolution time by 87% (from four hours to 30 minutes, including manual evaluation):
"The results have been very effective in terms of both speed and quality. The diagnostic insights provided by Chrome DevTools for agents and Modern Web Guidance gave us reliable references for fixing complex layout issues. We perform strict verification after every fix, and the current success rate and stability have significantly improved our release confidence."
—Yangjie Zheng, Head of Engineering, WeTV (Tencent)
note inc.
note inc., one of Japan's largest creator and media platforms with over 90 million monthly active users, used Modern Web Guidance alongside its in-house design system as part of an ongoing effort to modernize its Next.js frontend. Across a 180-run evaluation on its production codebase, Modern Web Guidance raised pass rates on modern web checks from 61% to 94% by steering agents to use native HTML and CSS features instead of custom JavaScript for scroll animations, tooltips, and accordions. It also increased proper LCP image prioritization by 28% across 431 merged PRs:
"Our mission at note is 'Start, and Keep on Creating,' so our platform has to stay fast and accessible for every creator and reader. As more of our code is written with AI coding agents, Modern Web Guidance helps them reach for modern, standards-based solutions instead of falling back on older JavaScript patterns. It also points out details that are easy to miss, such as image loading priority and form accessibility. Combined with our design system, it lets us keep improving note while keeping our UI consistent."
—Takehiko Itabashi, VP of Technology, note inc.
MetaMask
MetaMask, a self-custodial financial platform with more than 100 million downloads across approximately 190 countries, runs Modern Web Guidance as an automated review bot on every pull request to its open source browser extension, configured with just a three-line prompt. In its first five weeks, the bot reviewed roughly 480 pull requests and commented on 64 of them, leading engineers to fix 43 findings (mostly accessibility, HTML semantics, and forms issues that linters don't catch) with a median time of 15 minutes from comment to fix:
"The reviews are really helpful. They've helped surface and get our engineers familiar with modern APIs like Interest invokers and the Popover API. It hasn't increased PR review times, if anything it likely reduced them. The issues MWG caught would have otherwise required a human reviewer familiar with these modern web techniques."
—Francis Nepomuceno, UX Engineer, MetaMask
Ecosystem and community support
Modern Web Guidance started as an initiative within Chrome, but reaching this 1.0 milestone was a collaborative effort with numerous experts across the web community.
Thank you to the content area tech leads overseeing each web platform area, our browser partners at Firefox and Edge, the independent web standards and accessibility experts who authored and tested guides, and all of the open source contributors on GitHub who helped shape this release!
If you spot a gap in what coding agents know about the web, or want to help improve an existing guide, see the contribution guide to get involved.
Get started with Modern Web Guidance
To add Modern Web Guidance to your project, run the CLI installer from your project directory:
npx modern-web-guidance@latest install
Or if you already installed an earlier version, you can update to 1.0 by running:
npx modern-web-guidance@latest update
In addition to the CLI, you can install and update Modern Web Guidance directly through most popular coding agent plugin marketplaces, including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Antigravity, Copilot, WebStorm, Kimi Code, and Grok Build.

articles.title: Critical RCE Vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server
articles.body:
Critical RCE Vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server: Everything You Need To Know
Detect and mitigate CVE-2026-119618, a critical RCE vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server. According to Wiz data, 64% of cloud environments have resources vulnerable to CVE-2026-119618. Immediate patching is advised.
A critical synchronization vulnerability (CVE-2026-119618) has been identified in Apache HTTP Server’s HTTP/2 module (mod_http2). The flaw stems from a concurrent execution race condition within the assign_headers() function when handling shared resources. If successfully exploited, a remote, unauthenticated attacker can corrupt heap memory to achieve arbitrary code execution (RCE).
As of the time of this blog’s publication, no exploit is available and there are no reports of exploitation in the wild.
What is CVE-2026-119618?
CVE-2026-119618 is a critical, high-severity vulnerability involving a race condition in the Apache HTTP Server, which was independently discovered by Anthropic and Google Cloud’s Vulnerability Research Team.
Specifically, the flaw exists within the assign_headers() function of the HTTP/2 module (mod_http2). Due to improper synchronization when executing concurrent threads sharing resources, an attacker can trigger heap corruption. This memory corruption can ultimately be leveraged to achieve RCE on the hosting server, allowing unauthorized threat actors to execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of the web server process.
Wiz Research data: what’s the risk to cloud environments?
In cloud environments, a compromised Apache instance running containerized or virtualized workloads can serve as an entry point for lateral movement, potentially exposing adjacent microservices or cloud metadata endpoints.
According to Wiz data 64% of cloud environments have resources vulnerable to CVE-2026-119618, and 51% of cloud environments have publicly exposed instances. Note that this does not take configuration into account.
Which products are affected?
The vulnerability affects deployments utilizing HTTP/2 capabilities on the Apache HTTP Server within the version ranges outlined in the table below:
Which actions should security teams take?
Security operations and engineering teams should execute the following remediation and mitigation steps:
1. Upgrade Deployments
Upgrade Apache HTTP Server: Update affected installations to Apache HTTP Server version 2.4.71 or later. This release addresses the race condition in assign_headers().
Update Standalone Modules: If managing standalone mod_h2 builds from GitHub, upgrade the module to a version newer than 2.0.42.
2. Implement Temporary Mitigations
If immediate patching is not possible due to operational constraints, temporarily disable HTTP/2 support to eliminate the attack vector.
Edit the configuration file (such as httpd.conf) to restrict active protocols to HTTP/1.1 by removing h2 and h2c references:
# Restrict protocols to HTTP/1.1Protocols http/1.1
Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment.
A threat actor used IAM credentials from Qubole's AWS account to assume integration roles in customer AWS environments. Here's what we observed and how to hunt for it.

articles.title: Jensen Huang Resigns As Nvidia CEO
articles.body:
Jensen Huang Resigns As Nvidia CEO 13
			
		 	
				Jensen Huang has stepped down as CEO of Nvidia after 33 years leading the company, with CFO Colette Kress taking over as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent replacement.
"The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," said board chair Harvey Jones in a release announcing the news.
The abrupt departure follows revelations about Huang's affairs, including one with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes was a Chinese spy. CNBC reports:  Huang, 63, apologized on Sunday for being "unfaithful to my wife," though he provided no details about the affair with businesswoman Alice Huang, who has worked for a Chinese company and Nvidia customer called Megaspeed. Late Wednesday, The New York Times reported that the Nvidia CEO also had a separate affair, this one with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at the chipmaker. Later that afternoon The Times and other outlets reported that Nvidia's board met to discuss the company's future.
Jensen Huang denied allegations that he had compromised national security or Nvidia secrets after reports of the Alice Huang affair. The news sparked concerns that Nvidia knew companies based in Singapore and Malaysia had been evading U.S. export controls in accessing its technology. The board said on Tuesday that it had hired Wachtell Lipton to investigate the intelligence allegations.

articles.title: Nvidia’s stock drops as board reportedly preps to oust CEO Jensen Huang
articles.body:
Nvidia is reportedly planning to oust its co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang, who has led the company for the last 33 years, the Wall Street Journal reports. Sources told the newspaper that the Nvidia board is meeting as soon as Wednesday to determine Huang’s future at the company.
On Sunday, Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair with a woman purported by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy. On Wednesday evening, the New York Times reported that Huang also had an affair with an executive who reports to him.
Nvidia has become one of the most valuable companies in the world as it designs the chips that power the AI boom, but in the midst of Huang’s ongoing scandal, Nvidia stock fell about 8% in after hours trading on Wednesday. The stock is down about 11% in the past five days.
Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said. The company also has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan. According to Bloomberg, Nvidia is working with an outside firm to identify candidates that could potentially replace Huang as CEO.
SpaceXSI CEO Elon Musk late on Wednesday posted on X that hiring Huang “would be an honor.”

articles.title: Whoop just launched a social network
articles.body:
Whoop, the maker of screen-less fitness bands, is launching a social network on Thursday that lets its members follow friends and family and share their health data.
The network, called Whoop Humans, will be rolled out in the Whoop app to members at every membership tier at no extra cost. Members can follow anyone on Whoop and choose what to share, from sleep and recovery to workouts and achievements. Followers can react and comment; members can also attach photos and commentary to their data. It’s all opt-in, CEO Will Ahmed tells us.
Whoop already has a social feature, Teams, which a little more than half its customers use, according to the company. But Teams is built around groups and leaderboards, and everyone in a group sees everyone else’s information.
Humans is meant to be more intimate. Members decide who follows them and who sees what, so a trainer can track a set of clients without the clients seeing one another’s data, for example.
I found myself questioning how much a spouse wants to know about the other’s sleep score when Ahmed mentioned this particular scenario, so I asked him how else beta members used these newer social features. He said the company learned that people were more engaged when someone reported a low recovery score than a nearly perfect one, suggesting that the new feature may be particularly helpful for understanding when someone is struggling and might need attention.
Indeed, Whoop seems to be heading towards medical wellness. Like its most direct rival, Oura, the company is pushing faster and more aggressively into the wellness opportunity that an aging population presents.
Whoop had already added FDA-cleared ECG and atrial fibrillation detection, blood pressure insights, blood testing and medical-record uploads. Asked if older customers are gravitating to Whoop, Ahmed said, without offering specifics, that Whoop has seen “huge growth” among people over 60 over the past 18 months. He also said his was among the first companies accepted into a Medicare program that reimburses qualifying wearables that can show they improve health outcomes, and that it now has Medicare members.
He added that he expects families to be big users of Humans. (You can imagine adult children checking in on aging parents.)
But the company’s efforts to be thought of as the “brand for personal health,” raises questions, naturally, about privacy. Ahmed said members choose which metrics to share, can remove followers, and can switch on “stealth mode” to go dark for a few days without changing their settings. Activities marked sensitive aren’t shared by default, and Ahmed said health alerts and medical information aren’t shared at all. Members can also report any comment or photo that they deem disturbing, and the company said reported content is reviewed.
As for minors, Whoop’s minimum age is 13 for all members (higher in some countries), meaning customers of that age can share their data subject to consents and privacy settings. Asked whether a parent could follow a teenager’s data, he didn’t answer directly and pointed to the privacy controls.
Ahmed also said Whoop doesn’t sell member data. “Our product is not you; it’s the membership,” he said, adding that the company doesn’t license data to third parties.
He was candid about dealmaking. Asked about Oura’s announcement this week that it will pay $625 million for Counsel Health, a service offering on-demand physicians, Ahmed said he expects “more consolidation” among AI-focused, clinician-focused and wearable companies, and that Whoop is always on the prowl. Its deep relationship with members, he said, puts it “in a position to be an acquirer.”
He was more guarded about the company’s own finances, declining to share revenue or say whether Whoop is profitable. He did say that the company now has about 1,200 employees, membership on its software platform has increased more than 70% a year for three years running, and that it expects to have nearly 4 million members by year-end.
As for an IPO (the company raised a very big round earlier this year), he said only that Whoop “will certainly IPO in the future.” He also wouldn’t comment on Oura, which shelved its own IPO of up to $2.2 billion in September citing market uncertainty.
In the meantime, Whoop is widening its reach. The company announced that its devices will be sold through Ulta stores beginning next March (around 500 locations of the beauty retailer to start, and a target to retail in more than a thousand stores eventually). Indeed, Ahmed said Whoop’s female audience has more than doubled from last year.
As for competition, in addition to Google’s new Fitbit Air band, Whoop may soon have to contend with Apple, which is reportedly developing a Whoop-style band. But Ahmed mostly shrugged those concerns off, suggesting that building a product doesn’t guarantee success. Instead, he said, Whoop’s job is to stay true to the “aspiring” people it serves.

articles.title: I'm making LLMs work on small and old devices
articles.body:
Every device around you is more capable than it looks. TV boxes, old phones, single-board computers and routers all ship with CPUs, RAM and flash that sit idle most of the day. smolmaxxing is about unlocking that capability: finding the biggest language model each device can really run, then pushing it further with custom kernels, smarter memory use and weight streaming. Every claim is measured on the hardware itself.
Device #1 is a Xiaomi TV Box S (3rd Gen): Amlogic S7D, 4× Cortex-A55 @ 2.5 GHz, 1.9 GB of RAM (about 1 GB usable), eMMC flash, Android 14, no root. On it, this repo runs models from 260 K to 16 B parameters:
- Qwen3.5-0.8B: 16.8 tok/s (2.2× the stock 7.5; measured in the evening of 11-05, see §17).
- Qwen3.5-2B: 7.7 tok/s in real chat. The box's speed drifts by ~10 % over a day, so every step is measured back to back: §16 gave +11 %, §17 another +7 %.
- An 8B mixture-of-experts model (Moon-Beam-8B-A1B): 7.2 tok/s in real chat, its experts paged from flash on demand and prefetched one layer ahead (§19).
- A dense 1-bit 8B model (Bonsai-8B): 5.2 tok/s in real chat, up from 1.2: fully resident in a "headless" mode plus a lookup-table kernel (§19).
- A 16B mixture-of-experts model (Ling-mini-2.0): 5.1 tok/s in real chat, coherent over 600-word answers, the same expert pager applied unchanged (§20). Twice Moon-Beam's size, but not better per byte: bigger only helps on this box when the model is also better.
- A dense 9B model: 0.27 tok/s, streaming most of its weights from flash.
Device #2 is a first-generation iPad Air (2013): Apple A7, 2 cores, NEON without dotprod, 1 GB of RAM, iOS 12.5.7, jailbroken, CPU only. A 13-year-old tablet runs a 1.7B-parameter model at 24-26 tok/s (18-22 in long chats), a 4B one at about 10 tok/s, an 8B mixture of experts at about 3.5 tok/s (5 with half its experts, at a quality cost), and a 16B one at 2.6-4.5 tok/s, with their experts paged from flash, from a chat page in its own Safari. See Results on device #2.
Every step is written up experiment by experiment in EXPERIMENT.md (E1-E160).
The techniques aren't tied to one box. The 1-bit lookup-table kernel needs only base NEON, as the iPad shows; any ARM chip with dotprod gets the other kernels; and any Linux or Android device with more model than RAM can use the streaming engine.
"First run" is the first time each model ran on the box:
- 0.8B: the stock Q4_K_M file.
- 2B: the stock file, streamed from flash because it didn't fit in RAM. Its first build that fit ran at 4.8, so from there the gain is ×1.6.
- 4B: the stock file, which thrashed.
- 8B dense: the last 0.1 GB streamed from flash.
- 8B MoE: the first expert-pager run, without routing bias.
- 9B: streamed.
- 16B: started on the Moon-Beam recipe, so its gain is small.
On this box, the 2B is the best speed-quality balance. Ling-mini-2.0 shows that bigger isn't automatically better: it is twice Moon-Beam's size, but scores worse per byte and runs slower.
What we built, grouped by the bottleneck it attacks (details and numbers in What's in here):
Quality is English perplexity on a fixed 22 KB text, converted to bits per byte so models with different tokenizers compare fairly (lower is better). Speed is generation on the TV, measured either through llama-server with real chat requests ("chat") or with llama-bench ("bench").
* measured on the pruned head's positions (1.3 % of tokens fall outside it), so not exactly comparable; the stock full-vocabulary Q4_0 file scores 1.024.
Other small models, stock files (screening, §15 E54):
Granite 4.0 H 1B was the one model close to the 2B's quality. Rebuilt our way (E62), it runs at 5.29 tok/s, below the 2B's 6.55 at slightly lower quality: it carries about twice the 0.8B's weight bytes per token.
Physics of the box: one process can hold ~0.96 GB before Android starts killing things (~1.15 GB in headless mode, with the launchers and Google services force-stopped), and flash reads top out at 278 MB/s, with a lone ~1 MB random read costing ~6 ms. A model that has to stream X MB per token can never beat 278 / X tokens per second. That, not the CPU, is what limits everything above 2B, and why a mixture-of-experts model, which touches ~1 B of its 8 B weights per token, is the way past it.
10 tok/s at 8 B? Measured, not guessed (E98): Moon-Beam reaches 10.4 tok/s with 2 experts per token, but the text turns to gibberish; the best coherent setting is ~7-8 tok/s. Dense Qwen3-8B is Bonsai-8B at 1 bit, and the smallest Qwen MoE (35B-A3B) touches 3× Moon-Beam's weights per token.
A 2013 iPad Air: Apple A7, 2 cores, NEON without dotprod, 1 GB of RAM, iOS 12.5.7, jailbroken with Amethyst. Everything runs on the CPU with 2 threads and a 1,024-token context, cross-compiled from a Mac. The write-up is §21 of EXPERIMENT.md, and build steps are in ipad-air/README.md.
Only the Bonsai and Moon-Beam rows were measured on the latest build. The other rows predate the attention and sampler work below.
"Can't load": iOS 12 lets a process map at most about 1.7 GB, so stock llama.cpp fails on the 2.6 and 5.5 GB files before running a token. "First run" for Moon-Beam is the first expert-pager run (pool 8, no bias).
What we built on the iPad, grouped by the bottleneck it attacks:
How Bonsai-1.7B got from 2.75 to about 25 tok/s (same model file throughout):
In long chats (400-token answers), the three turns went from 15.4 / 7.6 / 8.2 to 21.8 / 17.9 / 18.4 tok/s through the attention work alone. The pruning threshold that holds long chats above 17 costs +0.42 % perplexity at 1,024 tokens of context, near the ±0.3 % noise floor; GGML_FA_EPS=0.0001 trades that back for about 15 tok/s.
An 8B model, through an expert pager. iOS 12 caps a process at about 1.7 GB of mapped address space (1.3 GB for the web server's user), so Moon-Beam-8B's 2.6 GB file can't even be mapped, and keeping fewer experts to make it fit more than doubles its perplexity (§21.7). Dense Bonsai-8B runs at 0.08 tok/s from flash. So the model file is rewritten with its experts last, only the 474 MB before them is mapped, and each layer keeps 14 experts in RAM, reading the others from flash with pread when the router picks them. Results match the unpaged model exactly. A small routing bias toward experts already in RAM (+0.3 % perplexity, inside the noise) brought it to 2.4-2.8 tok/s in about 600 MB (§21.8). Round 2 (§21.9) queues flash reads by when they're needed, prefetches the next layer's likely experts, and runs the experts through a lookup-table kernel for Q2_K: 3.4 tok/s, 40× the dense 8B, at +0.7 % perplexity on the full eval text. The flash is still the limit: each token reads about 53 MB at 266 MB/s. Wiring weights in RAM kernel-panicked the iPad, like a pool of 16 did before. Round 3 (§21.10) evicts by decayed use frequency instead of recency, for 3.5 tok/s at no quality cost. 5 tok/s takes 4 experts per token instead of 8 (+27 % perplexity); choosing the count per token adaptively turned out no better than a fixed count. A 16B model (§21.11): Ling-mini-2.0, 16.3B parameters with 256 small experts per layer, runs through the same pager at 2.6 tok/s with unchanged routing, 3.3 at +2.6 % perplexity and 4.5 with a strong cache bias, in under 580 MB. Its 5.5 GB file was assembled from two published quantizations over HTTP range requests and streamed straight to the iPad, since the Mac had no room for it. It is twice Moon-Beam's size at the same speed, but not a better model (+3 % perplexity).
Limits worth knowing. Bonsai is a 1-bit model and still gets facts wrong (in one test it called Mercury the closest planet to Earth). About 700 MB is the practical memory ceiling: 1-bit weights don't compress, so iOS starts killing processes past it, which is why the 4B needs a 512-token context. The jailbreak doesn't survive a reboot. The fast output head adds 2-3 s to the first prompt after each launch.
Kernels for Cortex-A55 (ARMv8.2 dotprod, no i8mm), as a patch on llama.cpp v0.8.0, each with an exactness test against a scalar reference:
Memory tricks:
- Pruned LM head: keep only the ~49-66 K most useful vocabulary rows, chosen by token frequency on English, code and 7 other languages. The other logits are scattered to −inf. Saves 0.2-0.5 GB and misses ~1 % of English tokens.
- Repack cache on flash (GGML_REPACK_CACHE): repacked weights are written to a file once and mapped afterwards. Models load in seconds.
Headless mode (tools/tv-llm-mode.sh on|off): a small foreground activity, then the launchers, Google services and other heavy apps are force-stopped, and svc power stayon keeps the animated screensaver (17 % of a core) away. Nothing persistent except stay-awake, which off restores. MemAvailable ~1000 → ~1300 MB. A fork-free guard (tools/tv-watch.c) replaced a shell loop that started ~25 processes a second and cost 10 % of the speed.
Expert pager for mixture-of-experts models (ggml-cpu/moe-pager-tv.inc):
- Experts live on flash: each expert tensor is overlaid with empty anonymous memory, and right after a layer's routing the missing experts are read with parallel O_DIRECT straight into their own addresses; a per-layer LRU pool (43 of 128 experts) keeps the rest. Kernels see an ordinary tensor. The GGUF's own expert bytes are hole-punched once the repack cache holds them, so the model costs one copy of its weights on flash.
- Cache-aware routing (GGML_MOE_BIAS): a small bonus for experts already in RAM cuts misses from 13 % to ~2 % for a measured quality cost (arXiv 2412.00099 has the idea on other models). Fewer experts per token (LLAMA_MOE_USED=6) is the other dial.
- Warm start from a list of each layer's most used experts, and pre-gated prefetch: layer L+2's router applied to layer L's hidden state, predicting what the router will actually pick (sigmoid, the model's own selection bias and the cache bonus), loads ~60 % of misses before they are needed.
- Why answers looped, and the fix: 2-bit experts break long-form coherence after ~250-300 words, and routing bias amplifies it. DRY sampling only hides it (the model paraphrases its loop); a repeat penalty of 1.15 over 256 tokens brings degenerate long answers from 12/13 to 1/13 on the TV (E99, E100).
Weight streaming for models bigger than RAM (ggml-cpu/stream-tv.inc):
- What stays in RAM: a chosen part of the weights stays resident. The rest lives in "stream zones".
- Prefetch: a hook on every matmul records the order the weights are used. Reader threads then fetch zone weights ahead of time with parallel 8 MB O_DIRECT reads straight into the weights' own addresses, at the flash's full 278 MB/s.
- Correctness: every compute thread waits until its weight is completely loaded, so a wrong prediction costs time, never correctness.
- Drop-behind: each zone weight is freed right after use.
- Verify mode: GGML_STREAM_VERIFY=1 compares every streamed tensor with the file. It found two silent-corruption bugs, which are fixed and documented in E48 and E50.
- Speculative decoding: with the model's own MTP head, verifying 2 tokens costs about one pass over the weights when the pass is flash-bound, so it pays off (+69 %). On the in-RAM 2B it lost (E31).
Profiling (env switches in the patch): GGML_OPPROF=1 per-op table, GGML_OPPROF=2 a node-by-node, per-thread trace of one graph (tools/optrace.py), LLAMA_UBATCH_PROF / GGML_CPU_PROF phase timings. They showed where a small model's time really goes (E57): ~71 % Q4_K matmuls, and only ~2 ms per token of barriers and scheduling.
Tooling:
- Streaming GGUF rewriter: adds a pruned head, extra tensors and metadata in one sequential pass, so Hugging Face → Mac → TV pipelines never store the model on the Mac.
- MTP fetcher: range-reads only the MTP tensors from safetensors.
- Memory guard: wraps every heavy run on the TV.
- Benchmark and perplexity harnesses, a model screener that streams any Hugging Face GGUF to the TV and scores it (tools/screen-small.sh), and a live token-stream web UI.
You need: the TV box (or another ARMv8.2 Android device) with network ADB, adb, zig (for static aarch64 musl builds), cmake + ninja, python3, and uv (for numpy).
export ADB_SERIAL=<tv-ip>:5555          # every script talks to the box through this
adb connect $ADB_SERIAL
# 1. llama.cpp v0.8.0 + the patch, cross-compiled for the TV
git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp third_party/llama.cpp
cd third_party/llama.cpp && git checkout 8642541 && git apply ../../patches/llama.cpp-v0.8.0-tvbox.patch
cmake -S . -B build-tv -G Ninja -DCMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME=Linux -DCMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR=aarch64 \
  -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=$PWD/../../zigcc/cc -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=$PWD/../../zigcc/c++ -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DCMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS=-static -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF -DGGML_NATIVE=OFF \
  -DGGML_CPU_ARM_ARCH=armv8.2-a+dotprod+fp16 -DGGML_OPENMP=OFF -DLLAMA_OPENSSL=OFF -DLLAMA_BUILD_TESTS=OFF
ninja -C build-tv llama-server llama-cli llama-bench llama-perplexity llama-quantize
cd ../..
adb -s $ADB_SERIAL shell mkdir -p /data/local/tmp/llm/patched25 /data/local/tmp/llm/patched
adb -s $ADB_SERIAL push third_party/llama.cpp/build-tv/bin/llama-{server,cli,bench,perplexity} /data/local/tmp/llm/patched25/
adb -s $ADB_SERIAL push third_party/llama.cpp/build-tv/bin/llama-quantize /data/local/tmp/llm/patched/   # used by tools/tv-quant.sh
zig cc -target aarch64-linux-musl -O2 -static -o gguf_recut tools/gguf-recut/gguf_recut.c && adb -s $ADB_SERIAL push gguf_recut /data/local/tmp/llm/
# 2. models: rebuilt from their Hugging Face sources straight onto the TV (see below)
tools/rebuild-models.sh 2b          # also: 08 4b b8 tb8 q9 mb lm caches
# 3. the live chat page (default: the 2B on patched25 with fp16 state), then open http://<tv-ip>:8090 from any device on the network
tv-llm-ui/start.sh
tv-llm-ui/start.sh stop
Other models:
# Moon-Beam-8B-A1B MoE, ~7.2 tok/s (first: `tools/rebuild-models.sh mb`, needs a native Mac build and ~9 GB on the Mac while it runs).
# start.sh turns on headless mode, the expert pager, routing bias, prefetch and the repeat penalty; POOL / BIAS / EXPERTS override them.
MODEL=mb-q2-h60.gguf tv-llm-ui/start.sh
# Ling-mini-2.0 16B MoE, ~5.1 tok/s (first: `tools/rebuild-models.sh lm`)
MODEL=lm2-q2-h60.gguf tv-llm-ui/start.sh
# Bonsai-8B 1-bit fully resident, ~5.2 tok/s (first: `tools/rebuild-models.sh b8`; the repack cache is written on first start)
MODEL=b8-q1-hml.gguf tv-llm-ui/start.sh
sh /data/local/tmp/llm/tv-llm-mode.sh off   # on the TV, afterwards: launcher and screensaver back
# Qwen3.5-0.8B, ~16 tok/s (first: `tools/rebuild-models.sh 08`, needs a native Mac build of llama-quantize)
MODEL=q08-q4k-h65p8.gguf tv-llm-ui/start.sh
# The 8B / 9B numbers below were measured with the build of that time (patched16); the current build has the same
# code plus §15-17. GGML_CHUNK_GUIDED=0 in SENV restores the old matmul scheduling. No fp16 state with MTP.
# Bonsai-8B 1-bit with streaming and no headless mode, ~1.2 tok/s (first run: `tools/rebuild-models.sh b8 caches`)
MODEL=b8-q1-hml.gguf BIN=patched25 EXTRA="-ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 -fa on -cram 0" \
  SENV="GGML_REPACK_CACHE=/data/local/tmp/llm/cache/b8c GGML_REPACK_RESIDENT_MB=800 GGML_STREAM_MODE=cache GGML_STREAM_WINDOW_MB=64" tv-llm-ui/start.sh
# Qwen3.5-9B with MTP, ~0.27 tok/s
MODEL=q9-iq2-h65-mtp.gguf BIN=patched25 EXTRA="-nr -ctxcp 0 -cram 0 -ub 16 -b 64 --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 1" \
  SENV="LLAMA_STREAM_RESIDENT_MB=600 LLAMA_STREAM_PIN=output.,blk.32. GGML_STREAM_WINDOW_MB=64" tv-llm-ui/start.sh
Everything on the box lives in /data/local/tmp/llm and runs as the adb shell user. The only system setting touched is stay-awake in headless mode (svc power stayon), which tv-llm-mode.sh off turns back off. adb shell rm -rf /data/local/tmp/llm removes it all.
The model files (0.5-4 GB each) are not in this repo. tools/rebuild-models.sh recreates every one from public Hugging Face files, streaming them through tools/gguf_build.py onto the TV. The SHA-256s below are of the files used in the experiments. Rebuilds of the 4B, Bonsai-8B and 9B files were checked byte-identical.
Ready-made downloads. The best file of each size class is on Hugging Face exactly as the TV runs it. They need the patched llama.cpp above; stock llama.cpp can't load the pruned head. Each card has the run command and the measured numbers:
Download with hf download hyperionaidev/<repo> --local-dir models/, then adb push the files to /data/local/tmp/llm/, with moe-warm-*.txt next to them. That replaces the 08 / 2b / 4b / mb / b8 / lm targets. For the 8B and 16B models, the first start writes the repack cache.
iPad Air downloads. Every model run on the iPad, where to get it, and its speed there. The three MoE files are our own builds, laid out for the iPad's expert pager and lookup-table kernel: they need the iOS 12 patch (ipad-air/), and any other llama.cpp loads them but gets scrambled experts. The rest are used exactly as published; the Bonsai models' fast layouts are built in RAM at load time. 53 experiments in all (E108-E160, §21):
The head-id lists in data/ were made by tools/vocab_select.py (Qwen3.5 tokenizer) and tools/head_select_tok.py (any tokenizer, via llama-tokenize), from the corpus tools/fetch_corpus.py downloads (Wikipedia + Project Gutenberg).
- On this box the 2B at 4 bits beats every bigger model at 1-2 bits. Post-training quantization below ~2.5 bits breaks normal models (E22, E23, E35). Models trained for 1-bit or ternary hold up, but at 4-8 B they don't fit without streaming.
- Past RAM, flash bandwidth sets the speed. The kernel's LRU is the worst possible policy for a cyclic scan bigger than the cache: it re-reads everything every token. Keep a fixed resident set and stream the rest yourself.
- Batching is free when you are flash-bound. Prompts and speculative verification cost about one weight pass, whatever their size.
- Measure, then verify. Two streaming bugs gave plausible speeds and wrong numbers; only comparing tensors with the file, and perplexity with a Mac reference, caught them.
- Small models are mostly vocabulary. Qwen3.5-0.8B's 248K-row head is a third of its weights; pruning it to 65K rows plus all-Q4_K took it from 7.5 to 12.1 tok/s (E55). Small models also lose more to 4 bits (+7 % perplexity vs +2.3 % for the 2B).
- Simulate before you write a kernel. Activation sparsity (E58) and a low-rank head (E60) both looked promising on paper; a quality simulation on the Mac killed each in under an hour.
- On an in-order core, count NEON ops as well as bytes. Tighter packing saved 20 % of the bytes and cost 2.5× the ops; undoing it made the 4B 33 % faster in chat (E76, E77). The 4-bit kernel is the opposite case, limited by RAM (E27), so the trick does not help the 2B or 0.8B.
- Check that every big matrix reaches the fast kernel. The 2B's head (65,668 rows, ~10 % of each token's weights) silently ran on the generic kernel for weeks because ggml only repacks row counts divisible by 8; four extra rows gave +5.8 % (E71, E72). The load log's repack buffer size gives it away.
- Most of the RAM was Android's, not the model's. Force-stopping the launchers and Google services for the duration (nothing persistent) let Bonsai-8B sit fully in RAM: 1.2 → 3.6 tok/s before any kernel work (E80). An animated screensaver and a guard that forked 25 times a second each cost another 10-15 % (E82, E88).
- For a mixture-of-experts model the flash is a cache miss, not a stream. A ~6 ms miss per expert means the pool hit rate decides the speed; routing toward cached experts and prefetching what the next router will pick turned 4.4 into 7.2 tok/s.
- Perplexity can't see loops. It scores one token at a time on clean text; the 2-bit model scored fine and still fell into loops in 12 of 13 long answers. Score long free-running generations too (tools/loop_stats.py), and compare models with different tokenizers in bits per byte, never in perplexity.
- Past 9B, count resident bytes, not parameters. The ceiling for a mixture-of-experts model here is the non-expert weights that must stay in RAM plus a useful expert pool. Ling-mini-2.0 (16B) keeps 279 MB resident and runs at 5 tok/s; Qwen3.6-35B-A3B would need ~870 MB before caching a single expert (§20).
- Guard the box. After two early kernel panics, every heavy run goes through a wrapper that kills it below 180 MB of free memory.
MIT. The llama.cpp patch is a derivative of llama.cpp (MIT). Model weights keep their own licenses, and the evaluation texts are Wikipedia excerpts (CC BY-SA 4.0).
Built on llama.cpp and llama2.c. Models from Qwen, unsloth (GGUFs and importance matrices), PrismML (Bonsai), Google (Gemma) and stories260K. The evaluation texts are excerpts from Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). The 🤏 logo is the pinching-hand emoji from Google's Noto Emoji (Apache 2.0).

articles.title: Talking Zen 6 with Mike Clark at AMD In-Depth
articles.body:
Hello you fine Internet folks,
I sat down with AMD’s Mike Clark to talk about Zen 6, the evolution from Zen 5 and what some of the differences are between Zen 6 and Zen 6c and what drove some of those changes.
Hope y’all enjoy!
The transcript below has been edited for readability and conciseness.
George Cozma: Hello, you fine Internet folks. We’re here at AMD In-Depth, where we’re talking about Venice. With me, I have a returning guest, Mike Clark. Would you like to tell the audience who you are?
Mike Clark: Hi, I’m Mike Clark, the original architect of Zen. Some people refer to me as “Zen Daddy.” I’ve been working on cores here at AMD for 33 years, and we’ve got another great one coming, so I’m very proud of the design team I get to represent here today.
George Cozma: I’ve had some hands-on time with Zen 6c. Let’s talk about the change that’s happened with Zen 6 and Zen 6c, what I refer to in my piece as the Zen 6 family. Why is it different from previous generations?
Mike Clark: Right. Starting with Zen 4, we’ve been going through this evolution of having two core families. Before, we were really just using the denser technology as an area play. In this generation, having learned a lot, as we were filling out that denser version of the core, we wanted to leverage it to add some extra IPC within the core. So if you look more in-depth at what we have, what used to be our classic design, we now think of as our high-frequency design. And our dense technology is now our top-of-the-line, no-questions-asked performance core, because we’ve also enabled the full L3 in that implementation, at 4MB per core. So we have 32 of those cores, 128MB of L3, and the highest IPC you can get in that core.
George Cozma: Awesome. So far, one thing I’ve noticed is that the vector scheduler is a bit bigger on Zen 6c. What was the reasoning for increasing that on Zen 6c?
Mike Clark: Well, that wasn’t the only thing we increased. One principle we follow is that we don’t want to create a delta between the two architectures that software has to be optimized for. We want them to have the same fit and feel, so the same optimizations apply to both. But because of its reduced frequency target, Zen 6c can have a little more capacity in the queues, since it doesn’t have to reach the maximum frequency the high-frequency core has to hit. The floating-point scheduler is just one example. There are other queues throughout the core that are larger in Zen 6c, to pull out a little more IPC and get a little more leverage in that SMT environment as well.
George Cozma: Interesting. Both Zen 6 and Zen 6c build on the design you had in Zen 5, and one of the interesting things with Zen 5 was the dual decode setup. Has the front end changed much to let a single thread make better use of both decode clusters?
Mike Clark: Yes. As you said, Zen 5 was a new foundation, with the ability to fetch two basic blocks and get them down the line. But it gets quite complicated with one thread running larger-footprint workloads, where some of it might be hitting the I-cache and some of it might be hitting the op cache, and you’re trying to get everything synced up. So we spent a lot of time optimizing that and making it more efficient from both a delivery and a power perspective: less power wasted, and more efficient delivery from that new front end.
George Cozma: Awesome. Going down into the execution engine, I also noticed that the number of integer multiply units has gone down from three to two. Could you talk a bit about what drove that choice?
Mike Clark: It really came out of the Zen 5 design, where we had a more unified scheduler. To make a scheduler simpler, you want the units it schedules into to be very uniform, and the way we had set up those schedulers, adding a third multiplier to the group it was scheduling into was easy and didn’t add complication. In Zen 6, we realized that to really scale out the architecture, we needed to go back to more distributed schedulers, which now schedule into the ALUs. We hadn’t seen much uptick from that extra multiplier on Zen 5, so to optimize the area and the schedulers, we went back to two multipliers.
George Cozma: Speaking of integer multiply, on the vector side you’ve added two more VNNI units. What was the impetus for adding them, and at what point in the design did you add them?
Mike Clark: As I said in the talk, these are long design programs. We weren’t designing Zen 6 to be an agentic core. When we started, no one was really even using that term. But Zen 5 was a whole new foundation for AI workloads, and we’ve always believed the core has a place in AI: orchestration, data type manipulation, smaller models. So we were always focused on making the core good at AI. It’s not going to beat a GPU, and that’s not the point. We realized we probably should have some more VNNI, given where we were seeing inference go, and the team rallied around that. It was kind of late, since these are long-lead projects and the floor plan was set, but the team rallied, we were able to squeeze a couple more VNNI pipes in there, and it was a big success.
George Cozma: Again on the vector side, one of the oddities of Zen 5 was that although the wires were all there, the load unit could only do two vector loads at a time. What changed within the Zen 6 core to allow four vector loads, assuming they’re either 128 or 256 bits?
Mike Clark: We can do the 256-bit loads. Since we were able to do two 512-bit loads, we already had 1,024 wires headed over there. Obviously, using them piecemeal versus as one contiguous set complicates the design. I think it’s something we always wanted to do on Zen 5, but with all the change and getting it working, we left that for the Zen 6 team, and they were awesome. We’re all really one team at AMD anyway, and sometimes things intersect at different points in the roadmap. This was the time to do it.
George Cozma: Speaking of bandwidth into the caches, the L2 in Zen 5 had some oddities where it couldn’t always hit 64 bytes per cycle on reads. What changed in Zen 6 to allow that? Because I’ve been able to measure it, and it does hit that.
Mike Clark: Honestly, sometimes you just don’t see some of these things. A lot of it was that we would be over-prefetching, and prefetches that hit in the L2 would be robbing L2 bandwidth. So we made sure we could sustain those prefetches alongside demand requests, reduce the conflicts, and deliver the full 64 bytes per cycle that we want.
George Cozma: Awesome. Circling all the way back to the front: the all-important branch predictor. There seems to have been a reduction in branch misprediction latency, so when you miss a branch, the number of cycles it takes to recover has gone down. What I also noticed, which is really neat, is that there wasn’t any reduction in accuracy. So how did you pull off not only a faster branch predictor, but one that’s even slightly more accurate than Zen 5’s already very accurate predictor?
Mike Clark: The branch prediction team, as you know, is very algorithmic. There’s lots of design space and lots of exploration, and AI has even been getting involved in helping us figure out how to optimize it. It’s a great optimization problem: the number of TAGE tables, how much information they hold, accuracy. So we set out to make a more efficient one. That was an area where we didn’t really want to grow; we thought we could be more efficient in the way we lay out the tables for prediction. And we’re always focused on our pipeline length. No matter how good a branch predictor you build, there are always hard-to-predict branches, and you’re always going to mispredict. So each generation, we’re monomaniacally focused on getting going again as fast as we can when we’re wrong. There are lots of unique tricks we pull to get that redirect back into the front end and get it flowing as fast as possible. And you’ve observed it, which is great.
George Cozma: Yeah. I haven’t had time on Zen 6 yet, but I have had time on Zen 6c, and in SPECint 2026 it matches your fastest Zen 5 server CPU. That’s very impressive, especially considering the clock deficit. Wrapping this all up and moving outside the core into the L3, there are obviously topology differences between the 12-core and 32-core CCDs. How much were you able to mitigate those differences inside the core, building up structures to tolerate latency, to compensate for the slightly increased L3 latency?
Mike Clark: As I always talk about, the design has to be balanced. As we grow the capacity of a structure, the new technology helps it shrink, so the physical distance doesn’t grow linearly, but unfortunately the distance does grow. Inside the L3, there are a lot of tricks I can’t talk about...
George Cozma: The secret sauce!
Mike Clark: [In order to] maintain bandwidth within the L3 mesh so we can keep delivering to the cores. And in the cores, we do grow the queues to handle those higher latencies.
George Cozma: Awesome. My penultimate question: Verano is adding LPDDR5X to the EPYC ecosystem. Were there any design considerations between LPDDR5X and DDR5 that you had to think about when designing the core?
Mike Clark: At the CCX level, we focus a lot on bandwidth per core. I think Mahesh talked a lot about the SDP ports, with 32-byte reads per port, so we try to make sure we have enough bandwidth between the CCD and the IOD. But we were already well provisioned for bandwidth with MRDIMMs, so that construction, the winglets and choosing a different memory technology, didn’t really have a major impact on how we built the core.
George Cozma: Awesome. Usually this is where I’d ask what your favorite type of cheese is, but since we already know that: have you tried any new cheeses lately?
Mike Clark: I have. My new favorite is Cotija cheese.
George Cozma: Oh!
Mike Clark: I’ve been eating a lot of tacos.
George Cozma: You’ve got to love Cotija on tacos. It’s absolutely amazing. Well, thank you so much for sitting down with me. If you like videos like this, hit like and subscribe; it does help with the algorithm. There are PayPal and Patreon links in the description, as well as a transcript of this on the Chips and Cheese website. Thank you so much.
Mike Clark: Thanks for having me, George. I always look forward to coming and talking with you about what this awesome AMD CPU design team has created, and you always have so many good questions. I wish I could answer more, since we do have to protect our secret sauce, but I really enjoy helping you understand some of our thought processes, the challenges we face, and how we’ve been able to overcome them.
George Cozma: Well, it’s always fun to sit down with you and talk, not just about what you’re doing, but also what the team is doing and what you’re looking forward to in the future. So thank you so much.
Mike Clark: Thank you.
George Cozma: I’ll see you in the next one. Have a good one, folks!
