We want them to have the same fit and feel, so the same optimizations apply to both. But because of its reduced frequency target, Zen 6c can have a little more capacity in the queues, since it doesn’t have to reach the maximum frequency the high-frequency core has to hit. The floating-point scheduler is just one example. There are other queues throughout the core that are larger in Zen 6c, to pull out a little more IPC and get a little more leverage in that SMT environment as well.
George Cozma: Interesting. Both Zen 6 and Zen 6c build on the design you had in Zen 5, and one of the interesting things with Zen 5 was the dual decode setup. Has the front end changed much to let a single thread make better use of both decode clusters?
Mike Clark: Yes. As you said, Zen 5 was a new foundation, with the ability to fetch two basic blocks and get them down the line. But it gets quite complicated with one thread running larger-footprint workloads, where some of it might be hitting the I-cache and some of it might be hitting the op cache, and you’re trying to get everything synced up. So we spent a lot of time optimizing that and making it more efficient from both a delivery and a power perspective: less power wasted, and more efficient delivery from that new front end.
George Cozma: Awesome. Going down into the execution engine, I also noticed that the number of integer multiply units has gone down from three to two. Could you talk a bit about what drove that choice?
Mike Clark: It really came out of the Zen 5 design, where we had a more unified scheduler. To make a scheduler simpler, you want the units it schedules into to be very uniform, and the way we had set up those schedulers, adding a third multiplier to the group it was scheduling into was easy and didn’t add complication. In Zen 6, we realized that to really scale out the architecture, we needed to go back to more distributed schedulers, which now schedule into the ALUs. We hadn’t seen much uptick from that extra multiplier on Zen 5, so to optimize the area and the schedulers, we went back to two multipliers.
George Cozma: Speaking of integer multiply, on the vector side you’ve added two more VNNI units. What was the impetus for adding them, and at what point in the design did you add them?
Mike Clark: As I said in the talk, these are long design programs. We weren’t designing Zen 6 to be an agentic core. When we started, no one was really even using that term. But Zen 5 was a whole new foundation for AI workloads, and we’ve always believed the core has a place in AI: orchestration, data type manipulation, smaller models. So we were always focused on making the core good at AI. It’s not going to beat a GPU, and that’s not the point. We realized we probably should have some more VNNI, given where we were seeing inference go, and the team rallied around that. It was kind of late, since these are long-lead projects and the floor plan was set, but the team rallied, we were able to squeeze a couple more VNNI pipes in there, and it was a big success.
George Cozma: Again on the vector side, one of the oddities of Zen 5 was that although the wires were all there, the load unit could only do two vector loads at a time. What changed within the Zen 6 core to allow four vector loads, assuming they’re either 128 or 256 bits?
Mike Clark: We can do the 256-bit loads. Since we were able to do two 512-bit loads, we already had 1,024 wires headed over there. Obviously, using them piecemeal versus as one contiguous set complicates the design. I think it’s something we always wanted to do on Zen 5, but with all the change and getting it working, we left that for the Zen 6 team, and they were awesome. We’re all really one team at AMD anyway, and sometimes things intersect at different points in the roadmap. This was the time to do it.
George Cozma: Speaking of bandwidth into the caches, the L2 in Zen 5 had some oddities where it couldn’t always hit 64 bytes per cycle on reads. What changed in Zen 6 to allow that? Because I’ve been able to measure it, and it does hit that.
Mike Clark: Honestly, sometimes you just don’t see some of these things. A lot of it was that we would be over-prefetching, and prefetches that hit in the L2 would be robbing L2 bandwidth. So we made sure we could sustain those prefetches alongside demand requests, reduce the conflicts, and deliver the full 64 bytes per cycle that we want.
George Cozma: Awesome. Circling all the way back to the front: the all-important branch predictor. There seems to have been a reduction in branch misprediction latency, so when you miss a branch, the number of cycles it takes to recover has gone down. What I also noticed, which is really neat, is that there wasn’t any reduction in accuracy. So how did you pull off not only a faster branch predictor, but one that’s even slightly more accurate than Zen 5’s already very accurate predictor?
Mike Clark: The branch prediction team, as you know, is very algorithmic. There’s lots of design space and lots of exploration, and AI has even been getting involved in helping us figure out how to optimize it. It’s a great optimization problem: the number of TAGE tables, how much information they hold, accuracy. So we set out to make a more efficient one. That was an area where we didn’t really want to grow; we thought we could be more efficient in the way we lay out the tables for prediction. And we’re always focused on our pipeline length. No matter how good a branch predictor you build, there are always hard-to-predict branches, and you’re always going to mispredict. So each generation, we’re monomaniacally focused on getting going again as fast as we can when we’re wrong. There are lots of unique tricks we pull to get that redirect back into the front end and get it flowing as fast as possible. And you’ve observed it, which is great.
George Cozma: Yeah. I haven’t had time on Zen 6 yet, but I have had time on Zen 6c, and in SPECint 2026 it matches your fastest Zen 5 server CPU. That’s very impressive, especially considering the clock deficit. Wrapping this all up and moving outside the core into the L3, there are obviously topology differences between the 12-core and 32-core CCDs. How much were you able to mitigate those differences inside the core, building up structures to tolerate latency, to compensate for the slightly increased L3 latency?
Mike Clark: As I always talk about, the design has to be balanced. As we grow the capacity of a structure, the new technology helps it shrink, so the physical distance doesn’t grow linearly, but unfortunately the distance does grow. Inside the L3, there are a lot of tricks I can’t talk about...
George Cozma: The secret sauce!
Mike Clark: [In order to] maintain bandwidth within the L3 mesh so we can keep delivering to the cores. And in the cores, we do grow the queues to handle those higher latencies.
George Cozma: Awesome. My penultimate question: Verano is adding LPDDR5X to the EPYC ecosystem. Were there any design considerations between LPDDR5X and DDR5 that you had to think about when designing the core?
Mike Clark: At the CCX level, we focus a lot on bandwidth per core. I think Mahesh talked a lot about the SDP ports, with 32-byte reads per port, so we try to make sure we have enough bandwidth between the CCD and the IOD. But we were already well provisioned for bandwidth with MRDIMMs, so that construction, the winglets and choosing a different memory technology, didn’t really have a major impact on how we built the core.
George Cozma: Awesome. Usually this is where I’d ask what your favorite type of cheese is, but since we already know that: have you tried any new cheeses lately?
Mike Clark: I have. My new favorite is Cotija cheese.
George Cozma: Oh!
Mike Clark: I’ve been eating a lot of tacos.
George Cozma: You’ve got to love Cotija on tacos. It’s absolutely amazing. Well, thank you so much for sitting down with me. If you like videos like this, hit like and subscribe; it does help with the algorithm. There are PayPal and Patreon links in the description, as well as a transcript of this on the Chips and Cheese website. Thank you so much.
Mike Clark: Thanks for having me, George. I always look forward to coming and talking with you about what this awesome AMD CPU design team has created, and you always have so many good questions. I wish I could answer more, since we do have to protect our secret sauce, but I really enjoy helping you understand some of our thought processes, the challenges we face, and how we’ve been able to overcome them.
George Cozma: Well, it’s always fun to sit down with you and talk, not just about what you’re doing, but also what the team is doing and what you’re looking forward to in the future. So thank you so much.
Mike Clark: Thank you.
George Cozma: I’ll see you in the next one. Have a good one, folks!

articles.title: Darling Development Update – Q4 2026
articles.body:
It's been a while since our last progress report, and a lot has changed. This update covers the biggest shifts in the project: our new policy on AI-assisted contributions, initial ARM64 support, and what we plan to work on next.
Our AI Policy
The biggest change in the project this year is not a feature, but a policy: we have adopted rules for AI-assisted contributions. We know this is a divisive topic that many open source projects are debating right now, and the concern about low-quality "slop" is a fair one. But in the hands of people who know the project's internals, an LLM can be a very powerful tool.
Developing Darling has always been a lot of fun, but it was also hard to see the light at the end of the tunnel. Let's face it: Apple is a huge company with many engineers shipping new features all the time, and a small group of volunteers is no match for that capacity. I started Darling in 2012, and until recently very few real-world macOS applications actually ran on it.
Darling has also never had the advantages that Wine enjoys. The surface of macOS applications is much smaller than that of Windows applications, so there is less interest in running them on Linux, and far fewer developers who know the internals of macOS well enough to help. That makes it hard to attract contributors, and just as hard to attract commercial backing of the kind Valve has provided to Wine. The scale of the platform is a problem too. Apple keeps adding frameworks that only ship with macOS: by one count, macOS 27 contains 464 public and 2,754 private frameworks, up from 273 and 878 in macOS 10.14. Wine can lean on Microsoft's redistributable runtimes, which tools such as winetricks fetch for users, whereas for most of Apple's frameworks there is nothing to download, and we have to implement them ourselves. Matching Apple's engineering capacity looked like an unsolvable problem for a handful of volunteers.
This year, that changed. Several forks appeared that make heavy use of AI, and they achieved impressive results. One of the most visible examples is a fork that runs League of Legends (see it in action on YouTube). VibeDarling has also gotten several original macOS applications working.
AI changes the equation. What used to be an unsolvable problem with few contributors is now financially realistic, and it lets us compete with Apple on something closer to level ground.
Refusing to use AI would have meant two things for us:
- We would have become insignificant. Various forks would be moving at extreme speed, while we continued at the same pace with very few things working.
- The community would likely have fragmented, as people moved to wherever progress is happening.
The policy is how we use this power responsibly. It is written as instructions for AI agents, but it binds the humans using them. Whoever opens a pull request is responsible for every line in it and must be able to explain it in their own words; maintainers' questions get answered by people, not by a bot. The rest of it encodes our clean-room rules: implement the documented contract rather than hacks for a single application, respect the macOS layering, isolate and label undocumented quirks, and never use leaked material or Apple's restricted source such as corecrypto. Nobody should use disassembly to produce matching code. Depending on local laws, it may be acceptable to use disassembly to document how something works and then reimplement it in a clean-room fashion: the agent that writes the code never sees the disassembly, only a separate behavioral description produced in another context.
ARM64 Support
Darling now has initial ARM64 support. This matters because ARM64 is the current main architecture for Apple hardware. Since Apple's transition to its own silicon, every new Mac has been ARM64-based, and the software being written for macOS today increasingly targets it first, or only. Without ARM64 support, Darling would be limited to an architecture that Apple itself is moving away from.
There is another reason we are confident in this support. The VibeDarling fork is being developed on ARM64, so its day-to-day work exercises the ARM64 code paths constantly. When the fork is folded back into the original Darling, we expect to have good support for this architecture from the start.
The Future
The Next Two Months
Our short-term goal is to get the work from all the forks merged back into Darling. For this we are using agent-driven merging logic, which has so far autonomously fixed many bugs, both in the code coming from the forks and in pre-existing bugs in Darling itself.
We plan to officially support three architectures: i386, x86-64 and ARM64 (aarch64). Our confidence in ARM64 comes from the fact that VibeDarling is developed on it.
Separately, I am slowly working on running ARM64 applications on x86-64 hosts by reusing Dynarmic. This is a long shot, so please don't count on it, but I'm curious to see how far it can go.
Longer Term
I expect to keep receiving a steady flow of patches from other contributors, so I can't speak for them. My own plan is to stabilize AppKit support and make the UI look nice.
I also have a few specific applications I want to get working, either because they are simple enough or because they are open source. Being open source gives the agents a better chance of discovering what the application expects from the system.
I would also like to start adding GUI applications to Darling itself, such as a configuration utility and a log viewer in the spirit of Console.app. Darling should come with native tools for managing it, and they will also serve as real-world tests of our AppKit support.
Contributing
Darling is a large codebase that can be daunting to contribute to, and we'd like to make it easier. If you want to help, even with a small fix, come talk to us on our Discord. If you use an AI assistant, please read our AI policy first: you are responsible for every line you submit, and you should be ready to explain it in your own words.
You can also support the project financially through our OpenCollective. The funds will be used to cover infrastructure and hosting costs, and perhaps LLM costs.

articles.title: A general purpose Apple Silicon layer for x86-64 PCs
articles.body:
A general purpose Apple Silicon layer for x86-64 PCs. It is a UEFI boot program with an arm64-to-x86-64 translator, a Metal driver for NVIDIA GPUs and a model of Apple silicon hardware. Stela presents a Mac mini (M2) and runs macOS 27.
Warning
Stela is still in development. It is slow and still may not boot on supported hardware. Fixes are on the way, please submit a GitHub Issue with your boot logs if you encounter an error!
An ahead-of-time and just-in-time compiler translates arm64e code to x86-64. It covers more than 3,000 AArch64 instruction encodings, maps guest registers to host registers and caches translated code.
The Metal driver compiles AIR, Metal's shader IR, directly to NIR, Mesa's IR, and supports the Metal3 and Apple7 GPU families.
- Download stela from the
releases page.
- Run sudo ./stela setup (Linux, macOS) or double-click stela.exe (Windows).
- Choose the USB stick, the installer, the macOS version and the Mac model, then confirm. Setup erases the USB stick.
- Boot the PC from the USB stick.
Download the new stela, plug the USB stick in and run:
sudo ./stela setup update stela
On Windows, open Terminal with Run as administrator and run:
.\stela.exe setup update stela
If Stela does not work, plug the USB stick into the computer that made it and
save the boot log. Include log.txt in your GitHub Issue.
sudo ./stela setup boot-log --output log.txt
On Windows, open Terminal with Run as administrator and run:
.\stela.exe setup boot-log --output log.txt
You need Rust, git, Python 3.10 or newer, and LLVM 21, 22 or 23 with Clang, LLD and libclang. On macOS, Xcode's Apple clang 21 or newer also works.
git clone https://github.com/tylertms/Stela
cd Stela
cargo xtask dist
This writes target/release/stela. The first build fetches and compiles
Linux, Mesa and LLVM sources and takes a long time.
Stela contains no Apple software. You are responsible for following Apple's software license agreement and terms of use.

articles.title: Gemini Decisions API
articles.body:
Gemini Decisions API: Fast, calibrated multimodal decisions
Today, we’re introducing the Gemini Decisions API, a new endpoint for fast, closed-set decisions powered by our new Gemini Decision 1 model (gemini-decision-1), available through the Gemini API in Google AI Studio.
The Decisions API gives you purpose-built primitives for bounded choices like tool selection, policy checks, model routing, and context grading. You can pass one multimodal input across text, images, audio, video, and PDFs (up to 256K tokens) along with up to 1,000 independent questions. Rather than generating answer text token by token, Gemini Decision 1 scores your candidate options in a single forward pass, returning probabilities and confidence scores in 150-250 ms end-to-end latency at $0.10 per 1M input tokens with zero output tokens billed.
Strong performance and calibration
On benchmarks spanning agent routing, reasoning, ranking, and multimodal understanding, Gemini Decision 1 leads across the suite, with the lowest calibration error.
Gemini Decision 1 scores options without token-by-token decoding, keeping median latency 50-100 ms of model compute (150-250 ms end-to-end), across multimodal inputs and contexts up to 16K tokens, remaining nearly flat from 1 to 100 questions per request. With zero output tokens billed, Gemini Decision 1 with the Decisions API is nearly 5x cheaper across the shared benchmark suite than Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite with the Interactions API.
Native multimodal evaluation across three decision types in one pass
Built on Gemini’s native multimodal architecture, Gemini Decision 1 can process text, images, audio, video, and PDFs directly in a single forward pass. You can combine modalities in one shared input, such as pairing a call recording with account metadata or a scanned PDF claim with damage photos, and tune resolution on image and video inputs to control visual detail and token cost.
You can evaluate multiple questions against that shared input in a single request, mixing yes/no checks, multiple choice, and rubric scores. Every answer includes a confidence score (from 0 to 1) so your code can route ambiguous cases to a fallback or human reviewer:
- noul (Yes/No): Estimates the probability that a yes/no condition holds, with optional true and false description criteria.
- choice (Multiple Choice): Selects from 2 to 255 choices, returning the winner and normalized probabilities for every candidate.
- score (Ordered Rubric): Grades inputs across an ordered rubric (starting at 0), returning a continuous weighted score and per-level probabilities.
The input field uses the same Content block format as the Interactions API. Here is how to check a photo of a breakroom counter, together with a text note, against all three question types in one request:
from google import genai
client = genai.Client(http_options={"api_version": "v1beta"})
result = client.decisions.create(
    model="gemini-decision-1",
    input=[{
            "type": "image",
            "uri": "https://storage.googleapis.com/generativeai-downloads/images/spill.jpg",
            "mime_type": "image/jpeg",
        },
        {
            "type": "text",
            "text": "Breakroom counter check before the 9 AM client meeting.",
        },
    ],
    questions={
        "has_spill": {
            "type": "noul",
            "instructions": "Is there an uncleaned liquid spill on the counter?",
        },
        "next_action": {
            "type": "choice",
            "instructions": "Which cleanup action fits the scene?",
            "criteria": {
                "wipe_with_cloth": "Small counter spill with a cloth or towel already nearby.",
                "dispatch_janitorial": "Large floor hazard, broken glass, or active leak.",
                "ready_for_meeting": "Counter is clean and ready.",
            },
        },
        "severity": {
            "type": "score",
            "instructions": "Rate the severity of the counter mess.",
            "criteria": [
                "Clean and ready.",
                "Minor localized spill.",
                "Major spill or safety hazard.",
            ],
        },
    },
)
How teams are building with the Decisions API
Teams across Google are already using the Decisions API as a low-latency control plane, shipping features simply by defining options rather than training custom classifiers or waiting on generative calls:
- Dynamic model routing in Gemini Notebook: Gemini Notebook uses the Decisions API as a real-time router to instantly direct incoming queries to the optimal model tier and thinking level for each request. The Decisions API classifies intent in milliseconds to serve everyday queries with up to 40% lower latency while reserving deep reasoning models for complex tasks.
- Rapid design iteration in Stitch: The new rapid canvas experiment in Stitch uses the Decisions API to generate playable wireframes of a product flow in seconds and to apply edits made by voice or tap almost instantly. When the flow feels right, one click hands the screens off to the full Stitch experience for deeper design polish.
- Emoji selection in CC: CC from Google Labs uses the Decisions API to pick the right emoji reaction from a palette of more than 200 options in a fraction of a second, so reactions appear instantly without adding latency.
- Safety layer for MCP tools in Search: Google Search uses the Decision API to detect adversarial behavior and content against adversarial evals with high efficacy within the latency envelope.
Stitch Rapid uses the Decisions API to design an entire product flow in seconds (1x speed).
Start building today
Gemini Decision 1 is priced at $0.10 per 1M input tokens and $0 for output tokens, with an API no-cost tier you can use in Google AI Studio for prototyping. Your shared input is billed once per request no matter how many questions you evaluate (each question adds only its own instruction and criteria tokens). There are no output-token charges, variable thinking-token bills, or separate audio transcription and OCR costs.
You can start building today by grabbing an API key in Google AI Studio, trying our Doorstep Parcels, Speed Sketch, and Find the Zoo Keeper demo apps, and following the Python, JavaScript, and REST guides in the Decisions API documentation.
Ecosystem integrations are rolling out across OpenRouter, LangChain, Vercel, LiteLLM, Pydantic AI, Pipecat, LiveKit, and OpenCode alongside the google-genai SDKs, with support coming soon to Gemini in Google Cloud.

articles.title: Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG
articles.body:
Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG
Maximum inner product search (MIPS) sits at the core of recommendation systems, search, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Given a query vector, MIPS systems search within a database of millions of candidate key vectors for the one that best matches the query. The original data point associated with that best-matching key is then used to handle the query: in RAG, the document that is best suited to answer the question is typically prefixed to the query.
As the number of keys grows to millions and vector dimensions reach thousands, the computational cost of running an exhaustive comparison of the query to all keys grows dramatically. Numerous approximate methods have been proposed to trade off accuracy for speed using clustering and quantization. While these baseline methods focus on the properties of the set of keys to build up clever indexing structures, their geometric arguments loosely assume that the set of queries itself will resemble that found in keys, or bypass any considerations about what the queries will look like. This can be problematic on two fronts: In the crucial RAG case, queries arise from short user-generated questions, whereas keys represent long, informative, and curated pieces of text, making keys and queries substantially different. Additionally, most MIPS use cases deployed in production target an existing base of users with a stable, well-characterized query distribution — a signal that generic, query-agnostic methods leave untapped. Crafting methods that work best for a likely source of inputs — rather than aiming for good performance on all possible inputs — is a central tenet of modern machine learning that helps redirect compute resources more efficiently.
In Amortizing Maximum Inner Product Search with Learned Support Functions, a paper presented at ICML 2026, researchers from Apple train small neural networks (NNs) — once, offline, for a fixed database of keys — that learn how to route queries toward their best match faster. Their approach trades off an upfront amortization cost to understand how typical queries tend to be matched in exchange for faster, more accurate retrieval at inference time through these small NNs.
The Basics of Maximum Inner Product Search
A fundamental principle in MIPS is to leverage the geometry of the set of keys to speed up search: Typical MIPS systems split the set of keys into k clusters — k is typically much smaller than the total number of keys n — keeping track of a representative centroid for each cluster. When receiving a new query, the system compares it with these k centroids. The query is then routed toward the cluster of the representative centroid it is closest to, and subsequently compared exhaustively with all keys stored in that cluster. If the database has n keys and k evenly distributed clusters, the effective number of keys that will be considered in that second step is on the order of n/k — a factor-of- k speedup when compared to the n comparisons done in the naive exhaustive approach. Unfortunately, this routing mechanism can result in errors, since centroid routing is not an exact approach, as illustrated in Figure 1 below.
MIPS as a Support Function
What makes MIPS interesting from a machine learning perspective is that it is built on a mathematical structure that had been largely overlooked before this work: The function that maps a query to the largest inner product with any key in a set is the support function of that set, a well-studied object in convex analysis. This function has two important properties: First, it is convex, so it can be approximated by a class of neural networks specifically designed for convex functions, input convex neural networks (ICNNs). Second, the gradient of that support function at any query returns the best-matching key itself.
The broad idea behind this work is to learn a neural network that can mimic the ground-truth support function (or its gradient directly) for a much lower computational cost. This can be achieved through a classical ML technique known as regression: one simply needs to precompute a large number of training examples formed by sampling input vectors (user queries) and pair them with the relevant output signal produced by MIPS (either the optimal score or the optimal key vector itself). All that is then needed is to train a suitably parameterized neural network to replicate the output given the input.
Two Ways to Learn Maximum Inner Product Search
If the regression problem were to be solved perfectly, according to the mathematical approach outlined above, the same neural network that is trained to mimic the support function could also output the optimal key by evaluating its gradient (through automatic differentiation). In practice, we observe that training separate, specialized networks for each of these two tasks works best:
The SupportNet neural network architecture can learn the support function directly, using a (loosely constrained) ICNN. The approach is mathematically principled and aligns with the convex structure of the problem. We find that this approach can shine when used to compute one support function per data cluster to improve routing quality.
KeyNet models learn to directly output the best-matching key vector when fed a query. A consistency loss derived from Euler’s theorem for homogeneous functions keeps their predictions geometrically grounded in the underlying support function, even though no convexity is explicitly enforced.
Both models are trained on examples drawn from the relevant query distribution: for each sampled query, the ground-truth best match is computed once via exhaustive search and stored, creating a supervised dataset that captures the MIPS solution landscape for the distribution of queries that actually matter.
Learned Routing with SupportNet
As shown in Figure 1, the simplest way to handle larger scales is to split the keys into clusters, compare the query to each cluster’s centroid, and route the query to the most promising clusters based on these k scores. This provides a cheap yet coarse rule that can be prone to mistakes because a centroid alone cannot account for the spread of its cluster. Indeed, a cluster can hold a key that sits far from its own centroid yet close to the query, and when the query is near such an outlier, centroid routing scores the cluster low and skips it, missing the true best match.
If one were given access to the support function of each cluster, then one would instead be able to do exact routing, since each support function quantifies exactly to what extent any key within each cluster can match the query with a large score. This is illustrated in Figure 2, in which the support function of each of the four clusters is plotted for a query that varies in the space of embeddings.
Leaning on this theoretical insight, we propose to learn these k support functions jointly with a trained SupportNet that can output k scores at once. We can then use the largest of these k scores to route any new query instead. The SupportNet model can answer a more useful question than a simple comparison to the centroid can: “How good is the best key inside this cluster for this query?” SupportNets are trained in a classic machine learning fashion, also known as regression: we generate sample queries that are drawn from the distribution (typically embeddings for text queries), compute the ground-truth support functions at those queries, and train a neural network to replicate these values.
We trained SupportNets of increasing sizes (XS, S, M, and L → 1%, 5%, 10%, and 20% of the database size) on Natural Questions partitioned into 128 clusters. Natural Questions is a retrieval benchmark that pairs general-knowledge questions with passages from a large document database, roughly 2.6M unique passages in our setup.
Figure 4 below shows the retrieval performance in terms of recall as a function of different notions of cost. Routing recall is the fraction of queries whose true partition, the one holding the exact best key, lands among those the router chooses to probe. For both plots, an exhaustive search is carried out in the top-s clusters matched with the query, where s grows as powers of two (1, 2, 4, 8, …, 128). Naturally, all methods reach a recall of 1 when they survey all 128 clusters.
The first tab shows that for a fixed retrieval performance the learned routers reach it at lower latency than centroid routing. The small SupportNet model hits 95% routing recall about 1.9× faster than centroid routing (1.74 ms vs 3.36 ms), and gains are even greater with the large model, which hits 97% in 1.74 ms. This plot explicitly factors in the additional compute incurred by running our small NNs rather than simply comparing to centroids.
The plot on the second tab looks exclusively at routing quality, neglecting the overhead incurred by running NNs. At a fixed budget of explored clusters, they find the right partition more often: scanning just 5% of the database, the learned routers recover the true partition ~90–93% of the time — up to 92.6% for the mid-size (M) — versus 87.5% for the centroid baseline.
Plugging Into Existing Indices
SupportNet routing replaces the simple centroid-based routing found in existing inverted file index (IVF) systems. With KeyNet, we can also keep the IVF system as is and just feed it a modified version of the query. In that scenario, KeyNet works naturally as a “query rewriter” in front of a standard approximate search index: predict where the best match is likely to be in embedding space, then ask your favorite IVF system to look there instead of starting from the original query. Because the IVF index is highly optimized, it can find the result faster when assisted by KeyNet. We also rely on regression to train KeyNets, as summarized in Figure 5: sample queries are matched with their ground-truth, best-matching key, and the KeyNet neural network is trained to reproduce that association.
We evaluated KeyNets of increasing sizes (XS, S, M, and L → 1%, 5%, 10%, and 20% of the database size) and in Figure 6 below, we show recall–cost tradeoffs for these different sizes. On the first tab, the search budget is wall-clock latency: reaching 99% recall takes up to ~8× less time with the largest model (0.23 ms vs 1.8 ms for the raw query). As before, the second tab focuses exclusively on the boost in “quality” provided by replacing the original query with its KeyNet transformation. The x-axis is the fraction of the database the index actually scans: scanning just 0.001% of the database, KeyNet-mapped queries retrieve the true key 89–97% of the time — up to 96.7% for the largest model (L) — versus 86% for the raw query, and reaching 99% recall takes up to ~11× fewer keys (0.009% vs 0.10% raw). Better recall for the same cost, or the same recall for a fraction of it.
We show examples obtained from the same Natural Questions dataset discussed previously, served through a FAISS IVF index. It is one of several datasets we studied, and the trend is consistent across them. Querying the index with KeyNet’s predicted key consistently beats querying with the raw question, across the full search-budget sweep.
Namely, Figure 7 below shows five Natural Questions examples: top-3 hits for the raw query versus the KeyNet-mapped query.
Which Network Should You Use?
The choice between the two ends up being a practical one. Use KeyNet when inference speed is the bottleneck and you just need to approximate the best key. Use SupportNet when you also want a calibrated score (for re-ranking, thresholding, or downstream use), or when compute is tight at small model sizes — a regime where SupportNet stays competitive. Both train similarly, integrate with existing approximate-search infrastructure, and are reasonably robust to mild distribution shift in the query patterns. Ultimately, a very large-scale MIPS system for which the set of keys is huge may require both: train a SupportNet router over all clusters, and then one KeyNet per cluster to help its regular indices zero in on the best key faster.
A New Direction for Learned Retrieval
Amortized MIPS reflects a shift in how retrieval can be approached when query distributions are known in advance — a common condition in production ML systems. By encoding MIPS solutions directly into network weights, the approach trades a one-time training (so-called amortization) cost for fast, lightweight inference and opens a practical path toward learned retrieval systems explicitly tailored to the queries they serve.

articles.title: Sunken SS United States Set To Become World's Largest Artificial Reef
articles.body:
Sunken SS United States Set To Become World's Largest Artificial Reef (pbs.org) 37
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from PBS: The historic ocean liner SS United States will be intentionally sunk Wednesday off the coast of the Florida panhandle. Live coverage of the sinking of the SS United States is expected to start at 1 p.m. EST, with the sinking expected at 2 p.m. EST. Watch live in the video player above. In its heyday, the SS United States crushed the trans-Atlantic speed record, which it still holds. The luxury ocean liner took only three days to cross from New York to Europe on its maiden voyage in 1952. Carrying presidents and Hollywood stars, the nearly 1,000-foot vessel was a technical marvel of its time. However, the rise of air travel and high operating costs sunk its economic viability, and the ship was pulled from service in 1969. The ocean liner sat at Philadelphia's Pier 82 for nearly 30 years.
After a contentious back and forth with a pier landlord over rent and docking fees, Okaloosa County in Florida eventually stepped in to purchase the ship and bring it to the Gulf of Mexico to become the world's largest artificial reef. The multi-million dollar project is also aimed at creating an economic development opportunity as a major diving attraction. "It was our goal to make sure that she wasn't lost forever," said David Lawrence, a member of the board for the SS United States Conservancy, the group that sold the vessel to the Florida county.
Like the ship's unconventional life, it will also have an unconventional sinking. Federal environmental and explosives rules prevent the county from using explosives. Instead, tanks inside the ship have been removed and large holes were cut into the decks. Once the valves are opened, water will flood the hull, sinking the ship. Resting at 180 feet below the surface of the water, the SS United States will join more than 500 artificial reefs in Okaloosa County, which the county relies on to support the underwater ecosystem.

articles.title: Congress to call Jensen Huang in to answer for alleged Chinese spy affair
articles.body:
Congress is gearing up to subpoena Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to answer their questions about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Bloomberg reports, citing two House Republicans.
The report comes a week after House Republicans Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford sent a letter to Huang asking him to appear before their committees for a joint, closed-door briefing in regards to his relations with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive and suspected Chinese spy.
House China committee Chairman Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that Huang has until the end of the day to respond to the request. If he doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed, said Moolenaar.
Mast, who chairs the House Foreign Affairs Committee, on Wednesday said his committee is preparing a subpoena for Huang to send if he doesn’t respond.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

articles.title: Jensen Huang accused of having another affair — with a Nvidia exec
articles.body:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is already under investigation after having admitted to having an affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. Now the New York Times is reporting that Huang is also suspected of having another extramarital affair, with a direct report of his at the company — Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare. Powell, like Huang, is married, the outlet says.
The Times says it was told of the alleged affair by five employees at the company. The sources said that Huang and Powell were captured on video “being affectionate at a San Jose, Calif., hotel” during a conference earlier this year.
Like many companies, Nvidia has rules discouraging superiors from having relationships with employees in subordinate roles, the Times notes. TechCrunch reached out to Nvidia for comment.
The company’s board has initiated an investigation into Huang’s publicly admitted affair. Additionally, two House Republicans said Wednesday that Congress is gearing up to subpoena Huang over the spy allegations if he doesn’t voluntarily respond to their summons to a closed-door briefing. Late Wednesday, after the reports of the second affair were published, the Wall Street Journal reported that the Nvidia board was preparing to oust Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993.

articles.title: Cancer vaccine for Yash, he's diagnosed with stage IV pancreatic cancer
articles.body:
rnafoundry.com/yash, manufactured at the RNA Foundry.
In January 2025, 32-year-old Yashdeep Bindal was diagnosed with stage IV pancreatic cancer. He had just returned to work after the birth of his daughter, Maya.
At the RNA Foundry, we are developing a personalized cancer vaccine for Yash. We’re sharing his tumour DNA, tumour RNA, matched-normal DNA and vaccine designs so that other researchers can help refine the work.
Get the data · See the lead design · Run the code · Contribute
The data guide describes each dataset, sample and reference scope. The file catalog lists locations, sizes and SHA-256 checksums.
Clinical timeline — diagnosis, treatments, scan findings and specimen collection.
- Stanford pathology and IHC — January 2025.
- Stanford STAMP — 31 January 2025.
- Caris tissue profiling — 22 February 2025.
- Guardant360 liquid biopsy — 21 October 2025.
Design #2 is the lead design, generated using matched-normal white-blood-cell DNA alongside tumour DNA and RNA. It contains 24 antigen regions in a 724-aa protein: 12 mutation, 5 splice, 5 CTA/self and 2 fusion regions.
- Selected antigens · protein · antigen order.
- RNA segment · coding DNA · annotated DNA segment.
- Methods · antigen-by-antigen review.
PolyA and any downstream extension are unspecified; nucleotide files contain the known segments. Design #1, generated without matched-normal DNA, is retained for comparison.
With Python 3.11 or 3.12, run from the repository root:
python3.11 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -e '.[mrna]'
yash-vaccine verify
yash-vaccine reproduce --output work/design-2-replay
These commands check and replay the lead design using bundled evidence and recorded predictions. They need no sequencing downloads or cloud account. The usage guide explains replay and alternative designs; the pipeline guide covers new raw-read processing and inference.
Fork the repository, add your work under designs/your-design/, and submit a pull request. Include your rationale, data sources, code, commands and useful results. Annotated protein or RNA sequences are welcome; label unspecified components explicitly. An analysis or antigen list can be contributed before a complete construct is assembled.
See CONTRIBUTING.md. Questions and ideas are welcome as GitHub issues or at yash@rnafoundry.com.
This is one approach to vaccine design. Alternatives could examine MHC class II targets, immunogenicity, antigen trafficking, or linker optimization for processing and presentation.
Shared data are in data/, designs in designs/, maintained helpers in src/, and upstream jobs in workflow/. See the agent guide, reference acquisition guide, provenance records, required credits and retained-source notices for details.

articles.title: Nvidia is reportedly preparing to fire Jensen Huang
articles.body:
Nvidia’s board is preparing to dismiss CEO Jensen Huang following a report from The New York Times about a second alleged extramarital affair, just days after he admitted to a separate affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, The Wall Street Journal reports. The second alleged affair was with an executive who reports to him, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, Kimberly Powell, according to the Times.
Nvidia is reportedly preparing to fire Jensen Huang
The Nvidia CEO had a second affair, allegedly with an executive who reports to him, The New York Times reports.
The Nvidia board will meet as soon as Wednesday night to decide on Huang’s future at the company, according to the Journal. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Verge.
On Thursday morning, Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation, saying CFO Colette Kress has been appointed interim CEO.
Huang and Powell, who are both married to other people, were allegedly captured together at a hotel in San Jose during Nvidia’s GTC developer conference in March, two unnamed sources told the Times. The Times has not seen the video. Rumors about a potential affair between the two had long circulated at Nvidia, an unnamed source told CNBC, partially because Powell does not have a health or science background.
Nvidia’s stock fell more than 7 percent in after-hours trading Wednesday.
Since Nvidia and Huang confirmed an extramarital relationship with Megaspeed executive and alleged spy Alice Huang and a subsequent investigation over the weekend, the company has said it retained former US attorney Joon H. Kim and his firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, to handle it, but today’s rumor suggests it won’t wait for those results to act. Last year, Huang hired crisis communications firm Heller known for handling public sex scandals, according to Wired. Its founder has advised several powerful men who faced public scrutiny, Wired reported, like former congressman Anthony Weiner and writer Jeffrey Toobin. Heller did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Verge.
Update, November 12th: Added note that Huang has now resigned.

articles.title: Court Says Trump Can't Use Leaks To Justify Spying On Journalists' LinkedIn DMs
articles.body:
Court Says Trump Can't Use Leaks To Justify Spying On Journalists' LinkedIn DMs (arstechnica.com) 27
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: The Trump administration's fight to stop suspected leaks of top-secret military information on LinkedIn can't sweep in "a vast number of confidential sources" of random journalists "who have no conceivable relationship" to the Department of Justice's investigation, an appeals court ruled (PDF) Tuesday. The order came after the DOJ asked LinkedIn to turn over 18 months of communications from targeted journalists who collectively published more than 1,000 articles on many different topics over that time period. The request was not limited to journalists involved in a controversial report from a news outlet that Trump said exposed confidential military information in a foreign country. (The outlet is not being named to protect national security secrets.) Instead, the DOJ cast a wide net, requesting extensive LinkedIn data on journalists who had any possible link to the journalists around the time the report was drafted.
The majority of journalists have LinkedIn accounts and publish their contact information to encourage sources to connect on the platform, LinkedIn argued. So allowing that government overreach went beyond harming targeted journalists and threatened to undermine a critical platform where journalists frequently connect with confidential sources, judges ruled. Even more concerning, the Trump administration secured a secrecy order barring LinkedIn from telling anyone about the sweeping request for a year. That left journalists unaware for far too long that their First Amendment rights had been compromised, judges ruled. "A request by the government to scoop up reporters' records wholesale and ascertain the identity of their sources would tip the balance against informed discourse in a manner inimical to democratic health," Wilkinson wrote. He criticized the lower court for approving the request simply because the records were technically feasible to collect, emphasizing that "serious security and speech claims are in tension in this case. There is space under law for both."
While declining to quash the order entirely, Wilkinson also directed the lower court to reconsider a limited exception to the government's secrecy order that would allow LinkedIn to notify an attorney representing the news outlet under investigation.
Bruce D. Brown, President of The Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press (RCFP), celebrated the ruling, saying: "This ruling is a big deal and will quickly become one of the leading opinions in the area -- one we will be quoting from it for a long time. The court recognized that confidential sources are the 'lifeblood' of investigative reporting and that dragnet demands from technology companies to reveal those sources violate the law."

articles.title: Apple Is Killing Its Support Community Forum Next Week
articles.body:
Apple Is Killing Its Support Community Forum Next Week 42
			
		 	
				Apple is shutting down its Apple Support Community forum on November 20, ending a user-to-user support platform whose history stretches back to the 1998 launch as the Apple Tech Exchange. The forum is already read-only, and Apple has not said whether the nearly three decades of community posts will be preserved or disappear when the site closes. Here's the full banner notice that's currently displayed on the website: 
"The Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state. You can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site. We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products."  Apple told MacRumors that it decided to sunset the forum after a careful evaluation of strategy and customer needs.

articles.title: ExcalidrawZ: Local Native Excalidraw on macOS/iOS
articles.body:
Excalidraw is an excellent drawing tool. ExcalidrawZ keeps the familiar Excalidraw canvas, then adds native file management, iCloud sync, history, export, AI assistance, MCP integration, and Apple-platform interaction details around it.
Non-App Store version
- Download the latest .dmg from Releases.
- Open the .dmg and drag ExcalidrawZ into Applications.
ExcalidrawZ manages drawings as real app documents instead of loose browser downloads.
- Organize drawings with groups and custom file sorting.
- Work with ExcalidrawZ library files, local folders, and temporary external files.
- Open and edit .excalidraw, .excalidraw.png, and .excalidraw.svg files directly.
- Sync app-managed files across macOS, iPadOS, and iOS with iCloud.
- Keep file history checkpoints so important changes can be reviewed and restored.
ExcalidrawZ records checkpoints for app-managed drawings, so you can review earlier versions and restore important work when needed.
The canvas remains compatible with Excalidraw while the surrounding app is built for Apple platforms.
- Customize toolbar tool order; number shortcuts follow your configured order.
- Use Apple Pencil on iPad, including familiar undo and redo gestures.
- Use mouse and trackpad scroll and zoom gestures on iPad and iPhone.
- Import PDFs and convert Mermaid diagrams into editable Excalidraw content.
Use Excalidraw collaboration when you want to draw with others.
ExcalidrawZ includes an AI assistant designed for canvas work.
- Ask AI to read, create, and revise drawings.
- Attach images and let AI use visual context when needed.
- Use proposal previews before applying AI-generated content to the real canvas.
- Control whether each file is visible to AI.
- Use AI from compact iPhone toolbars, iPad floating panels, or the macOS inspector.
ExcalidrawZ can expose the current app as an MCP server for compatible AI clients.
- Basic mode provides the familiar excalidraw-mcp drawing workflow.
- Optimized mode adds deeper ExcalidrawZ integration for current-file editing, file navigation, history, canvas inspection, export, library workflows, and math tools.
- Connect local MCP clients through the app-hosted HTTP endpoint.
ExcalidrawZ includes richer tools for technical drawings and study notes.
- Insert LaTeX-rendered formulas.
- Render function graphs with configurable axes and styles.
- Use reusable math templates and AI-assisted formula generation.
- Edit inserted math images later from the canvas.
For sensitive drawings, ExcalidrawZ adds protection around both storage and AI access.
- Lock files with local authentication.
- Encrypt locked files and their checkpoints.
- Use a Recovery Key for fallback access.
- Keep locked content hidden from AI; AI can work through proposal canvases instead.
- Use encrypted backups as an additional recovery path.
ExcalidrawZ supports common export and sharing workflows.
- Export images, editable Excalidraw files, and PDF.
- Preserve editability when exporting .excalidraw.png and .excalidraw.svg.
- Share through clipboard, files, and the system share sheet.
- Archive app-managed files for backup.
ExcalidrawZ can open, import, edit, or export common Excalidraw-related formats:
- .excalidraw
- .excalidraw.png
- .excalidraw.svg
- PDF import and export
- image export
Welcome to my Discord server to share suggestions or report issues for ExcalidrawZ.
- The Excalidraw core used by ExcalidrawZ is also open-source. You can find it here.
Create Config/Overrides.xcconfig relative to the repository root, alongside Config/Project.xcconfig:
DEVELOPMENT_TEAM = YOUR_TEAM_ID
ICLOUD_CONTAINER = iCloud.com.yourname.ExcalidrawZ
APP_GROUP_IDENTIFIER = group.com.yourname.ExcalidrawZ
Replace these example values with identifiers registered to your Apple Developer team. The shared configuration leaves DEVELOPMENT_TEAM empty; set your team in the local overrides. The app and QuickLook extension must use the same App Group. All targets, including the extension and tests, inherit the team from Config/Project.xcconfig, which includes your local overrides. These overrides apply to all build configurations.
Create Config/Secrets.plist relative to the repository root. The project already references this file and includes it in both app targets' resources. The app's configuration loader stops with Unable to load Secrets.plist if the file is missing or invalid.
For local drawing development, this minimal configuration is sufficient:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
    <key>COLLAB_URL</key>
    <string>https://example.com</string>
</dict>
</plist>
COLLAB_URL must be a valid absolute URL. The example URL is a placeholder for local drawing work; to test collaboration, replace it with the URL of your deployed collaboration-enabled Excalidraw web client.
Optional string keys are ONEDRIVE_CLIENT_ID, GOOGLE_DRIVE_MACOS_CLIENT_ID, and GOOGLE_DRIVE_IOS_CLIENT_ID. Configure your own OAuth client IDs when developing the corresponding integrations.
Config/Overrides.xcconfig and Config/Secrets.plist are ignored by Git and should stay local.

articles.title: PostgreSQL 18.7, 17.12, 16.16, 15.20, 14.25, and 19 RC 2 Released
articles.body:
The PostgreSQL Global Development Group has released an update to all supported versions of PostgreSQL, including 18.7, 17.12, 16.16, 15.20, and 14.25, as well as the second release candidate of PostgreSQL 19. This release fixes 52 security vulnerabilities and over 140 bugs reported over the last several months.
There are several issues that may require you to take extra steps after updating, which are described in detail below. See the "Updating" section for more information on post-update steps you may need to take.
For the full list of changes, please review the release notes.
This is the final release of PostgreSQL 14. PostgreSQL 14 is now end-of-life and will no longer receive security and bug fixes. If you are running PostgreSQL 14 in a production environment, we suggest that you make plans to upgrade to a newer, supported version of PostgreSQL. Please see our versioning policy for more information.
The following security vulnerabilities are closed in this update release. You can find more details about the vulnerabilities and their affected versions in the links below:
ALTER ... SET DATA TYPE executes arbitrary code (CVSS v3.1: 8.8)dblink and subscriptions can append to arbitrary files (CVSS v3.1: 8.1)INSERT ... ON CONFLICT can read or modify rows despite auto-updatable view WHERE condition (CVSS v3.1: 5.4)pg_basebackup can use backup manifest content as a format string (CVSS v3.1: 3.7)EXECUTE privilege on cast functions (CVSS v3.1: 3.1)RECORD typmod use-after-free executes arbitrary code (CVSS v3.1: 8.8)plperl prepared-query use-after-free executes arbitrary code (CVSS v3.1: 8.8)dict_int reads beyond zero-length tokens (CVSS v3.1: 4.3)COPY error context uses freed field storage (CVSS v3.1: 4.3)DROP OWNED can remove restrictive row security policies from non-owned tables (CVSS v3.1: 5.4)MERGE can place the wrong row in a trigger transition table (CVSS v3.1: 5.4)vacuumdb --missing-stats-only lets a database owner execute code as the vacuumdb user (CVSS v3.1: 7.2)pg_restore executes arbitrary code due to missing non-plain archive validation (CVSS v3.1: 8.8)tsvector_delete() heap buffer overflow executes arbitrary code (CVSS v3.1: 8.8)ts_rank_cd() heap buffer overflow may execute arbitrary code (CVSS v3.1: 8.8)pg_dump not-null constraint name allows SQL injection (CVSS v3.1: 8.8)return_next() use-after-free executes arbitrary code (CVSS v3.1: 8.8)pltcl reentrant result conversion use-after-free executes arbitrary code (CVSS v3.1: 8.8)reindexdb index name quoting allows SQL injection (CVSS v3.1: 8)security_barrier analysis can expose hidden values through indirect expressions (CVSS v3.1: 4.3)REINDEX CONCURRENTLY does not block DROP INDEX during index functions (CVSS v3.1: 8.8)REASSIGN OWNED bypasses role SET and CREATEDB checks (CVSS v3.1: 4.3)plpgsql record-field type confusion executes arbitrary code (CVSS v3.1: 8.8)pg_show_all_settings() use-after-free discloses memory (CVSS v3.1: 4.3)
This update fixes over 140 bugs that were reported in the last several months. The issues listed below affect PostgreSQL 18. Many of these issues also affect other supported versions of PostgreSQL.
pg_trgm GiST indexes
that could cause searches to miss matching rows. You need to reindex after
updating;  see the "Updating" section.missing chunk number errors.
If you've encountered this issue, after updating, you'll need to reindex. See
the "Updating" section.NOT NULL NO INHERIT constraints on partitioned tables in all
cases, including CREATE TABLE ... LIKE. Previously, this could allow a
partition to contain NULL values when it should not. See the "Updating"
section for how to find and repair affected constraints.bpchar without a
length, which could cause index-only scans to return wrong results. If you have
B-tree indexes on pg_control file, and avoiding
truncated or zero-padded copies of files such as postgresql.auto.conf that
are replaced while the backup is running.CLUSTER or
VACUUM FULL) when a row had been updated by a subtransaction that later
aborted.LATERAL references, outer joins, self-join elimination
on tables using inheritance, DISTINCT ON in a subquery with set-returning
functions, and queries using non-deterministic collations.RANGE-partitioned
tables when a query filters only on the leading columns, DEFAULT partitions
on tables using MINVALUE or MAXVALUE bounds, and concurrent updates that
could silently skip rows that should be updated.SERIALIZABLE
isolation. Previously, concurrent updates that should have failed with a
serialization error could succeed.WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE when the target row is concurrently deleted.
Previously, a WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET action could run instead, giving
incorrect results.JSON_TABLE and JSON_VALUE that could return incorrect
results.psql to accept
multiple COPY ... FROM STDIN
commands in a single command string. The fix for CVE-2026-6464 caused AT TIME ZONE in a FROM clause or a target alias named set, tsvector
and tsquery values that could fail to reload.
This release also updates time zone data files to tzdata release 2026f.
Beginning in November 2026, Canada's Northwest Territories (America/Inuvik)
are on year-round UTC-06 and Manitoba (America/Winnipeg) is on year-round
UTC-05. This release assumes their TZ abbreviations will be CST and EST
respectively (though this could change). It also reflects that Cuba will stay
on daylight saving time this winter, and that the EST5EDT, CST6CDT,
MST7MDT, and PST8PDT zone names now use their indicated UTC offsets for
old timestamps instead of the history of their associated city-named zones.
All PostgreSQL update releases are cumulative. As with other minor releases,
users are not required to dump and reload their database or use pg_upgrade
in order to apply this update release; you may simply stop PostgreSQL and
update its binaries.
If you suspect that a GIN index is affected by one of the corruption issues fixed in this release, you should reindex it, for example:
REINDEX INDEX your_index_name;
If you use pg_trgm, you should reindex any GiST indexes that use the
gist_trgm_ops operator class.
If you see missing chunk number errors when reading a table, you should
reindex the table, which also reindexes its TOAST table, for example:
REINDEX TABLE your_table_name;
If you use incremental backups, we recommend taking a new full backup after updating and using it as the basis for subsequent incremental backups.
If you use partitioned tables, the following query finds NOT NULL NO INHERIT
constraints on partitioned tables:
SELECT conrelid::regclass, conname
FROM pg_constraint
WHERE contype = 'n' AND connoinherit
  AND conrelid IN (SELECT oid FROM pg_class WHERE relkind = 'p');
You can remove unwanted constraints with ALTER TABLE ... DROP CONSTRAINT ....
Constraints you want to keep should be repaired with
ALTER TABLE ... ALTER CONSTRAINT ... INHERIT, which will fail if any of the
table's partitions contain NULL values in that column.
If you have B-tree indexes on bpchar columns (that is, columns declared as
bpchar without a length), you should reindex them after updating. Columns
declared as char(n) are not affected.
Users who have skipped one or more update releases may need to run additional post-update steps; please see the release notes from earlier versions for details.
For more details, please see the release notes.
This release marks the second release candidate of PostgreSQL 19. As a release candidate, PostgreSQL 19 RC 2 will be mostly identical to the initial release of PostgreSQL 19, though some more fixes may be applied prior to the general availability of PostgreSQL 19. PostgreSQL 19 RC 2 also includes the fixes in this update release that apply to PostgreSQL 19.
The planned date for the general availability of PostgreSQL 19 is November 19, 2026. Please see the "Release Schedule" section for more details.
To upgrade to PostgreSQL 19 RC 2 from earlier versions of PostgreSQL, you will
need to use a major version upgrade strategy, e.g. pg_upgrade or
pg_dump / pg_restore. For more information, please visit the documentation
section on upgrading:
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/19/upgrading.html
If you use pg_upgrade and have indexes that use
full text search,
pg_trgm, or
fuzzystrmatch, please
review the
"Migration to Version 19"
section of the release notes, as you may need to reindex them after upgrading.
Several bug fixes were applied to PostgreSQL 19 during the RC 1 period. These include:
JSON_ARRAY() and JSON_OBJECT()
expressions over arrays, composite types, and range types to be used in
expression indexes, generated columns, and partition keys, as these indexes
could become out-of-date. If you created any of these objects while testing
PostgreSQL 19, you need to drop or redefine them before upgrading, as
pg_upgrade will fail to recreate them.GROUPING SETS
queries, where a column not included in the current grouping set could show a
value instead of first_value() and nth_value() when using
IGNORE NULLS with
some EXCLUDE frame options.LISTEN /
NOTIFY queue becoming
stuck if a session is interrupted while reading notifications.work_mem
limit based on the planner's row estimate.
For a detailed list of fixes, please visit the open items page.
This is the second release candidate for PostgreSQL 19. Unless an issue is discovered that requires a delay or an additional release candidate, PostgreSQL 19 should be made generally available on November 19, 2026.
For further information please see the Beta Testing page.
If you have corrections or suggestions for this release announcement, please send them to the pgsql-www@lists.postgresql.org public mailing list.

articles.title: Anthropic IPO
articles.body:
Anthropic’s Initial Public Offering
AI will have a vast impact on the world. Anthropic is a public benefit corporation dedicated to securing its benefits and mitigating its risks.
“We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history. If managed well, it could rapidly accelerate scientific innovation, greatly increase economic growth rates, bring cures for major diseases within reach, and solve problems that have resisted generations of human effort.”

FAQs
- What is the timeline for the IPO? The IPO process begins with a roadshow starting on November 10th (EST). Subject to regulatory clearance, the final IPO share price is expected to be set on November 18th (EST), and shares are expected to begin publicly trading on November 19th (EST).
- What is Anthropic offering in this IPO? Anthropic is offering shares of its Class A common stock to the public, which will trade on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT”.
- How can I participate in the IPO? You can request shares through a participating brokerage platform. To participate, you must have an active account and submit an indication of interest through their platform.
- Am I eligible to participate in the Anthropic IPO? Your brokerage account or investing app will confirm whether you’re eligible when you submit your request to participate.
- At what price will the shares be offered? The final IPO price is expected to be determined on November 18th (EST), based on regulatory clearance, investor demand and market conditions.
- When will I know if I received shares of Anthropic? Your brokerage account or investing app will confirm your allocation on the first day of trading, which is expected to be November 19th (EST).
- What is the difference between buying in the IPO and buying after the stock begins trading? Shares bought in the IPO will be purchased at the offering price, which is expected to be set on November 18th (EST). Shares bought after Anthropic starts trading will be purchased at the prevailing market price at that time.
- Will I receive all the shares I apply for? There is no guarantee that any investor will receive all or any of the shares they apply for in the Anthropic IPO. However, you should be ready to purchase all the shares for which you apply.
- What is the prospectus? A prospectus is a regulatory filing that provides detailed information about Anthropic’s business, financial statements, risk factors, management team, use of proceeds, offering details, among other items. Investors should review the prospectus closely before investing.

articles.title: Pulling the Lever in a Subway Problem
articles.body:
Hi! I'm the person who pulled the brake. What I saw:
The train starts pulling out of the station. Someone begins shouting that their arm is caught in the door. I look over, see that the door is closed somewhere between their elbow and wrist, but it's not clear exactly where with their jacket on. People, including me, start shouting to pull the brake, but no one does. The train keeps accelerating, and it looks to me like once we get to the end of the station they're going to lose their hand. I get to the back of the car and pull the brake.
After the train stops, the man manages to pull his arm into the train, with his bag still on the outside. If he'd let go of his bag I think he would have been able to do this sooner, but he was panicking as I suspect most people would with their arm half out of the train like that.
I was pretty shaken up, and didn't end up blogging about it, but it came up again at one of our effective altruism dinners. This got me thinking about ways that philosophical problems do and don't translate into real life.
In this situation the stakes were lower than in the traditional trolley problem, and the situation is closer to Scanlon's Transmitter Room (What We Owe to Each Other, quoted jokingly here). The worst case was someone's arm being badly injured, maybe permanently. On the other side was delaying the whole line for an hour, perhaps losing ~4 years of waking life in total (~25k people * 1hr / 16 / 365 = 4.3y). But were these the real stakes?
I now think his arm probably wasn't caught in the door. That's what it looked like to me, and I was very sure at the time, but people who were closer disagree:
 I was in the car too -- I could tell that it was just his bag in the
 door, but in a split second, I was having a hard time telling how big
 his bag was, and I wasn't about to guess how wide the tunnels were
 since he wasn't letting go of his bag when the train started
 moving. I'm glad u/cbr ran to pull the brake -- I was one of the
 folks yelling to passengers to hit the call button to get the T to
 stop, and everyone at that end of the train just seemed to freeze.
 —zapdot
And:
I think what the above poster is saying is that there was a lot of
miscommunication inside the car. I watched it happen from the outside
and I never saw the dude's hand in the door. I saw him pulling the bag
with both hands then I saw the brake come on.
—dizzyrags
This illustrates a major way philosophical problems can fail to translate to real life: we're always acting under uncertainty, without knowing the consequences of our options. People understand this, and often "fight the hypothetical", but needing to make decisions when you really don't know whether you've read the situation correctly is a key part of real life morality. We need to make decisions that are robust to us having misinterpreted the situation.
(When Julia found herself in "drowning child" situation it was similar: the hard part was assessing the world, not whether to act.)
The other big way this differs from a textbook thought experiment is that it's not clear that the "inaction" case actually would have avoided a train delay. If I'd been right about his arm, I expect once the accident happened he would have been screaming even more, and I or someone else would have pulled the brake anyway. Which might well mean a worse delay, since now there's an injury involved too.
Which illustrates another way that intuitions built from philosophical problems can lead us the wrong way: this didn't occur to me at the time. It's hard to think very far ahead in an emergency, but morality problems often suggest a frame of mind where we have time to fully reason out the likely effects of each of our options. If I had thought this through it would have been an additional point in favor of pulling the brake. Or maybe I would have thought even further ahead: "if I do not pull the brake, I will become a famous example of a calculating (derogatory) utilitarian. I MUST NOT DO THAT."
Another thing I learned is that the suggestion Cialdini makes in Influence (quoted in Yudkowsky's Bystander Apathy) to point to one single person and ask them for help doesn't reliably work. When this happened I wasn't near the brake and I pointed to the person next to it and shouted something like "you, the brake!" They didn't, so I ran down the train and did it myself.
One philosophical idea that did transfer to real life is the Unilateralist's Curse. Perhaps the reason no one else on the train pulled the lever is that they all correctly perceived that the person was only in danger of losing their bag and not their arm. The one person (hi!) who came to a different conclusion still delayed the train for everyone. I don't think that was fully what happened here, since others were also shouting to pull the brake (though they were not independent observers). But since the "it's ok" position was harder to communicate, I think part of what happened was what we could call "expressivity bias", where an idea that was harder to express lost out, combined with it just being very hard to integrate diverse viewpoints under time pressure in a stressful situation.
As someone who had often speculated about philosophical problems, the experience of being in one was very stressful, and it's not one I hope to repeat.

articles.title: Jane Street – Our software engineering interviews are changing (a little)
articles.body:
Over the last few years, LLMs have changed how software gets built and that’s no different for us at Jane Street. Most of our engineers now use them every day not only for writing code, but also for reading, debugging, and reviewing code, and plenty of things that aren’t code at all.
We’ve talked about this recently in a podcast on how we use AI in our development, and in a post on formal methods that touches on how agentic coding is reshaping the way we work.
Our coding interviews haven’t changed, though. The questions we ask software engineers today are the same style of question we’ve been asking for years: sit down with an interviewer or two, program through a problem together, and talk as you go.
That style has served us well and the key goals remain the same: we want to see how you solve problems, structure your work, communicate, and collaborate in the pursuit of excellent software development. But the shape of the job has evolved, and we think our interviews should evolve, too. As generating code has become arguably cheaper than ever, other parts of the job have come to matter even more: taste about what to build, choosing abstractions that last, and making sure what got built is actually correct, among other things.
So this summer we started trialing some new kinds of interviews in our onsites for campus candidates. Broadly, they involve less code-writing, and lean more higher-level, focusing on software design, on verifying the quality, structure, and intention of code, and on using LLMs to produce code. Most rounds will continue to be traditional coding interviews, conducted without LLM assistance.
We know this sounds vague, but that’s intentional: the formats are still evolving, and we’d rather not describe something in detail today that looks different in six months.
A few things worth knowing:
- Not every onsite includes these new rounds yet, and when you come on-site we’ll give you a heads-up about what to expect.
- The rest of our process is unchanged. If you’ve read our earlier posts about interviewing here, they’re still accurate.
- While we find LLMs incredibly valuable as part of our daily work, we also recognize that not everyone has deep experience working with them. You shouldn’t feel like you need to have a highly worked out methodology for working with agents in order to do well in our process. In the end, we’re looking for people with great instincts for building software, and we don’t feel like we need an LLM to evaluate that.
- Different folks have integrated LLMs into their workflows in different ways and to different degrees, and we don’t expect you to have a particular setup or to use them for everything. What we care about is that you think clearly about the tools you use: what they’re good at, where they fall short, and when to reach for something else.
- As has been the case for some time, our more experienced candidates’ interviews will continue to be more varied, featuring a range of interview styles, from producing software to designing systems and discussing prior work.
As always, we’ll keep iterating, and we’ll write more when there’s more to say.
If you’re interested in working with us, apply on our website!
